p.emphasis: A kitchen whose owner had not brewed coffee for two months.

section.subtitle: Prologue
section.p: Yukio Kurosawa's kitchen held the smell that holds in kitchens of people who drink coffee once a day and never rinse the pot after.

He knew this. He made coffee every morning and washed the dripper after. But over the last six weeks the dripper had stood more often than it had been used; the filter hung in it wet, then dry, then wet again; and a film of old grounds clung to the walls of the moka pot, which he had not brewed in for a long time — it had stood there since the days he lived in the prefectural dormitory — and the tin on the shelf that had once held beans had been empty for twelve days.
He knew this, and this morning at six he decided not to make any at all.

He stood at the kitchen window, in his socks, and looked out at Maruyama Park. The snow lay thin, dark at the edges of the paths. A crow sat on the nearest lamppost. It watched him the way it always watched him. He did not nod.
Then he stepped away from the window.

On the kitchen sill, next to the bronze ashtray he never filled at home, stood two identical white porcelain figures. Without faces. One was his own, from Hachirodate, from Toshi's plot; he had taken it himself after the arrest, and it had stood there ever since. The other was from Kamishiroi, from the shelf above the altar — Ogawa had let him take it after the firemen carried the altar up out of the basement. The two figures stood side by side, and the morning light fell on them the same way.
He dressed.

The same coat — black wool, mid-thigh. Dark gray scarf. Leather shoes, soles resoled twice. The paths of Maruyama crunched under them with the same dry crunch as two winters ago, and last winter. The city had changed nothing beneath him.
He did not turn toward headquarters.
He reached Susukino in forty minutes on foot. He did not take the subway. The subway was for the times something was burning.

The alley off Minami 4-jo 6-chome kept its silence at this hour. An automatic ramen brazier a block up stood dark, the shutters down. Two thin cats by the dumpster watched him longer than they needed to, then parted.

The doors of the izakaya Kingyo were closed. The sign — not taken down, the old red fish on wood — held on the nails he and Sato-san had driven in together in the autumn of 2019, when a typhoon had torn it off. A handwritten note on the door: "しばらく休みます" (Closed for a while). Sato's hand. A second line beneath it in another hand, clerical, added later: "Return key to Minami precinct — 011-XXX." The building manager had added that some three weeks ago, when she understood the tenant was not coming back.
Kurosawa stood at the door.
He had come here twice in the first month after he was discharged from the hospital. Both times he had stood and read the note. Both times he had walked away.
Today it had been two months.

Two hours earlier, in his mailbox downstairs, there had been a yellow slip notifying him of a registered letter — as of the first of the following month, the landlord was terminating the lease on the izakaya premises, since the rent had not been paid and the tenant was unreachable at any of the contacts provided. Below, the standard paragraph about vacating the premises by the fifteenth.
He put the slip into his coat pocket. Not into his notebook. Into the pocket, next to his lighter.

The window at Kingyo was old, double-glazed, put in back in the nineties. On the inside, a paper concertina screen behind which nothing could be seen. To the left of the door, brickwork, three courses down from the frame.
He took off his scarf. Wrapped it twice around his right hand and tucked the end into his palm.
He struck once with his elbow. The glass held.
Struck a second time. The inner pane cracked on the diagonal from the upper right corner.
The third — and the outer went to cobweb.

He wrapped the scarf tighter and knocked the central shard through with the heel of his hand. Three layers of glass fell inward onto the wooden sill and past the sill, onto the floor, in small pieces, like ice off a roof.
He did not hurry.
He pushed his hand through the opening and found the inner latch. It gave at once; it was an old latch that Sato had loved because "it knows my fingers."
The door opened inward.
He stepped into Kingyo the way one steps into another man's room while he sleeps.
Inside, it held the smell that holds in the kitchens of people who have kept a kitchen for forty years and, for two months, have not.

Soy that had settled into the board and had not been rinsed off with hot water. A thin film of oil at the base of the gas stove. Rust from a tap that dripped rarely and slowly and left a ring on the bottom of the sink. A faint cat-smell — not the animal, but the smell that starts up in an empty kitchen in the second month. And over all of it — Peace tobacco, old, not fresh, that had soaked into the ceiling wood over the years and had not left it.
He stood at the threshold and did not move.

The counter was clean. Eight seats. The stools — three black, five brown — stood straight, tucked under the edge of the counter the way Sato tucked them before closing. Three glasses on the upper shelf above the counter, upside down, bottoms up, the way they were set out to dry. Behind the counter, on a wooden peg — the white cook's shirt. It was not on the peg. The peg was empty.
He registered this the way one registers a missing signature on a report.
He walked behind the counter.

On the work surface behind the counter, a small pack of Peace without filters. He knew this pack. He knew where Sato kept it — on the wooden shelf between the brazier and the socket for the refrigerator. He opened the lid with one finger. Counted.
Fourteen cigarettes. Two empty slots on the right.
Sato opened a new pack on Tuesday evening. Thursday morning, when Kurosawa came in for tea before his shift, the pack usually held thirteen. On Friday, nine. On Sunday, three.
Fourteen meant a pack from which two had been smoked. Which meant the beginning of Wednesday. Which meant, roughly, when Sato had last locked Kingyo.
He put the pack back exactly in the corner from which he had taken it.
The kettle by the brazier was cold. A thin ring of scale on the bottom. It had not held water for a long time.
He went round the counter the other way, to the register.

The register — old, mechanical, with levers — stood on a low wooden cabinet by the entrance, where it always stood. The glass top clean; someone (Sato) had wiped it a last time. Beside it on the cabinet: the brown leather order pad, a pencil with a blunt point, a magnet for receipts, a change dish with one five-yen coin and one one-yen coin.
And an envelope.

Cream. Heavy stock. No address, no writing. It lay exactly in the middle of the cabinet, clean, as if just brought in. No dust on the envelope. No dust around the envelope either. Someone had wiped the cabinet with a cloth under it when they set it down.
Kurosawa did not pick up the envelope at once.
He stood over it for half a minute.
Someone had been here. Not a week ago and not two. Recent. Perhaps yesterday.
The glass — the glass he had just broken — was still settling on the sill behind his back with a small sound.
Then he lifted the envelope by an edge between two fingers. The flap did not hold on its own — the paper still remembered the hand that had closed it.
Inside lay one thing.

A newspaper clipping folded in two. The print matte, the paper aged over time to that dry gray shade that comes to newsprint over ten or fifteen years. The headline short. The defendant's name. The venue. Tokyo, winter.
In the lower right corner, a photograph of a young Inspector Yukio Kurosawa, just off the courthouse steps. Black coat. The face of a man who had not slept for three nights.
Around the face, a neat circle. Red felt-tip. One motion, carried through.
He held the clipping between two fingers. He braced his other hand on the corner of the cabinet.

He knew this clipping. Not from the newspaper. From memory — and now no longer from memory. From the envelope Ogawa had silently set on his desk a year and a half ago, after the Toshi case, and said: "This was left in my mailbox. Not yours. That matters."
That envelope — Ogawa's — was now in headquarters archives, in the safe, in the file "Kamishiroi. Physical evidence. Copies." The original — under seal.
And this — was here.
The second.

Which meant: the Doll Maker knew Sato would not come back to Kingyo. Which meant: the Doll Maker had set the envelope on the register after Sato locked Kingyo from the inside — that is, on Monday evening, that is, together with Sato, that is, perhaps by his own hand on Sato's shoulder.
Kurosawa slowly folded the envelope back around the clipping. He put it into the inside pocket of his coat — not into his notebook, into the same pocket that held the yellow lease-termination slip.
Two things side by side, in a coat.
He stepped out from behind the counter. Walked to the door. Turned once — toward the empty peg where the cook's shirt was not — and closed the door behind him.
The glass under his feet crunched the same way — the pieces that had fallen inside and the pieces that had fallen out.
On the threshold he stood another half minute.
Then he took the pack of Peace he carried with him from his pocket and smoked one — standing with his back to the sign, his face to the alley — long and slow, down to the filter, as always.
The sky above Susukino was coming up gray.
He crushed the butt against his sole and put it in a small tin in his pocket. He let the scarf down from his cut hand and wound it around his throat.
He walked toward headquarters.
Behind him remained a broken window, an empty izakaya, an empty peg, and a register cabinet wiped clean beneath an envelope that no longer lay on it.
Sato had not come back.
Kurosawa had known that already. Now he knew that he was not coming back — and that a clipping with a red circle was on its way not to one man, but to two.

p.emphasis: The chief was putting him forward, out loud. Two men behind glass were counting how long it would take.

section.subtitle: Chapter One
section.p: The Hokkaido Prefectural Police Headquarters stood on the corner of the same intersection it had stood on ten and twenty years ago: concrete, glass, a portico too wide, under which in winter a wedge of snow always drifted in from the side where the wind always came.
Kurosawa entered at eight forty-seven.
The guard behind the partition — Mori, the same one — had his collar unbuttoned to the second button and nodded. It was clear he felt a little ashamed of that second button.
"Kurosawa-keibuho."

He had not gotten used to the suffix. Keibu he had carried for six years. Keibuho — a supervisory grade, the lieutenant-width gap between him and Ogawa — had been nailed to him four weeks ago, along with a warm note from the prefectural chief in which the word methodical was underlined twice and the word result did not appear.
"Mori-san."

The elevator went up slowly, as always. It smelled of wet cloth from somebody's coat. On the wall inside — a new poster, white on blue, with a red circle in the middle: "Prevention of Chain-Collision Accidents on Mountain Routes in Winter." Kurosawa looked at the red circle longer than he meant to.
The elevator chimed on the fourth floor.

The Missing Persons unit held the same faintly stifling warmth as last winter, and the winter before. The heating drove hard along the ceiling. Down along the baseboard a thin band of cold from the concrete slab held. Three desks in one room. Ogawa's glass partition to the right. The calendar on the wall crooked on one pin — a new one, January, with a photograph of a red bridge under snow, the same bridge that had hung there two years ago.
Sasaki was already at her computer. She had come in at seven, if habit still held.
"Good morning, Kurosawa-keibuho."
"Good morning."

She looked at his face once — a short, careful glance. Not at the scar over the eyebrow — she had stopped looking at that back in November — but at the way he set his right hand on the corner of the desk. She knew this motion. He made it when he was returning to neutral gestures after something he did not intend to recount.
Sasaki opened her mouth, thought better of it, closed it.

He hung his coat on a peg. Tucked the scarf into a pocket; the scarf had fine cuts on the inner side, and the wool held them neatly and did not shed. He took out a small metal thermos, unscrewed the cap, poured. His second coffee of the day. He drank standing.
Behind the glass partition Ogawa looked up, knocked a knuckle on the glass and jerked his chin — over here.
Kurosawa went in.

Ogawa was fifty-six. The last six weeks had added one extra fold from nose to corner of mouth, left side. He had a habit of keeping that fold ironed out by conversation — when the conversation was there, it disappeared — but at nine that morning he was not ironing it out.
"Sit."
"I'll stand."
"Sit down, Kurosawa."
He sat.

Ogawa looked at him longer than he needed to before saying the next line. Beyond Ogawa, past the glass of his office, in the outer room, through the far interior blinds — movement. Two men. One short, in a gray suit. The other taller, in black. They stood and watched this way.
Kurosawa did not turn his head.
"Behind the partition — two guests from Tokyo," Ogawa said evenly. "You don't notice them yet. I don't introduce you yet."
"NPA or Ministry?"
"Both."
Ogawa allowed himself a short pause. Then he opened a thin gray folder on the desk, spread it with two fingers, turned the first page. He did not need to look at it. He looked at the ceiling.

"Over the last six weeks in Hokkaido — three reports that don't pass through the usual filters. Sato Eiji, izakaya in Susukino — that one you already know. Nakamura Aoi, thirty-one, Kita 24-jo — the report came in this morning, the mother called from Niigata at six forty. The third — Ito Kazuo, fifty-two, an intercity coach driver, Asahikawa–Sapporo; the report was taken at the Asahikawa station yesterday evening. They look different. Different districts, different ages, different genders. By protocol, three separate cases."
"By protocol, three separate departments."
"By protocol — yes."
Ogawa closed the folder.
"Off protocol — all three will be on your desk by noon."
Kurosawa did not move. He only turned the thermos with his right palm onto the ring of damp it had left on the desk pad, so the ring would not go into the wood.
"Ogawa-san."
"I know what you want to say."
"No. You don't."
"Then say it."
"I'm not ready to lead a group."
"You already lead it. Since last Monday. You just haven't said so out loud."
Ogawa ran a hand down his cheek.

"Kurosawa. At the general briefing at ten I'll say three things. First — that from the first of the month a working group is being formed within Missing Persons under the internal name serial disappearances. Second — that you are at its head, group leader, with full authority to interrogate and to initiate unscheduled operational actions, reporting to me personally. Third — that Sasaki-junsa-bucho works with you as a second officer in the group, not as escort, not as stenographer, but as a second officer with the right to independent action under your coordination."
"Forensics?"
"Endo-san handles forensics on a separate line. Technical forensics — separate. I'll speak to that separately, once we have a budget."
"Prosecutor?"
"Fujiwara knows. He is not delighted. He does not like you. But he does not like anyone, and that is stable."
Kurosawa looked at the folder.
"Those two behind the glass — will they be at the briefing?"
"They'll stand by the far wall. Silent."
"Which of them will say goodbye to me first — them or the prefectural chief?"
Ogawa looked at him for a long time.
"Kurosawa. This is not a joke."
"No. It's a serious question."
Ogawa leaned back in his chair. Folded his arms across his belly, the way he always did when he was thinking out loud.

"First — me. If it comes to it. You don't need to know that, but I'm telling you, because you have to lead this with your eyes open. From where I sit — you have four to fourteen months. If you show me a map in four months, they will widen you. If you show me a face in fourteen, they won't touch you until pension. If neither — you will be quietly transferred to Kushiro."
"Kushiro is not the worst town."
"Not the worst. But not Maruyama."
Ogawa looked somewhere past him.
"Go."
Kurosawa stood up. At the office door — he turned.
"Ogawa-san. Thank you for not asking whether I'm ready."
"I didn't ask, because I know the answer."
"Yes."
Ogawa looked at the calendar on the far wall. He said nothing more.

Outside the office, the two men from Tokyo were no longer standing by the far blinds. They had shifted to the narrow sector between the copier and the printer — a place from which they were not immediately visible. The one in the gray suit inclined his head slightly toward Kurosawa. The one in black — did not.
Kurosawa crossed to his desk. Sasaki, at her own, did not look at him directly, but her fingers on the keyboard paused for a second. Then moved again.
He sat. Opened the first page of the day.
"Sasaki."
"Yes."
"In five minutes — at my desk. Bring your folder. And your thermos."
"Thermos?"
"We'll go after the briefing. Kita 24-jo."
"Nakamura."
"Yes."
She nodded.
He did not look at her as he spoke. He looked at the calendar with the red bridge and thought about how the town on the calendar was Otaru, as always on the January page.
Otaru was where Sato had been born.
The briefing took nine minutes.

In the large room on the second floor there were twenty-three officers. Two from Forensics, three from Organized Crime, twelve from various district stations, two from Traffic, four of his own. The two guests stood by the far wall, as Ogawa had said. Silent.

Ogawa spoke evenly. He announced the group. He announced the name. He announced Sasaki. He did not name the three who would be on Kurosawa's desk by noon. He said only: "Serial disappearances of adults, different profiles, common methodology. Kurosawa-keibuho leads."
Kurosawa stood by the window, hands behind his back. He did not speak.

One of the younger investigators in the second row — Tachibana from Toyohira — when Ogawa had finished, raised a hand. Asked about jurisdiction. Ogawa answered. Another, from Traffic, asked about access to the JR databases and the bus companies. Ogawa answered. The third question — quiet, from the back — was formed by the man in the gray suit. Not everyone could hear him.
"You speak of a series. Do you have grounds for calling this a series rather than simply three coincidences in a month?"
The voice was level. Tokyo standard, no admixture. He did not give his name.
Ogawa looked at him. Not at Kurosawa.
"Kurosawa-keibuho."
Kurosawa lifted his hand from the sill. Turned.

"Three individuals," he said. "Sato Eiji, Nakamura Aoi, Ito Kazuo. Each of them has kept, for more than half a lifetime, one old piece of text in open access — a blog, a diary, a forum. Each of those texts contains one personal detail unknown to the subject's immediate circle. In all three texts, by our preliminary data, one micro-edit has been made in the last three weeks — a space, a punctuation mark, an invisible unicode character. That is the signature of a methodology known to us. That is the grounds."

He spoke evenly, without pauses. It was untrue by exactly one detail: he had data on Sato, he had a suspicion on Aoi (Ogawa had just handed him the folder in which Sasaki was to verify precisely that detail), and he had only the report on Ito, without any preliminary reading of the digital trace. Three out of three, he had only for one.
But he said it the way people say things when three of three are confirmed. And he knew the man in the gray suit would not hear the difference. Not in this room.
The man in gray nodded once. Did not say thank you.
The one in black was writing in small pencil on an uncovered form.
Ogawa closed the briefing.
Twenty-three men dispersed slowly. Kurosawa remained standing. Sasaki, in the second-to-last row, did not move either.
The two from Tokyo went out last. The one in gray — at the door — stopped for a second. Did not turn. Then went out.
Ogawa came over to Kurosawa.
"You didn't have data on Ito."
"I didn't."
"You said you did."
"I said there were grounds."
Ogawa almost smiled at the corner of his mouth.
"Kurosawa. From this minute — every 'there are grounds' you speak in their hearing, I want on paper by evening."
"It will be."
"Who was he?"
"The one in gray?"
"Yes."
Kurosawa was silent.

"Tanaka," said Ogawa. "Tanaka Ryosuke. NPA, Interprefectural Crimes Division. Forty-eight. Careerist. Does not like Hokkaido. Does not like unorthodox methods. Does not like me personally, going back to the time I blocked him from a Sapporo posting twelve years ago. He is here officially as an observer on the topic 'Methodological support for regional units handling serial cases.' In reality — to watch you."
"For how long?"
"As long as he can hold out here without normal Japanese food. In our canteen we have one yamidzu and ton-jiru. He likes sushi rolls with tuna. In Sapporo there are no sushi rolls with tuna."
"Not much of a profile."
"It's what I have. Go."
Sasaki was standing by her desk when Kurosawa came back into the unit.
The thermos in her hand was new — not the black one from last year, but gray, metal, larger.
"Kurosawa-keibuho."
"Yes."
"You told him we had data on Ito."
"I said there were grounds."
"I heard you say it."
"You are right. I said we had. We don't."
"Are we going to Asahikawa?"
"No. Kita 24-jo first. On Ito we'll go through the Asahikawa district station, I'll call from the car. We'll have the wife by evening."
"All right."
She did not move. She was looking at the floor under his desk.
"What is it?"
"Late last night I went into the archive and pulled Sato-san's blog. Livedoor. The one about tofu."
"I know."
"I found an entry from the twelfth of June, two thousand and eight. I read it through."
"And?"
"There is one invisible character between paragraphs. Unicode U+200B. It is definitely there."
"That's confirmation. That's good."
"That's not why I'm telling you now."
He looked at her.
"Then why?"
Sasaki lifted her eyes.
"I checked my mixi. Private. My younger sister has her own."
"Nao."
"Yes."
She said nothing more. She held the thermos in her hand and did not set it on the desk.
Kurosawa looked at her for one second. Then looked away.
"Let's go."

He pulled on his coat. From the inside pocket he took the yellow lease-termination slip for Kingyo, put it in the top drawer of his desk, and locked the drawer. He left the cream envelope in the coat.

Behind the glass partition Ogawa was saying something into the phone. One of the two men from Tokyo — the one in gray — had returned to the outer room, was standing by the far wall and watching. Kurosawa and Sasaki walked past him to the doors. Tanaka did not nod. Kurosawa did not nod either.
The elevator went down slowly.

He was thinking about how ten minutes ago he had said the word methodology aloud without the right to it before either the prosecutor or his own conscience. He had done that before only with Ogawa, and Ogawa had a habit of covering that imprecision from behind, the way one covers the shoulder of a junior partner in kendo. Now Ogawa would cover him publicly — that is, in front of Tanaka. That is, in front of the man who was writing those imprecisions down on a form without a cover.
In two weeks he would either be closed by that form or forgotten by it.
He did not know which of the two he would prefer.
"Kurosawa-keibuho."
"Yes."
"Tanaka-san. The one in black — who is he?"
"I don't know. Ogawa didn't say."
"He's not NPA."
"No."
"Ministry of Justice?"
"More likely."
Sasaki nodded, the way one nods when the answer was needed only to fix the silence of the next five minutes.
The elevator doors opened onto the lobby.
"Sasaki."
"Yes."
"About Nao I will speak with you. Not today. But I will speak."
"I know."
She stepped out first into the cold light of the portico. He followed.
The snow held under the soles with the same dry crunch he had walked in with that morning.
Only now he was not walking alone.

p.emphasis: At the bottom of the clean cup there was a crumb. Fresh.

section.subtitle: Chapter Two
section.p: The drive to Kita 24-jo took twenty-three minutes — along Kita 5, then Kita 12, then a left toward the station overpass and six more blocks north. Sasaki at the wheel. Kurosawa in the passenger seat, phone on his knee, a warm scarf spread across the knee and, on top of the scarf, a sheet on which four lines had been written by her at six forty-two that morning:

p.emphasis: "Nakamura Aoi. 31. QA engineer. Ezo Systems. Did not come in on 30 October. Mother calling from Niigata."

section.p: Below, in a smaller hand:

p.emphasis: "Mother says: Aoi has not picked up since Monday. Reads LINE, doesn't reply. Twice a year."

section.p: He read it for the third time.
"Twice a year she doesn't pick up?"
"The mother said 'once every six months, when she snaps — she doesn't pick up for two or three days.' I put it more tersely."
"When was the last time she 'snapped'?"
"The mother doesn't remember. Says, around April."
"About what?"
"She didn't say."
Kurosawa folded the scarf. Looked at the traffic light.
"How long did you talk to her?"
"Twenty-two minutes. She cried three times. Not out loud. Quietly."
"An educated woman."
"Primary-school teacher. Retired. Widow."
He nodded.
The light changed. Sasaki started forward.

The building on Kita 24-jo was seven floors, panel construction, from the nineties. Balconies with white aluminum frames. On every fourth one, laundry hung out, despite the two below zero on the thermometer. The residents of this district liked to dry laundry until it froze.
Apartment 402.

The building manager brought the spare key eleven minutes after they called. He came out in a down jacket over a house cardigan, keys on a lanyard — forty-two, forty-three, a wife who opens the door for him with suspicion at any hour. He walked them silently to the door and stood behind them while Kurosawa pulled thin latex gloves onto his fingers.
"Aoi — quiet. No complaints ever. No guests ever. Pays by home banking on the first of each month. The last transfer — first of November, as always."
"When did you last see her?"
"On the stairs. Maybe two weeks ago. Not less. Maybe more. I don't notice people like her."
Kurosawa nodded. Lowered the handle.
The door opened smoothly and quietly.

The apartment was 1LDK, a narrow entry hall, kitchen-living to the right, bedroom in the back on the left. Warm — not hot; the thermostat was set at eighteen, and someone had held it there on purpose.
Kurosawa stepped into the entry hall.

One pair of sneakers on the genkan. Onitsuka Tigers, white with a red stripe, size 24. The inner edge of the right heel was worn more than the left — by about two millimeters. She put her weight on the right foot; an old habit from small ankles. The sneakers stood straight, toes to the door, no dust on them.
He took off his own shoes. Set them beside hers, also toes to the door.
Sasaki, behind him, did the same, quietly.
"Manager," Kurosawa said over his shoulder, "we'll be here an hour. If anyone tries to come in — stop them."
"Yes."
The door closed behind them.
He went into the kitchen-living room.

The window faced north, onto a closed courtyard with parking and a laundry rack. A thin blanket of gray light lay on the table under the window. The table was low, white, IKEA. On the table — one MacBook Air, closed, the charging cable wound into a neat loop by the upper right corner. To the right of the MacBook, a white ceramic cup. The handle of the cup turned toward the window.
He came up to the table without touching.
Crouched. Looked at the cup from the side.
The cup was clean. The inside was white, dry. The handle wiped. Along the rim — no lip mark.
He straightened up, walked around the table, looked at the cup from the other side. The same.
Then he leaned in and looked into the cup from above.
At the very bottom — under the oblique fall of light from the window — lay one small dark-brown crumb. The size of a cumin seed, perhaps smaller. Not a stain, a body — solid, with relief.
He turned to Sasaki.
"Sasaki."
She came over and leaned in.
"Coffee."
"Yes."
"Ground. Fine."
"Fine."
He straightened.
"The cup is clean. The walls are dry. The handle is wiped. On the bottom — a fresh crumb of ground coffee."
Sasaki did not answer at once.
"Yesterday she could have drunk coffee, washed sloppily, the crumb settled."
"She could have."
"But."
"But there is no coffee grinder in the apartment. No filter machine. No moka pot. Not a single jar of beans in the kitchen."
He opened the upper cupboard over the sink.
The shelf — three boxes of tea. Genmaicha, Sencha, Hojicha. One small jar of Nescafé Gold instant, two-thirds full. The lid not fully closed.
"Instant."
"Yes."
He closed the cupboard.
The second cupboard — plates, two bowls, two cups, all the same, from the same set. The third — rice bowls, three chopsticks in a stand, the stand empty.
Nowhere — ground coffee.
He came back to the table.
"Someone was here with their own coffee."
"Or brought it."
"Or sat down to drink with her."
He did not add the third.
Sasaki took an evidence bag from her belt pocket. Opened it. Kurosawa used tweezers to move the crumb from the bottom of the cup into the bag. The bag was sealed, labeled.
"Call the response team now?" Sasaki asked quietly.
"No. Not yet."
He wanted to go further in.

The bedroom was narrower than expected — a little more than a niche. A futon bed on a wooden frame, the blanket flung back two-thirds down, the way one flings back a blanket when getting up and not intending to come back. Two pillows — one flat, one fuller; she slept on the flat one.
Kurosawa looked.

On the flat pillow, the mark of a temple, oval, deeper on the southern side. On the nightstand to the left, glasses in a thin frame, the arm turned toward the bed, the way a person sets them down who sits up, takes them off as a last action, and lowers herself onto the flat pillow. Beside them, a water glass. Half-full. On the surface of the water a thin film of dust.
Half-full and with dust — that meant not two days. A week.
The blanket had been thrown back on Thursday.
"The mother reported her missing on the first of November."
"Yes."
"But she didn't sleep here Saturday night."
"Yes."
He opened the wardrobe.

Nakamura Aoi's clothes hung in the wardrobe the way clothes hang for a person who knows she will come back here today, and tomorrow, and Thursday. On the left, sweaters stacked, colors from the darkest on top to the lightest at the bottom; on the right, hangers with blouses and jackets; on the lower shelf, seven identical pairs of white striped socks and one pair of gray. Nothing shifted. Nothing missing to the eye.
Kurosawa ran his fingers along the tops of the sweaters.

One sweater from below was not where it should have been. The color order broke at the fourth step from the top: dark blue lay above olive. That does not stay that way for a person who folds by gradient.
Someone had pulled out a sweater. Put it back in a greater hurry than she would have.
"Sasaki. Here too."
Sasaki looked, nodded.
He left the bedroom.

The work corner was the right corner of the kitchen-living room, under a tall lamp on an arc bracket. A low table, wooden. On the table — the MacBook, a switched-off Bose desktop speaker, two folders with papers, a box of Muji pens, black 0.38, six of them, and a cobalt dish with two paper clips.
And an empty rectangular place the width of a palm.
Kurosawa leaned over the table.

The place was half a millimeter lower than the surface of the table. A faint outline — the thinner dust had not settled where for years something had been laid down and picked up, laid down and picked up. Size — about thirteen by nineteen centimeters. Plus or minus.
"Moleskine."
"What?"
"A Moleskine used to lie here. Hardcover, standard L. Thirteen by nineteen. Did the mother say?"
Sasaki nodded.
"The mother said that Aoi never leaves the house without a notebook. It's in her bag or on her table. Always. Almost like a body."
"The bag is on the genkan."

Kurosawa went into the entry hall and lifted the bag — gray canvas, long handles. Unzipped it. Wallet, keys, glasses case, two Muji pens, a tube of hand cream, a small plastic container with two mints, a dry-cleaner tag for a suit dated last Thursday, two pages of printed code with small notes in green marker.
No notebook.

He put the bag down as it had been. Turned it in one motion by the strap so the clasp faced toward the door — Aoi set the bag down exactly that way, and the thin mark of the clasp on the genkan mat, a millimeter to the right of center, said so.
He came back to the table.

"The notebook has been taken," he said quietly. "Keys, wallet, work papers — all here. Bag here. Sneakers here. Blanket thrown back on Thursday. Sunday evening she did not come back. Someone was here today or yesterday."
Sasaki stood with a hand on her phone. Not dialing.
"Kurosawa-keibuho. Response team?"

"Yes. Now yes. Bring in forensics from the department — Ogawa will confirm by voice, I'll call myself. Tell them, no sirens — quietly, two cars, no publicity until evening. We'll canvass the neighbors ourselves first, then them. And — Sasaki."
"Yes."
"Pull from the dust on the table — right from the spot where the Moleskine lay — a sample. Not around the edge, from the center, from the surface layer. With the thinnest tweezers. Not with a glove."
"You think the dust layer was smoothed after it was taken."
"I want to see what it was smoothed with."
Sasaki put her phone down. Pulled thin metal tweezers from a case. Crouched over the table, very low.
Kurosawa straightened.
He walked once more, slowly, through the kitchen-living room. He looked not at the objects one by one, but at what lay between them.

The bookshelf by the door to the bedroom: twenty-two spines. Technical books on the left, cookbooks in the middle, thin books of poetry on the right. Three or four Moleskine notebooks from previous years — with colored ribbon bookmarks — stood on the lower shelf, leaning against each other. He took out the first — leftmost, oldest. The date on the first page — 2019. Entries in Japanese, small hand. He did not read.
The second — 2020. The third — 2021.

The fourth — 2022. In the middle of it — he turned it with a finger — a thin strip where one page had been cut out. With a knife or blade. Neatly, along the spread. No trace of the torn edge remained; those who tear pages from their own diaries leave the gesture differently, and the one who cut here knew where the blade should press.
He put the notebook back. Did not show Sasaki yet. He only showed when a clue became a fact, and a fact became paper.
The fifth — 2023. The sixth — 2024. The seventh — 2025. The eighth — 2026.
The 2027 was not in the bag. It was not in the wardrobe. It was not in the entry hall. On the table — only an outline in dust.
The twenty-seventh — taken.

In the bathroom, one black brush on the sink, SunStar Ora2 toothpaste, the towel's tail looped on a hook. The mirror wiped not to the end; in the lower right corner a vertical streak from a water splatter that someone had missed. Someone — Aoi. Someone — not Aoi. One drop had dried since Monday, another over it — fresher, from yesterday or the day before. A thinner layer. Kurosawa looked at that overlap for three seconds and did not say it aloud.

In the corner of the shower cabin, a tiny rectangle of light color on the beige tile, the size of a little fingernail. He crouched. Looked closer. The tile there was cleaner than its neighbors; someone had pressed something sticky or damp against it — tape, a sticker — and pulled it off. Aoi did not keep stickers on tile. Whoever had — had not kept it there long.
He did not tell Sasaki about this. Not yet.
The response team came in forty-eight minutes — two cars, quiet, no siren, as he had asked. Forensics in white. Three of them. Nods, professionalism, no one said an extra word.
Kurosawa and Sasaki went out to speak with the neighbors.

The neighbor to the left — 401 — a woman about sixty-five, in a pastel tracksuit, hearing aid in her right ear. She had seen Aoi rarely. The last time — "the Monday before last, in the lift, with a bag from Seiyu." Did not notice at what time. Did not notice with whom.

The neighbor to the right — 403 — a single man of about forty, working from home, background music behind the door. He had seen Aoi "about two weeks ago," once heard "it seemed like someone was unlocking a door after midnight" — "maybe her door, maybe another floor, I get confused now." To the question "when exactly after midnight" he answered: "maybe Thursday? maybe the night going into Friday?"
The upstairs neighbor — 502 — was not home.
Kurosawa returned to the fourth floor. Knocked at 402.

"Keibuho," said the senior forensic officer. "The door was locked with a key, not the latch. The upper lock not engaged. Aoi walked out of here, turned off the light in the entry hall, closed the outer lock, took the key with her."
"Or someone with her key."
"Or."
"Prints?"

"Many. Hers, most likely. One cup, table, door handle, wardrobe. We'll take samples at Ezo Systems tomorrow for cross-check. We'll lift them. But — no fresh foreign prints on anything obvious. Whoever was here — cleaned up after themselves completely. Or was in gloves."
Kurosawa nodded.
The forensic looked at him.
"Keibuho. Is this the thing again?"
"Yes."
The forensic stood a moment, then dropped his chin and went back into the apartment.
They were driving away from Nakamura's building at half past one.

Sasaki at the wheel. Kurosawa in the passenger seat, phone on his knee. He called the Livedoor archive, called mixi support, called the corporate secretariat at Ezo Systems, called the Asahikawa district station, asking for Miho Ito's report to be sent by scan that same day. Each call — one minute, two, three. He counted them on the fingers of his left hand.
Between the sixth and seventh call — Sasaki.
"Kurosawa-keibuho."
"Yes."
"The mother. Aoi's. She needs to be met. She's flying in on the evening flight from Niigata."
"At what time?"
"Arrives at 19:40. She has no one here to meet her. Her aunt in Sapporo, with whom Aoi lived — at a conference in Kyoto until Friday."
"We'll meet her."
"Both of us?"
"You'll meet her. I'll come to the hotel to see her. Not to the airport. I don't want the first conversation at arrivals."
"Yes."
Sasaki was silent for a few seconds.
"Aoi," she said, looking at the road, "in twenty-two calls with her mother did not once say she trusted anyone in Sapporo."
"The aunt?"
"About the aunt she has one phrase: 'the aunt doesn't want extra words.' She said that back in September."
"Whoever drank coffee at her place — not the aunt."
"Not the aunt."
Kurosawa did not answer at once.

He was thinking about this — about how someone had sat across from her in the kitchen, brought their own ground coffee in a small packet, made themselves one cup, drank; she drank tea from her Nescafé Gold or green from the cupboard; they talked. Someone talked for a long time. Someone knew how to talk for a long time with a woman who is silent. Someone she had let into the apartment more than once — because the first time she would not have set that cup so the handle faced the window: the handle faced the window because she knew from which side her guest would sit, and had set the cup in advance.
"Sasaki. That cup was prepared."
"I know. I saw."
"So she was waiting."
"Yes."
A pause.
"Keibuho. One request."
"Yes."
"The mother doesn't yet know about the Moleskine."
"I know."
"I want to tell her myself."
"About what exactly?"
"About the fact that it's gone."
"Why you?"
"Because she will cry, and I do not want the first person she hears it from to be someone whose face she then keeps seeing."
Kurosawa looked at her sidelong.
She was watching the road. She held her thermos — gray, metal — between her knees, the way one holds a hot thing that does not belong to one.
"All right," he said. "You tell her."
"Thank you."
He added nothing more.
In the car, when four blocks from headquarters remained, he tipped his head back and closed his eyes for five seconds.

In five seconds he managed to think one thing: that Nakamura Aoi had not slept in her apartment on Sunday night, that her Moleskine 2027 had been taken, that on the bottom of her clean cup a fresh crumb of a stranger's ground coffee remained, and that this meant the Doll Maker — or, more precisely, the man before the Doll Maker — drank coffee.
Then he opened them.
"Sasaki."
"Yes."
"When we're back at headquarters — Endo. At once."
"What to ask?"

"One question. Whether there is already, in the database, any fresh case from the last three weeks in Sapporo in which a crumb of ground coffee was found in the apartment of a victim on a piece of tableware that the victim herself did not use for coffee."
"So Aoi isn't the first."
"Maybe not."
"Or this is a new signature."
"Or this."

Kurosawa looked at his hands on his knees. He had not taken the latex gloves off until the car; he had taken them off at the wheel, dropped them into a bag. His palms smelled of powder and someone else's kitchen. He rubbed them together.
"Sasaki."
"Yes."
"The crumb in the cup — not a mistake. The Doll Maker does not make mistakes of that kind. If he left it — he left it on purpose. It's a sign."
"A sign of what?"
"Not a sign to us. A sign to her."
"To her?"

"To Aoi. So that when she comes back — or does not come back — and someone else walks into that apartment, whoever walks in would see that cup the way I saw it. Would see that someone had drunk coffee there with her. Would see that she had let someone in. Not a stranger."
Sasaki did not answer. She kept one hand on the wheel, the other on the gear lever — at the corner she was downshifting for the right turn into the headquarters garage.
"Keibuho."
"Yes."
"You think — it's for the mother."
"Yes."
"For Aoi's mother from Niigata."
"Yes."
"So that when she comes in, she will understand: my daughter let someone into her own home."
"Yes."
Sasaki exhaled briefly, almost inaudibly, through her nose.
"That is cruel."
"That is the level of cruelty we call method."
Sasaki nodded. She did not move her hand to the thermos. Did not move her hand to the phone.
She just drove.
Kurosawa looked at the road.
In front of headquarters, on the portico, in the wedge of snow on the north side, two men in dark coats stood. He recognized Tanaka's silhouette from three hundred meters out.
"Keibuho."
"Yes."
"He's waiting for us."
"I know."
"Do we mention the crumb?"
"No."
Sasaki nodded again, slowly, very slowly.
The car went down into the basement garage.

p.emphasis: "National 39 remembers me." — an entry from twenty-three years before today.

section.subtitle: Chapter Three
section.p: Miho Ito's report came in by scan from the Asahikawa district station at sixteen forty-eight.
Kurosawa printed it while the printer was still warm. He took the sheet with both hands, put it on the desk under the high lamp, sat.

The report was written by hand. Blue ballpoint. The handwriting was schooled, neat, with a slight forward slant — the hand of a woman who had spent forty years filling out charts in an infirmary and had learned to write so that any chart could be read by anyone in any light. Surname — Ito. First name of the person filing — Miho. Date — 1 November 2027. Surname of the missing man — Ito Kazuo. Date of last contact — 30 October 2027, 21:47, LINE message "arrived, ate, going to bed," Nagayama, Asahikawa.
In the "circumstances" field, three lines.

"On 31 October my husband left for the morning shift — the Asahikawa–Sapporo route, JR Hokkaido coach, the 06:20 run. He did not appear for the return run 15:40 in Sapporo. Does not answer LINE, phone off. Last seen by colleagues at the transfer point in Sapporo at 12:14, smoking on the crew balcony."
In the "additional" field, one line in a smaller hand:
"Has driven the same route for twenty-one years. Never missed a run."
Below, a signature, the stamp of the receiving sergeant, the time.
Kurosawa read the line about twenty-one years twice.

He knew this category of person. Drivers who do not make mistakes on a route for twenty-one years — those are not the ones who keep their hand steel from discipline. Those are the ones who keep their hand steel because it shook once and, after that once, they did not allow themselves the right to shake again. He had worked with witnesses from this category several times. They do not forget details of accidents that did not happen. They remember every car that overtook them, in the same place, over twenty-one years.
Kilometer 743. He had something at kilometer 743.
Then he set the sheet aside and went back to the computer.

LiveJournal, as a living organism, died in 2019, when the Russian parent holding company moved the servers and changed the privacy terms so that private diaries could be read via a direct URL. Whoever knew about it closed the door behind themselves. Whoever did not — left themselves open.
Kurosawa opened the side panel of the browser. Typed into the search: "north wheel jp livejournal."
The second result.

The profile of user north-wheel-jp — registered 4 March 2003, last log-in 12 January 2027 (less than a year ago). Avatar — a photograph of the iron counter of a coach wheel, taken close up. The profile description — three lines, in the old early-2000s internet style:
"Driver. Hokkaido. I read poets. I do not read news."
Five tags: "road," "night," "snowstorm," "Issa," "solitude." The last tag used twice in twenty-three years.
Total posts — 89. The last — 12 January 2027, four lines of a haiku, no signature, no comments.
Kurosawa scrolled down.

Posts from 2027 — four. Posts from 2026 — three. Posts from 2025 — two. Then rarer and rarer, with a break at 2010–2018 (about one post a year), and a cluster at 2003–2009, when the author had written eight to twelve posts a year.
He opened the archive for 2004.
The list of entries for November 2004.
"8 November 2004, 04:22 — Untitled."
He clicked.
"Six years ago on this night I hit someone. National Route 39, the Kamikawa Pass, in the snow. I did not stop. I did not look. I am still at the wheel. National 39 remembers me."

One paragraph. No signature. No comments. No tags. Time of publication — 04:22. That is, the same hour at which the event in 1998 had happened (he was counting by the author himself — that is, that "six years ago on this night" was 8 November 1998, in the morning hours).
The post was open. Not private. Not friends-only.
Kurosawa looked at the screen longer than he needed to.

Then he opened the LiveJournal diff-archive — that gray service he knew about through a Ukrainian journalist who had lived in Sapporo in 2015 and left behind a set of bookmarks. The diff-archive kept snapshots of entries on various dates from 2004 through 2027.
He compared the entry of 8 November 2004 in the snapshot from June 2010, from May 2016, from November 2022, and from November 2027.
The first three — identical to the character.
The November 2027 snapshot differed by one character.
At the end of the line "National 39 remembers me," after the period, there was one space that had not been in the previous versions.
The date of last edit, extracted from the archive metadata: 21 October 2027, 03:11 night hours.
Ten days before 31 October — that is, before the day Ito had not come out from under the awning of the crew balcony in Sapporo.
Kurosawa leaned back in the chair. He rubbed the scar above his eyebrow with his palm — not because it itched, but because it was the gesture with which he held something inside himself.

One space. One. At the end of a line. To read that space, either no one could or one person could. On the same day, in the same week, the same had happened in Sato's tofu blog. In Aoi's private mixi — the same week, by their preliminary data on a punctuation mark. And now — here.
He noted the three edit dates on a sheet in a small hand:
"Sato — 4 October. Aoi — 19 October. Ito — 21 October."
Interval — from fourteen to seventeen days. Different posts. Different platforms. The same signature.

And — all three posts about the same thing in a person's life. In Sato's case, the one Michiko had mentioned once: "once a year he shows me a post he wrote at night and later deleted." That post had been deleted, but not from the archive. In Aoi's case — a private entry about a clinic in Niigata when she was fifteen. In Ito's — this.
Each one's worst night.
He put his hand on the phone and called Asahikawa.
Ito's wife picked up at once. Her voice was not tears, but the state of voice that comes to women who have cried three mornings in a row and are now in the hour of pause between fits.
"Ito-san."
"Yes."
"This is Kurosawa Yukio, Prefectural Police, Missing Persons Unit. I have your report."
"Thank you for calling. Three people have already called me today. You are the fourth."
"I am the one who leads."
"I understand."
He paused, briefly, as was customary.
"Ito-san. I have one question for now. We'll talk in full tomorrow — I'll come myself. But one now. In 1998, in November — did something happen to your husband? Something that changed him?"
At the other end — silence.
Then, a deep breath in. Not tears.

"I don't know the details," Miho said slowly. "I only know that in November of ninety-eight he came home from a run out of Kushiro — we were still living together in Sapporo then, I had just become pregnant with Ryohei — and he lay down for three days. Not ill. Just lay down. On the fourth he got up, shaved, went to work. A month later he resigned from Nippon Express. Six months later he took a job with JR, driving the Asahikawa–Sapporo coach. Twenty-one years since."
"Did he tell you why?"
"Never. I asked twice. The second time he answered, 'Miho, there are things a person carries in place of cargo. My cargo carries me back the same way.'"
Kurosawa closed his eyes.
That line was not his own. That was from Issa.
"Ito-san. One more question. Did your husband keep an online diary?"
"No. We didn't even have internet at home until 2010. He has a button phone."
"At work? A computer?"
"At work, yes, in the dispatch room. But for timetables. He isn't —" she broke off. "Why? Is there something on it?"
"There is one old post from 2004. I just read it."
"On what?"
"On LiveJournal. It's an English-language platform, Japanese people rarely used it, but at the time it was popular among those who wanted to write anonymously."
"What does it say?"
Kurosawa looked at the screen.
"About 1998. Nothing more."
At the other end, a long pause. Then the even, almost administrative voice of a woman who had worked forty years in an infirmary:
"Kurosawa-san. I will make you tea. Come tomorrow."
"I will come."
"In the morning. Not after noon. In the afternoon my son comes."
"In the morning."
"Thank you."
She hung up.
Kurosawa sat for some time with the phone on his knee. Then he put it on the desk.

He held two things in his head at once: a woman in an infirmary uniform who would offer him tea at ten in the morning in a panel building in the Nagayama district, and the line of Issa about the snow that a branch holds for one more second, and one more, and one more, until it breaks. Ito had read that line for twenty-one years. He read it as counsel — as an instruction to hold the branch — and not as a warning.
The Doll Maker, Kurosawa thought, had read it as an instruction too. Only from the other side.
Miho in Nagayama with the tea — tomorrow.
Endo at the morgue — tomorrow.
JR dispatch — tomorrow.
The pass — the day after, and not alone.
He looked at the LiveJournal screen for north-wheel-jp again. Scrolled down. The last post, the one from 12 January 2027, four lines of haiku. He read them slowly:
"The road is longer than the memory that carries it. The snow does not ask."
Not Issa. Ito himself.
Kurosawa closed the tab.

Sasaki was standing in the doorway of the unit. She came in and sat on the corner of his desk, not at her own — on the corner of his, sideways, the way she used to sit last year, when she still didn't know how to talk with him about work without paper in her hands.
The gray metal thermos in her right hand.
"Keibuho."
"Yes."
"Endo asked for another half hour."
"For what?"

"To search the database for fresh cases with a coffee crumb. She has two prior matches — both from district stations, not ours. One from Kitami, four months ago. One from Hakodate, six months. Both closed as 'left of own accord.' Both — women in their thirties, living alone, a crumb of ground coffee found on clean tableware. In Kitami — on the bottom of a teapot. In Hakodate — on the bottom of a teacup."
"Someone had come to drink with them."
"Yes."
"Have those two been found?"
"No. One is still missing. The other — no body found, the case closed for lack of criminal indicators. The mother of the second still calls the district station once every two weeks."
Kurosawa nodded.
"Will Endo file it formally? Enter it into our case?"
"She says she will, but wants to speak with you face to face tomorrow. About another matter."
"What matter?"
Sasaki looked at him briefly, then out toward the window.
"About 2022, keibuho."
Kurosawa looked at her.
"About my brother."
"Yes."
"What about him?"
"She didn't say."
Kurosawa did not move for a moment. Then he lowered his head half a centimeter — a motion meaning: I have heard, I am holding this aside until tomorrow.
"All right. Tomorrow."
Sasaki did not stand up right away.
"Keibuho. Ito. What did he write?"

"One paragraph. About the Kamikawa Pass, the night of 8 November 1998. He hit someone and did not stop. The post is open — public. The Doll Maker added a space after the period of the last line. The twenty-first of October, at night."
"Twenty-first of October."
"Yes."
"Sato — the fourth, Aoi — the nineteenth."
"Three nights in October. One after another. One week."
Sasaki drew breath once. She held the thermos with both hands now.
"He took all three in one week. Maybe in one day. Toshi said so."
"Toshi doesn't make mistakes about such things."
"And it means that while you and I were driving to Kita 24-jo today — he already had the list for all nine."
Kurosawa looked at her.
"Nine."
"He has nine doors in each of his houses."
"Yes."
"Three is the beginning."
"Yes."
She stood, hip against the corner of the desk.
"Keibuho. I know you'll say 'let's take it one step at a time.' But tell me one thing now: of the nine, how many can we still reach in time?"
Kurosawa looked past her for a long moment — at the far wall, where the January calendar with the bridge hung crooked on one pin.
"I don't know," he said. "I think four. Maybe five. Not more."
Sasaki nodded.
"Then we have to go to the pass."

"No. Not yet. First, to Miho tomorrow. Then Endo. Then, through the Asahikawa district station, to JR dispatch for the camera footage from the crew balcony in Sapporo at 12:14 on the thirty-first. Only after that — the pass, and not alone. With traffic. With the locals."
"That's three days."
"That's three days."
Sasaki nodded again. Took her notebook from the desk.
"Keibuho. One more thing."
"Yes."
"Tanaka."
"Yes."
"He was waiting for us. We didn't go down to him. He came up. I didn't let him in here — I said you were on a call."
"Thank you."
"He wants, by end of week, a full 'methodological justification' — on paper — for our group."
"He'll have it."
"You'll write it yourself?"
"Ogawa and I. Ogawa will sign off on it."
"All right."
She stood up.
At the door she turned.
"Keibuho. About Nao."
"I remember."
"No, just one thing now."
"Yes."
"Her edit — the fifteenth of October."
Kurosawa looked at her.
"The fifteenth."
"Yes. Probably on the first day. That is, of these — four. Three known and one."
"Nao — in Niigata?"
"She's not there any more. I moved her this morning."
"Does she know?"
"She knows what I told her: 'I think you may be being watched, stay with our parents, don't go online from home in these two weeks.' She listens. She's the younger one, she listens."
"Good."
Kurosawa was silent. Then said, evenly:
"Sasaki. You will not be alone in this."
"I know."
She went out.
At half past seven he switched off the monitor.

He folded the printout of Miho's report in two and put it into the inside pocket of his coat, next to the cream envelope and the yellow lease-termination slip for Kingyo, which he had never taken out of the morning drawer — had forgotten.
No, not forgotten. Had not wanted to.
He pulled on his coat, wound his scarf — now the wool held also the smell of the latex gloves from Nakamura's apartment — and went out into the corridor.
The elevator held the same faintly stifling warmth.
In the lobby, behind the partition, Mori-san had gone; he had been replaced by the night man, younger, with some longer surname Kurosawa did not remember. The younger one nodded. Kurosawa nodded.
On the portico — again the wedge of snow. The two from Tokyo were not standing there. One crow was standing on the nearest lamppost, and it watched him longer than crows watch.
He went on foot.

In the pocket of his coat, next to the envelope and the printout and the yellow slip, there was now also one more thing: a small sheet folded into fours, with three dates and one word, "nine," underlined twice — once for each of its halves.
He did not know what he would do with it tomorrow.

He knew only that on the way back toward Maruyama, tomorrow, he would go to Miho Ito in Asahikawa, drink tea, and then go on — alone, without Sasaki — toward kilometer 743. Not to find anything on the road.
To stand there and listen to the wind.
Issa, he thought as he walked, Issa wrote about snow in branches. Never about snow on a highway.
Ito had read him for twenty-one years.
Choosing what not to see.
At the crossing by the old Shinto shrine, where a red cat with a scar across the bridge of its nose lived, Kurosawa stopped. The cat sat on its stone. Looked in his direction. Kurosawa looked back.

"February twenty-third, two thousand and two," he said quietly, not expecting the cat to listen, "Ren gave me for my birthday a small pocket edition of Issa, with a red spine. I read three haiku from it and put it on the shelf. It's still there."
The cat blinked once.
Kurosawa went on.

He had not thought of Ren since Monday. Since Monday he had thought about Sato, then about Aoi, then about Ito. Sasaki had said today, "Endo wants to talk to you about 2022, keibuho," and Ren had come back into his head by that name. Ren always came back by name, not by image. The image was in a frame on the kitchen wall next to Ayano, and Kurosawa had not looked at it directly for weeks.

He knew how to work with that. He had done it twice: in 2015, when he buried his mother; in 2024, when Ayano disappeared. He held the name to the side. He kept walking down the street. He did his work, and the name stood the way a man in the next subway car stands — you look at him from the side of your eye, until there is a reason to turn your head.
Endo would turn his head for him tomorrow.
He knew.
He only did not yet know what she would see there.

Two blocks from Maruyama, the light on the seventh floor of the furthest building in the block went off at the same moment as the temple bell. He reached his entrance, punched in the code, walked into the warm lobby. Ryoko did not come out of her door — her granddaughter was visiting today, he had been hearing voices through the wall since yesterday. He went up the stairs; the elevator in their building was running on one bearing, and in the evenings Kurosawa spared it.

At the door of his own apartment he stood for a second without putting the key in. Listening. Behind the door — the silence that holds in empty apartments to which someone will come back in a minute. Only that silence.
He went in.

p.emphasis: Three posts. One week. One choice.

section.subtitle: Chapter Four
section.p: The livedoor archive was kept alive in Tokyo on servers no one had cared about for a dozen years. That was the best guarantee against deletion: what no one needs, no one strikes out — it simply stops being turned off.

Kurosawa opened the blog at six in the morning. Outside the window it was still night — that particular Sapporo dark, when snow has not yet fallen but the air already knows it will. Ryoko was up in the kitchen downstairs; he heard her running water. He poured his own — twenty-two grams, three hundred and thirty grams of boiling water, as always — and did not drink. The cup stood to the left of the keyboard, slowly readying itself to be forgotten.
kingyo-oyaji.livedoor.blog.

He knew this blog. He had read it back in twenty-one, when he first started dropping in on Sato-san to sit for a while after work and had wanted to understand why a man who poured saké in silence had once written about tofu as if it were a prayer. Forty-three entries. The last one — June 2010. About autumn, which tofu knows before others do.
Now he was opening it not as a reader.
Kurosawa went through the first ten posts in reverse — from last to first — and was not looking for content. He was looking for shadow.

A space inserted where there could not be one. A comma shifted by one character. A timestamp missing one minute in the morning. A unicode void between paragraphs — the same U+200B the Doll Maker had once left in Murata's post the year before. This was not autograph for autograph's sake. This was a way to verify that access still worked, that the backend still opened — and, probably, a way to fix the date the victim had been chosen and locked into the list.
The ninth post from the bottom had a strange silence.

"Tofu and Autumn Rain," 12 June 2008. Between the third and fourth paragraphs — an interval that looked like an ordinary empty line, but when the text was copied to a terminal became visible. One zero-width character. U+200B.

Kurosawa reached for an "edit" button he did not have. He had only what the archive administrator saw at backup: the edit history. He had paid Kenji for access two weeks ago — in case something needed looking at.
Timestamp of the edit: 4 October 2027. 03:14 a.m.
Ten days before Sato-san disappeared.
Kurosawa felt the skin at the back of his neck cease being skin for a second and become parchment. It passed. He stood up, went to the sink, poured water into a glass. Drank it. Came back.
He was not surprised. He had been looking for exactly this. But to see was not the same as to predict. To see is when the skin forgets whose it is.
He copied the timestamp into a separate file. Named the file metronome.txt. Still empty. That would change.
At seven Sasaki came in.
She brought two tuna onigiri and a sheet of paper. The onigiri she put beside the keyboard. The sheet — between his hands and the cup.
"You said 2channel," she said.
"I did."
"Otaru, 1998, September. Thread 'port, old stories.' Thirty posts. I pulled an archive snapshot from the forty-seventh minute — before the author of one of the posts took the post down."
Kurosawa read the sheet.
One handle, kanata-1959. Eight lines.

cite.p: "Pier number three. The night after the typhoon. The clamp was rusted — I knew. The wave went out and came back. He held on. Then he didn't. I stood forty seconds and listened. Once he called out. Then there was only water."

section.p: No name. No date more specific than "after typhoon Vicki." No mention of whom. Only one person who stood forty seconds and listened.
Sasaki did not sit down. She stood behind him and waited.
"Kanata," said Kurosawa. "Distant. 1959 — year of birth."
"Yes."
"Did you check the wife?"

"Michiko Sato, 'snow-kingyo' on LiveJournal. Five hundred and ninety-eight entries, 2004–2014. One entry, 2007, September: 'He told me one story. Not all of it. Then he showed me an old post he wrote at night, then deleted. I did not ask anything.'" A pause. "He wrote from a port café. Otaru, September 1998. That's the same one."
Kurosawa folded the sheet in two. Did not look at Sasaki.
"Next?"
"Next — I'll go to the Otaru Nishi archive," she said. "They should have the school kendo club rosters from 1974. I want to find who Kenta Ono was. The second Kenta. The nephew."
"Not nephew," he said. "Cousin. On the mother's side. Back then, in 1998, he was twenty-two."
She looked at him.
"You already know."
"I guess. He wrote about it in eight lines, without naming him. You don't name the one you still see."
Sasaki nodded. Took her laptop. Walked to the door.
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."
"The onigiri are getting cold."
"I know."
The door closed behind her softly.
Kurosawa went back to the screen. He did not eat.
The second post was found in Nakamura Aoi's LiveJournal before noon.

Kenji came into the unit at ten, brought three laptops, the cat Miso in a carrier (the cat was asleep), and silently set everything on the corner desk. Kurosawa showed him the file metronome.txt with one line — Sato-san's timestamp. Kenji looked at it for four seconds.
"Give me victim two," he said.
"Aoi Nakamura. mixi, old profile, aoi_smoke. Private, but after the 2020 leak readable through a direct URL. Entry of 3 February 2011."
"One minute."

The minute stretched to twenty-seven. Kenji did not do anything extra. He opened three terminal windows, ran three different diff scripts against three different archive mirrors of mixi (Kenji knew of two of them; of the third only Kurosawa knew, and the surprise in Kenji's eyes turned out to be useful — Kurosawa noted that Kenji was capable of being surprised). Then Kenji turned the monitor.
"One period became a comma."
"Where."

"'名前を付けたら、覚えてしまう.' (Once you name a thing, you can't help remembering it.) In the version before 15 October — a period. In the version after 19 October — a comma. The original post from 2011 had been edited once in eight years. This is that once."
"Timestamp."
Kurosawa opened metronome.txt. Added a second line.
4 October. 19 October. Difference — fifteen days.
"The third," he said.
"Ito Kazuo. Your long-hauler. LiveJournal, north-wheel-jp. Entry of 8 November 2004, the one about the Kamikawa Pass."
"One minute."
This time — eighteen.

"One space added at the end. After '国道39号は私を覚えている.' (National 39 remembers me.) Before — period and line end. Now — period, space, line end. The author of these posts never did that; he has eighty-nine posts, nowhere at line's end is there a trailing space."
"Timestamp."
Kurosawa opened metronome.txt.
Three lines.
• 4 October 2027, 03:14. Sato Eiji.
• 19 October 2027, 02:41. Nakamura Aoi.
• 21 October 2027, 03:07. Ito Kazuo.
Kenji pushed back from the keyboard a few centimeters.

"Kurosawa-san. These signatures are an audit trail to himself: he keeps a list of who he has edited so he doesn't confuse them — memory for nine people over many years is unreliable, and a signature inside someone else's post is more reliable."
Kurosawa nodded slowly.
He looked at the screen. Three nights. One September week before it — silence. One week after — silence.
The dates said nothing on their own until he had aligned them with what was already in his head.

p.strong: All three edits — within the middle of October 2027.

section.p: All three in the same three weeks in which, by his hypothesis, the Doll Maker had kept a ready list in his head and been making his last checks before the act. Not "in one day," as Toshi had said. That was a simplification. In reality — across a short cycle, when the hand that chooses had already chosen and was only verifying that all three were still in place.
But Toshi had not said "one day" by mistake. Toshi had said "find the day" — that is, the point of origin, the moment of choice from which the countdown had begun.

Kurosawa did the arithmetic in his head. If the Doll Maker made one edit per person as a test of access and a fixing mark — then between choice and edit he might have three days to three weeks. The earliest edit — 4 October. The latest — 21 October. Difference — seventeen days. If the test access takes on average a week — then the choice was made a week before 4 October.
That is, somewhere at the end of September, the beginning of October, 2027.
He opened a calendar. 27 September — Thursday. Thursday, the day Toshi publishes a haiku. Kurosawa opened 5channel.

The haiku for 27 September 2027. Toshi's post from the detention center could not have gone out — but back in July, on the second-to-last Thursday before the arrest, Toshi had put up his last haiku while free:
「三つの窓 夜のなかで 同じ光」
Three objects. One abstraction. One point in time.
Kurosawa leaned back. He looked at the ceiling. For a long time.
Kenji did not interrupt.
Miso woke up in the carrier and mewed softly.
At five in the afternoon Sasaki came back from Otaru.

She had found Kenta Ono on the roster of the kendo club at Otaru Nishi, class of 1974 — second dan, left-handed, had stopped at a slightly higher level than Sato. Died in the port in 1998. The mother is still alive, eighty-two, in a nursing home in Sapporo. Sasaki had found out the address but did not go. She knew it would be Kurosawa, and she knew Kurosawa would not go to see her before Sato was alive in a hospital bed.
"Have you eaten anything?" she asked.
"Not yet."
The onigiri lay on the desk, soft and cold.
Kurosawa took one, bit, did not taste, swallowed. The other he left.
Sasaki said nothing about it.
She put her notebook in front of him, open to a page with a diagram drawn in pencil — three crosses connected by short lines, and one point above them, from which three arrows ran down to each cross.
"It's not three," she said.
"I know."

"It's one choice that broke into three. He was not hunting one by one. He opened your list — I mean, those six or seven people in Hokkaido who fit the filter — and put down three ticks in one evening. After that there was only the calendar."
Kurosawa looked at her diagram longer than she was counting on.
"Sasaki," he said. "I have to go to Toshi."
"I know."
"Tomorrow."
"I know."

She took the notebook. Stood by the window. Looked out at the headquarters courtyard, where under a lamp one man in uniform was smoking, his face turned aside, the way a person does who does not want to be seen in that posture.
"He knew where he would go for each of them," she said quietly. "Two weeks in advance. And in those two weeks he did not hurry."
"Yes."
"You understand what that means for Ayano."
Kurosawa closed his eyes.
"I understand."
"He chose her the same way. Once. On one evening. Three years ago. And then waited."
Kurosawa did not answer.
He opened metronome.txt and added a fourth line, empty, without a date. The cursor blinked over it for three minutes. He did not fill it in.
Outside the window snow began to fall — thin, dry, still soundless. The Doll Maker, somewhere seven hundred kilometers from him, was closing a laptop in a kitchen Kurosawa did not yet know.
Kurosawa closed his laptop earlier than he wanted to. It was a gesture. Gestures were sometimes all he could afford himself.
"Sasaki."
"Yes."
"Tomorrow at eight. Detention center."
"I'll drive."
She went out. Kurosawa was left with cold coffee, an empty onigiri on a paper wrapper, and three dates in a file that had settled into a shape he was not yet ready to name aloud.
Metronome. He had chosen the word two weeks ago, when he did not yet know whether he would find its work in three different archives on three different nights. Now the word was accurate.
The Doll Maker had a metronome. And the metronome kept time.

p.emphasis: Kettle cold. Shirt missing. Hair — four weeks.

section.subtitle: Chapter Five
section.p: The izakaya Kingyo had stood in its place on Susukino Minami 4-jo 6-chome for as long as Kurosawa could remember anything in this block. Half-basement entrance, six steps down, the sign — a goldfish once painted by Sato-san himself with boat paint — the yellow faded to the color of butter left out in a kitchen. The note "しばらく休みます" (Closed for a while) still hung on the door. The rain had wetted and dried it perhaps eight times over.

The door-glass Kurosawa had broken in the prologue — the small diamond-shaped pane by the handle — had not been replaced. In its place was plywood, nailed up in haste. By whom, Kurosawa did not know. Some neighbor, probably. Sato had many neighbors who did not ask.

Sasaki stood on the top step and waited while he worked the lock. There was no key — there was a short metal hook that Hokkaido Prefectural Police handed to every detective in the first year of service, and no one knew how to use it.
Kurosawa opened it in forty seconds.
"You've done this before," Sasaki said. Not a question.
"Once. Not here."

The door gave inward, softly. Inside it smelled of what izakaya smell of when they have not worked for two months: old soy sauce that has finished evaporating; oil thickened in the fryer to the density of wax; and a third thing — wood that has soaked in smoke for forty years and breathes it when it is quiet around it.
Sasaki turned on a pocket flashlight. Kurosawa did not.
He knew this kitchen by touch.
Inside, everything was where it should have been.

Two counters — one for guests, one for work. Eight seats. Four chairs around a low table in the corner. A ceramic pitcher of water in the entry — the same style as the one in Kamishiroi — but here it was a real one, pre-war, with a thin crack around the neck that Sato had glued twenty years ago with rice paste. Sasaki ran the beam along the counter. Dust lay evenly — the even dust that settles in a closed room over eight weeks. No prints. No traces.
On the little shelf over the counter — a pack of Peace without filters. One.
Kurosawa came up, took it, weighed it in his palm.
"How many?" Sasaki asked.
He flipped the flap open. Counted with a finger.
"Fourteen."
"Out of twenty?"
"Out of twenty."
He put the pack back. Exactly in the place it had been.

Sasaki turned the flashlight onto the register. The register stood closed. On top of it — a fresh flat patch, about ten centimeters long — the trace of an envelope that had lain there several weeks and had then been taken. Kurosawa had taken it himself. Cream envelope. Newspaper clipping. A face circled in red. He still had it in the drawer of his desk in the unit.
"Nothing fresh here," said Sasaki.
"There shouldn't be anything fresh here. There should be something exact."
"Exact of what."
"Exact to what he loved."
Sasaki looked at him.

Kurosawa went behind the counter, into the kitchen corner. That was no longer the guest side — that was his territory. Sato had stood here every evening from six to one for forty years. A thick board of thin cherrywood on the work table, worn in the middle to a pale yellow; a steel bar above it with magnets, on which two knives used to hang — now one, ceramic. The other was not there. Kurosawa looked at the empty spot longer than was necessary.
"The knife," he said.
"What."
"He took one knife."
"Sato."
"No. The one who led him."
Sasaki came up, shone the light on the bar. The empty magnet gleamed.

"The knife is steel," Kurosawa went on. "Wooden handle. Yanagi-ba, thirty centimeters. He kept it for fish. Cut for thin sashimi. He never worked meat with the ceramic one, ceramic doesn't take meat. Which means the one who led him knew the difference. Or Sato picked it up himself. Or he was told to bring something with him."
"What could he have been told to bring."

Kurosawa did not answer. He opened the drawer under the work table. Inside lay three clean white towels, folded the way Sato folded them every evening after washing: three folds, corner to corner. One towel missing. Kurosawa closed the drawer.
"The peg," he said.

Behind Sasaki's shoulder, on the low peg by the exit from the kitchen into the corridor — where Sato hung his white cook's shirt between shift and shift — the shirt was not there. The peg was clean, no web, no dust on the edges. Someone had wiped it with a hand.
Sato never wiped that peg on purpose. He simply hung on it.
"The cook's shirt is gone," Sasaki said quietly.
"Gone."
"He put it on before he went out."
"He put it on. Or it was already on him. But no one takes another person's clothing off a peg when they are taking that person away by force. Only someone leaving of his own accord takes it."
Kurosawa closed his eyes for a second.

Sato had gone out in his shirt, in a clean apron, with a yanagi-ba knife wrapped in a clean white towel. That is how a cook goes out who has received an invitation to someone else's kitchen. That is not how a person goes out who is being abducted.

Sasaki found the hair on the spare fish knife — the one lying on the work table separately, under a light lid. Sato always kept it there: a small helper knife, for scaling a small saury or carp. The lid did not sit tight. In the gap between lid and handle, one hair had fallen.
Grayish. Fine. Four centimeters.
Sasaki lifted it with tweezers. Held it up to the light on both sides.
"Fresh," she said. "Not ten years old. About four weeks. Maximum five."
"His."
"Maybe. Maybe not. We'll have to check."
Kurosawa looked at the tweezers.

"It's his. He dyed in September." He stopped himself. That was foolish — to say such a thing about a man like Sato, who had never in his life dyed his hair. Sasaki paid no attention. Kurosawa corrected himself: "It's his. That was his gray. Grayish, yellowed at the tips from smoke. No one else our age goes gray like that."
Sasaki put the hair in a bag. Wrote on it with a marker, cap up: SATO / KING / kitchen-4wk / 15.11.2027.
"Four weeks ago," she said, "he was still coming in here. Already after the abduction."
"Yes."
"He came on his own or he was brought."

Kurosawa looked at the pack of Peace on the shelf. Fourteen of twenty. Sato smoked his pack over two days. That meant that between the day he vanished in the prologue and the day this pack was last opened in his hand — three days. Not more. The pack had been left here between the abduction and something.
"He was brought," Kurosawa said.
"For what."
"To take something. To leave something. To show him something."

He stood a moment longer. Then went over to the coat rack in the corridor. Behind the rack — a photograph Sato had hung in the nineties: he and Michiko, taken on the pier at Otaru, both younger than he was now. Michiko is laughing. Sato is not laughing — but he holds her by the arm, and the way he holds her is more than a smile. The photograph was in place. Kurosawa touched the frame with the tip of a finger. The dust came off in an even strip.
"Sasaki."
"Yes."
"He came here to say goodbye."
She turned the flashlight in his direction. Not to his face — to his chest. She saw he was standing in front of the photograph.
"To whom."

"To Michiko." He took his finger from the frame. "It was his way. He went to her grave three times a year. But coming to this kitchen was easier — she stayed here longer. He would smoke one cigarette, look at this photograph, look at the tableware, then leave. He did this four times a year, in the week of their anniversary. He had to do it on the fifth of November."
"Abducted on the thirty-first of October."
"Yes."
"And brought here on the fifth."
"Yes."
"The Doll Maker knew about this ritual."
"Yes."

Kurosawa moved back from the photograph. He walked to the counter. Sat on one of the stools — the third from the right, the one he always sat on — and put his hands on the wood, the wood that had remembered his forearms for as many years as he could remember.
He did not cry. He looked at the empty register.
