Sato had been walked out along his ritual. The Doll Maker did not take people crudely — the Doll Maker took people inside their own forms. Sato had gone of his own accord because he had been allowed to say goodbye — and the way he had been allowed, Sato took as understanding. Older people rarely meet strangers' understanding out loud. When they meet it, they follow it, as one follows a mother's voice.
"Kurosawa-san," Sasaki said quietly.
"Yes."
"You want to say something aloud."
"No." He stood up. "Let's go."
At the door Sasaki hung back.
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."
"You came here on Sunday. A week before the prologue. You told Ogawa you didn't open a case."
"I came. I didn't know. I thought he had just closed for a few days."
"You saw him last."
"October twenty-seventh. In the evening. I drank green tea here, at this counter. He was silent. That was normal."
"Did he say anything."
Kurosawa thought.
"One thing. He said, 'Kurosawa-keibu, you've lost weight again.' I didn't answer. He poured me a second cup. That was all."
"That — was all."
"That — was all."
Sasaki nodded. Went out onto the steps. Kurosawa closed the door behind him. There was nothing to lock with — the hook only opened, it did not lock. He put the plywood back in place.
The note "しばらく休みます" swung on a draft and stilled.
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."
"He will go willingly into the next ryokan too. If we don't get there in time."
"I know."

Sasaki walked to the car. Kurosawa stayed on the top step for a minute. Took a cigarette from his pocket — not Peace, his usual Mild Seven Light — rolled it between his fingers, did not light it. Put it back.
He still had four in the pack. Not today.
He came down to the car.
Outside, the snow was falling — the same that had started overnight — and now you could hear it falling.

p.emphasis: "Find the day. He chose them on one day."

section.subtitle: Chapter Six
section.p: The Sapporo Prefectural Police detention center held its light the same way it had held it a year ago: a green fluorescent calm without cause and without time. Kurosawa went through two metal detectors, handed over his watch, handed over his pen and his phone, kept his notebook — new, not yet opened — and the thermos.

The thermos was not the one from last year. That one had stayed on the metal table in front of Toshi then, and Toshi had not drunk, and Kurosawa had not taken it back, and afterward one of the guards had washed it and put it in the personal-effects cabinet of the detainee. Kurosawa had not asked about it. He had bought a new thermos a month after his discharge, from a shop near the station — a plain steel half-liter, no writing. Screw cap. Water — not green tea.
When you drink green tea at the detention center, Toshi looks at that cup, and Kurosawa did not want him looking.
The guard nodded. Kurosawa went into the interview room.
Toshi was already sitting.

He did not stand. Did not look. Hands lay on his knees calmly, as always. In seven months in the detention center he had lost weight — not much — and the bone at his temple had become more visible. Shaved bald. Dark blue work trousers, a gray shirt. All the same.

Before him on the table lay a thin sheet of paper with one question. Kurosawa recognized the handwriting of Investigator Kawaguchi — he wrote the questionnaire every Tuesday and picked it up on Thursday, and in seven months Toshi had returned three hundred and twelve sheets with no answer.
Toshi took the sheet, folded it in two, laid it neatly on the edge of the table.
"You came."
"I did."

Kurosawa sat down. Put the thermos in the middle of the table. Unscrewed the cap. Poured water into a plastic cup — brought in beforehand, from a small bag — and set the cup between them, closer to Toshi but not so close that he would have to reach.
Toshi looked at the cup. Did not thank him. Did not take it.
Kurosawa screwed the cap on. Put his hands on the table. Opened the notebook. He had no pen — the pen had been taken at the entrance. The notebook was to have something to look at.
He did not look.
He looked at the wall to the left of Toshi's head.
Toshi looked at the wall to the left of Kurosawa's head.
The minutes in the interview room had their own physics. The first five — inertia. Then — vacuum. Then again inertia, in the other direction.

Kurosawa sat twenty-seven minutes without moving. Toshi sat twenty-seven minutes without moving. The guard behind the glass shifted from one foot to the other twice. Once — at the twelfth minute. The second time — at the twentieth.

At the twenty-eighth minute Toshi slowly — with that economical movement Kurosawa had always noticed in him — reached out his hand to the plastic cup. Took it. Did not raise it to his lips. Put it back.
At the twenty-ninth — he turned the cup a little with a finger.
At the thirtieth — he said, without looking:
"Sato-san."
"Yes."
Silence.
"Nakamura Aoi. Ito Kazuo."
"Yes."
Toshi nodded. Very briefly. Once.
Kurosawa opened his mouth — and closed it. In place of words he passed a palm along the edge of the notebook. Toshi waited.
"Three edits," Kurosawa said at last. "4 October. 19 October. 21 October."
Toshi did not react.
"But it is not three choices. It is one." Kurosawa laid his palms one on the other on the table. "Yes?"
Toshi looked aside. At the wall to the left of Kurosawa.
"Find the day," he said. "He chose them on one day."
"Which."
Toshi did not answer.
"End of September," Kurosawa said to himself, quietly. "Thursday."
Toshi did not change his expression.
"The twenty-seventh."
"The twenty-seventh," repeated Toshi. Not as an affirmation. As if trying the word for taste.
"You say 'the twenty-seventh.'"
"I say nothing, Inspector. I repeat what is yours."
Kurosawa looked away.

He knew this game. Toshi played it the same way he wrote haiku — with method and without blood. Never directly. Never by lying. Only by repeating what you yourself had said — and if you said something right, letting it stand. If you said something wrong, repeating it too, in the same even voice. The difference was in how long his eyes held on the empty wall between the words.
"The twenty-seventh of September," Kurosawa said once more.
Toshi's eyes stayed on the wall for one second longer than usual.
Kurosawa closed the notebook.
"Sato went of his own accord," he said after a pause.
Toshi nodded. Once.
"You knew he would go of his own accord."
"He always went of his own accord."
"You saw him."
"No." A pause. "I knew he always went of his own accord because you knew him."
Kurosawa turned his head. Looked at Toshi for the first time in the conversation. Toshi did not look at him.
"You knew Sato-san from my conversations," Kurosawa said. "You never saw him."
"Yes."
"I talked about him in Furano."
"Yes."
"About which side, exactly."
Toshi thought.
"You said once, 'He is the only person with whom I can be silent and not feel guilty.' It was in December 2024."

Kurosawa did not answer. He did not remember whether he had said it. He believed he had. He knew Toshi did not invent things of that kind — Toshi did not have a fantasy of that small a kind. Toshi kept details the way one keeps a rosary: each in its place.

He wanted to ask why Toshi had told this to the Doll Maker. He did not ask. He knew the answer. Toshi had told it not as betrayal — Toshi had told it as a person who shares with his spiritual director an observation about another person who is suffering. In Toshi's frame this was not an informing. This was compassion.
Kurosawa had long ago stopped being angry with Toshi over form. Now he was angry only over content.
"You understand," Kurosawa said, "that there is one more in two weeks."
Toshi did not answer.
"Or not."
Toshi looked at the plastic cup.
"Or not," he repeated after him, quietly.
"Do you know?"
Toshi was silent for a long time. At the edge of where silence stops being silence and becomes refusal.
Then he said:
"He has taken as many as he wanted. He counts, as I told you once. Nine."
"Nine in rotation," Kurosawa said. "Yes."
"Three new. One old one has gone earlier."
Kurosawa went still.
"Who."
"Do not ask."
"Who went."
Toshi held a very long pause. Kurosawa heard the guard behind the glass shift from one foot to the other — this was already past the standard minutes — a third time, at the thirty-seventh minute.
"The one who was long ago," said Toshi. "He stopped repeating."
"What does that mean."
"It means," said Toshi, "that when a victim stops repeating the old dream — she becomes unneeded. He lets her go. Sometimes into death. Sometimes into a new life — but not her own. Not she herself."
Kurosawa felt his fingers dig into the edge of the notebook. He unclenched.
"Who," he said again.
Toshi looked at the cup — and, for the first time in the conversation, at Kurosawa.
"Don't ask me," he said. "Ask Endo."
Kurosawa sat another five minutes.
Toshi did not look at him anymore. Looked at the wall.
The cup stood between them, full. Toshi did not drink.
At the forty-second minute Kurosawa screwed the thermos closed. Took the notebook. Stood.
"Thank you," he said. Not for anything in particular.
Toshi nodded.
Kurosawa walked to the door.
"Inspector."
Kurosawa stopped without turning.
"Yes."
"You will come again."
"Yes."
"Bring, please, green tea. Not water."
Kurosawa was silent for a long moment.
"All right," he said. "Next time."
He went out.

The guard locked the door behind him. The click was low, short — the same as last year. Kurosawa walked down the corridor to the effects room, took his watch, took his pen, took his phone, and only at the exit from the building put his coat on.
Outside, the snow was falling.
Sasaki was waiting in the car. He sat down on the right. He said nothing. Neither did she.
They drove two blocks. Kurosawa opened the notebook. In it there was one word, written by Toshi-with-his-pencil-in-his-head:
He closed the notebook.
"Sasaki."
"Yes."
"To Endo."
"Now?"
"Now."
She turned the wheel.
Two blocks on, it was already dark. The snow was falling evenly.

title.p: The One Who Came Three Times

p.emphasis: A thin voice. Rain on the veranda. A sheet of paper.

section.subtitle: Chapter Seven
section.p: Toshi was not yet Toshi then. He was Brother Jisai, twelfth year at the monastery, thirty-seventh year from birth. He shaved his own head every Tuesday, with a dull Feather razor he kept apart from the razor for his hands. He knew his face only when he washed.

Abbot Gensho, then still sixty-four, not seventy-two, kept him on pilgrim reception. It was a post for one who did not want to speak. You met a person at the gate, bowed, pointed to the stone for shoes, showed where to wash the hands, poured tea, showed the bed — and all these movements together made four sentences in a day. Sometimes five.
He remembered that pilgrim the first time — not because the man stood out in any way. Because he did not stand out.
He came on Thursday evening. Rain.
A young man — around thirty — in a gray coat. No umbrella. Not wet — he had come from the bus stop under the awning. Someone had shown him the way. He knew.
One suitcase. Not a rucksack.
Bowed correctly. Not deep, not shallow. Bowed like someone who had learned to bow somewhere else — not here.
The voice was thin. Not feminine. Just thin. That happens when the throat is soft from someone who speaks little.
"I'm told you take three nights here."
"We do."
"Thank you."

Jisai showed the stone for shoes. The pilgrim took them off. Set them straight, heel to heel. Jisai looked — not out of profession, but out of the body. He always looked at how a person set their shoes down. It said more than the eyes.
The shoes stood perfectly.
Second night.
The pilgrim went to the library.
That was allowed — to pilgrims who asked. Not many asked. The abbot made the decision — nodded.

Jisai brought tea at eight. Knocked. Went in. The pilgrim sat on a cushion at a low table — not with any book — but before his own sheet. Was writing. Not fast. Not with a pencil — with a thin brush-pen. Jisai saw only what he caught in a glance: three lines, short, with pauses between the ideograms that were noticeable to eyes accustomed to old bindings. Haiku.
He set down the tea. Bowed. Went out.
In the corridor he stopped.
Stood, looking at the plank of floor in front of him.
He could not have said why.
Third night.
Jisai did not bring the tea. The younger brother did — Getsui. Jisai sat in his own room. Looked at the wall. Was not meditating. Listened to the rain.
At half past nine there was a knock at the door.
"Brother Jisai."
He opened.
The pilgrim stood there. No coat. In a gray shirt. Hair dry.
"Forgive the disturbance. I'm told your name is Jisai."
"Yes."

"I'll leave something for you in the library. Do not take it. I do not leave it with the abbot — I'm in a hurry. But I wanted someone from the monastery to read it. Not necessarily you. Perhaps in some year."
"What is it."
"A bound sheaf. Thin. No name. Haiku."
Jisai nodded.
The pilgrim bowed. Went.
Jisai closed the door.
The rain came.

He did not go to the library until morning. Not out of curiosity — out of discipline. The abbot said: pilgrims leave what they leave. We do not read on the go. We put it on the shelf. In ten years, when we forget whose it is — then we read it.

In the morning the pilgrim left. Took his shoes. Took his suitcase. In the entry hall he bowed to Gensho — Gensho bowed back. Jisai stood behind a pillar and watched. The pilgrim said something to the abbot — Jisai did not hear — and left.
Gensho turned to Jisai.
"How long was he here."
"Three nights."
"Who brought him."
"He knew the way himself."
Gensho nodded. Went to his room.
Jisai went into the library.
On the third shelf from the top — where things pilgrims brought were kept — lay a thin sheaf. Eight sheets of rice paper, sewn with black thread. No name. No date.
Jisai took it. Put it back. Did not unfold it.
Discipline.
He forgot about it for eight years.

Toshi sat in his hut. It was the second week after he had come out of the room. Memory came back in portions: not as images, but as the form of the body — how to stand, how to hold a cup, how not to ask.
He opened the laptop for the first time in eight months.

He did not know why he went to 5channel. His fingers knew. He went into an old thread — "Silence and Its Sides" — where twenty-three handles were silent most of the time. Read thirty posts from different authors.
At the twenty-third — he stopped.
A haiku. The same method. Five — seven — five. One object. One abstraction. One point in time. No scar.
He recognized it.

He could not have said what. The rhythm. The way of placing a pause before the third ideogram of the second line. The way of avoiding banalities. The way of not rhyming an image with an image. This was not a handwriting — this was a hand.
He opened his own shelf. Took down the thin sheaf. Eight sheets, black thread. No name. No date.
Unfolded it.
Eleven haiku. By the same method.
The same one.
Toshi sat for a long time, looking at the sheet.
Then — for the first time since memory had begun to return — he laughed. One short exhale through the nose. Not joy. Recognition.
The one whom he now knew as his return to himself — had come to him back in nineteen.
Had come three times, as a pilgrim. Three nights. Had written haiku in the library. Had left a sheet on the shelf. Had known that Jisai was the man who would one day read it.
Had known it eight years before Toshi knew him.
Toshi now remembered one more thing that he had not mentioned to Inspector Kurosawa in the conversation in December.
The pilgrim, on the third night when he had knocked at his door, had said one more thing. Jisai had paid it no attention then. It was an incidental remark, courtesy.

"Brother Jisai," the pilgrim had said, "on the shelf behind your abbot stands the same faceless figure that stands at my sister's home. I saw it yesterday when he was showing me the calligraphies. That is a rarity."
Jisai nodded. Did not ask where the sister lived.

Then, in 2019, on Abbot Gensho's shelf there did indeed stand a small white porcelain faceless figure — a cone, smooth, about fifteen centimeters high. Toshi had never asked where the abbot had got it.

In 2027, in his hut — on the altar, in the corner — there stands one exactly like it. It was given to him by a woman he does not remember and whom he was not allowed to look at. Her voice — thin. He heard her for three nights as he returned to himself. She held him by the hand while he cried, and did not ask why. That was the sister.
He could not say whether that was the same sister the pilgrim spoke of in 2019. But one thing was certain: the figure was the same.
Toshi had given Inspector Kurosawa half of this in December 2024.

Then, in the detention center — already after the second arrest, in 2026 — he had repeated the half: the pilgrim, the quiet voice, three nights, the sheaf. Kurosawa had received it. Toshi had not spoken of the second half — that he had recognized the hand in 2027. Had not spoken of the sister. Had not spoken of the figure on Gensho's shelf.
Not out of protection of the Doll Maker. Toshi did not protect him — he had nothing to protect the man from, who was beyond protections.
He had not said it because Kurosawa, had he heard, would have taken two wrong steps:

First, he would have driven to Gensho and started asking about the figure. Gensho did not remember him — Gensho was old, his hands trembled, he confused the names of pilgrims from the last ten years. Kurosawa would have made himself angry for a wasted trip.

Second — Kurosawa, learning that the Doll Maker had come under the guise of a pilgrim and that Toshi had not recognized him then, would have begun to ask himself whether Toshi had recognized him then and lied. That would have poisoned the conversations in the detention center.
Toshi did not want to poison the conversations. The detention center was the only place where he and Kurosawa sat across from each other without the Doll Maker between them.
He kept silent out of love — if that word could apply.
He knew Kurosawa would not use him — yet.
He knew Kurosawa, when there was less time left, would come to him and bring green tea. And then — perhaps — Toshi would tell him the second half. Or — perhaps — he would not manage in time.
Toshi closed his eyes.
The rain in Furano fell the same way the rain had fallen in Reisen-ji in 2019 — evenly, without intent.
He opened his eyes.
The plastic cup of water stood in front of him. Empty. The detention center.
Time had shifted half a step again.

p.emphasis: "One molar, Kurosawa. Only one. But not that one."

section.subtitle: Chapter Eight
section.p: Machiko Endo tossed her last cigarette into the ashtray outside the door of the morgue and stepped in — not to greet anyone — so that nothing would distract her for the next hour and a half. She closed the door with her shoulder. Turned the key. It was her ritual. The key turned not against outsiders — against herself, so she would not step out to the café around the corner before she was done.

On the lower floor — the place her friends in the police called the basement, though technically it was a semi-basement with proper windows under the ceiling — she had three fridges, two work tables, one archive cabinet with twenty-two drawers, and one shelf with a cup, a box of Lipton, and one bottle of Nikka behind the box. She had not touched the bottle for three weeks. That was a good sign.
She turned on the light. The fluorescents came on with that short half-second delay Endo knew better than her own name. She set the thermos on the work table. Pulled a folder off the shelf.
The folder was the same one she had kept on her table for seven months.

p.strong: 黒澤 蓮 / KUROSAWA Ren / DOB 1979.04.12 / DOD 2022.02.17 (protocol).

section.p: She opened it. Not because she did not know its contents by heart. Because on paper it became different — concrete.
Endo did not love Kurosawa as a person. She loved him as an obligation.

In 2019 he had found her sister. Not alive — the body — by a bridge, in a marsh, after seventeen years of searching. Endo had said one line to him then: "Kurosawa-san, you think I'm thanking you. I owe you." He did not answer. That is his way of taking on obligations — not taking them on with words.
Now she had to return that obligation. Not to her sister — to Kurosawa. And she was returning it without hurry.

Endo did nothing in a hurry. It was a profession. The dead do not hurry, and the living who hurry make mistakes in the morgue, and Endo had seen three dozen such over twenty-two years — all reassigned to other posts or quietly let go.
She sat down. Opened the odontologist's protocol from 2022 — the one on top of the pile.

Three pages. Signed by Dr. Iwamura Ken'ichi, age as of 2022 — seventy-one. Retired in 2023. Died in 2025. In 2022 he was doing relief work at the forensic center — that was his third job, after private practice and teaching. Endo had known him since student years. Back then he was precise. In 2022 — no longer.
The description of the dental arch in the protocol was standard, laconic. On the lower left M1, a notation: "present, no serious defects observed, restoration minor."

Endo set the protocol aside. Took from the same folder Ren's old dental file. She had obtained it two weeks ago — by lawful request through the investigation — from the private dental clinic Sapporo Odonto, where Ren had been treated since 2015.
The file was four times thicker than the protocol.
Entry of 8 March 2018:

cite.p: "Patient Kurosawa Ren. Complaint: pain in the lower left jaw. Examination: M1 lower left — vertical root fracture, consequence of trauma (patient reports a fall from a bicycle in February 2018). Extraction indicated. Performed. Patient consented to subsequent implantation."

section.p: Entry of 22 April 2018:

cite.p: "Nobel Biocare Active implant placed, titanium post 11 mm long, 4.3 mm diameter. Temporary crown. Patient satisfied."

section.p: Entry of 15 June 2018:

cite.p: "Permanent crown, metal-ceramic, seated. Hygiene satisfactory. Next examination — May 2019."

section.p: Endo opened the third document in the folder. It was a table she kept herself, in pencil, on graph paper. Three columns: "what should be," "what is recorded in the 2022 protocol," "conclusion."
On the line "Lower left M1":
• Should be: metal-ceramic crown on a titanium post of a Nobel Biocare Active implant.
• Recorded in the protocol: molar present, restoration minor.
• Conclusion: discrepancy.
Endo ran a fingernail under that last word. Her nails were cut short, like those of everyone who worked with their hands; the polish was clear, so no one would see it chipping.

A titanium post does not burn in a fire with a fuel-tank explosion. It deforms but stays. A metal-ceramic crown cracks — yes — but the post remains. An odontologist writing a protocol — even under stress — could not confuse a natural root with a titanium post. That is not a question of experience. It is a question of instrument. Titanium does not pass through an x-ray as bone.
One of two things was the truth.
Either Dr. Iwamura had committed gross negligence in 2022 and, now dead, could neither confirm nor deny it.
Or the tooth in the mouth of the body in the burnt car in February 2022 — was not the tooth of Ren Kurosawa.
Endo took a second folder from the shelf. A thin one.

Inside lay one sheet. On the sheet — two names. Both were dentists. Both from Hokkaido. Both worked at different clinics, both were among those to whose backups the Doll Maker might have had access in 2020–2023. Endo was running her small OSINT, telling neither Kurosawa nor Ogawa. She loved OSINT the way a cook loves someone else's recipe — without admitting to the love.
One of the two dentists was the brother of a subcontractor at the firm Yuki-Kogei. Not much of a connection — but in Hokkaido everyone knew everyone within two handshakes.
Endo had not approached this dentist directly. She had only written his name on a sheet and put the sheet in the folder.
That would be for later, she thought — though she did not call it "for later" aloud. She called it "what comes after."
Another sheet, under the first:

A request for isotope analysis of tooth enamel — the typical method for determining a person's regional origin from the ratio of strontium and oxygen in the teeth. Endo had submitted the request two weeks ago to a Tokyo lab, through official channels, through Ogawa, paying out of her own budget.
Results were due in two weeks.
Endo looked at the clock on the wall. Half past eleven. Lunchtime. She had not eaten.
The call from the departmental secretary came at twenty past one.
"Endo-sensei, Kurosawa-keibuho is here. And Sasaki. They're downstairs."
"Let them up."
Endo did not stand up. Did not straighten her lab coat. Took the folder — both, the thin one hidden under the thick — and set it on the table.

Kurosawa came in first. Thinner. The scar on his brow white, which one day in poor light would be pink. Did not take off his coat — only unbuttoned it. Sasaki behind him, hair cut short, no makeup, with a thermos.
"Endo-san," said Kurosawa.
"Kurosawa."
A pause.
"I was told to come to you," he said.
"By whom."
"Toshi."

Endo nodded. Was not surprised. She had known that one day Kurosawa would come from exactly this side. She had only not thought it would be today. She had been counting on next week — after the isotope analysis. Then she would have had two more arguments and one less span of time.
"Sit."
He did not sit. Sasaki sat.
"Endo," said Kurosawa. "Ren."
"Yes."
"Speak."
Endo opened the folder. Turned it to face him. Pointed a finger at the odontologist's protocol.
"One discrepancy. Lower left M1. On the medical record — a Nobel Biocare implant, titanium. On the 2022 protocol — a normal molar."
Kurosawa was silent for a long time. Then he sat.
Sasaki looked at him sidelong. Said nothing.
"One mistake," Kurosawa said quietly. "It could have been the odontologist's mistake."
"It could have been," said Endo. "It also could not have been. But the odontologist is dead. You can't ask him."
"And?"
"And I have no second proof. One is not proof. Two is proof. I have the means to obtain a second."
"How."
"Exhumation."
Kurosawa closed his eyes. One second. Two.
Sasaki moved her hand toward the thermos, then drew it back.
"How long," said Kurosawa.

"For permission — up to a week. I need your signature — you are the only living blood relative. Your mother in Sendai, she is in dementia, her signature will not be accepted legally. For the procedure itself — three weeks. For the conclusion — up to a month. All told, five to six weeks."
"You are certain that you are right."
"No." Endo looked him in the eyes. "I am certain that I am not mistaken in what I don't know."
"What does that mean."

"It means," she said, "that I am not asserting the body is not Ren. I am asserting the tooth is not the right one. The difference is that from the first assertion follows horror, and from the second — work."
Kurosawa nodded slowly.

"One more thing," said Endo. "I've submitted a request for isotope analysis of the enamel. Privately, on my budget. The results will come in two weeks. That will tell me whether the person in the grave is from Hokkaido or from another region."
"That's not a Ren-test."
"That's not a Ren-test," she agreed. "That's a looking-for-who test."
Sasaki spoke for the first time.
"Endo-san." A pause. "When did you understand?"
Endo looked at her.

"In May. I was rereading the protocol for another reason — there was a case related to Nobel Biocare, we had to cross-check markings. That was when I saw that Ren's M1 had an implant and the protocol did not. I closed the folder then and put it on the shelf. I did not open it for seven months."
"Why."

"Because," said Endo, "there was nothing to open it for. Kurosawa had grief, and I had a hypothesis. A hypothesis without a request is not a profession, it is gossip. I waited until Kurosawa himself began asking questions that required such a request. He began last week."
Kurosawa looked at her.
"How did I begin."

"You came to me on Monday," said Endo, "and asked whether I could give you a list of unsolved deaths in Hokkaido in the winter season involving a car fire. You put a question about method. That is a professional question. Not a question of grief. That was when I opened the folder."
Kurosawa looked at the table for a long moment.
"Let me sign," he said.
Endo opened the third drawer. Took out a form. Laid it before him. A pen — her own, not his — set beside it.
Kurosawa signed. Date. Name. Degree of kinship — "younger brother."
No reservations. No questions.
Sasaki looked out the window.

Endo took the form — she herself looked at the signature longer than she needed to — put it in the folder. The thin folder — with two names and the sheet about the isotope analysis — she moved to the lower drawer. Locked it. Put the key in the right pocket of her coat.
Kurosawa stood.
"Endo-san."
"Yes."
"How long will you still keep that folder in the lower drawer."
Endo looked at him.
"As long as necessary," she said. "Don't ask me that question again. I know what I'm doing. You know that I know."
Kurosawa nodded. Walked to the door.
Sasaki stood up, nodded to Endo, followed.
On the threshold Kurosawa stopped.
"Endo."
"Yes."
"Thank you."
"Don't thank me before there's a result."
He nodded. Went out.
The door closed.
Endo sat another five minutes.

Then stood up. Went to the shelf. Took the Nikka bottle from behind the Lipton box. Unscrewed it. Did not pour into the cup — poured into the plastic tumbler she kept for coffee — a finger's width. Drank.
Set the bottle back.
Turned off the light.
Went out into the corridor. Locked the morgue door. Turned the key twice in the lock — away from herself — and slipped it into the same pocket where the drawer key already was.
She did not go to smoke behind the morgue but on another street, a block away. Not because she did not want to meet anyone. Because she wanted to walk a little.
The snow fell evenly.
Endo thought one thing she had not told Kurosawa:

If the body in the grave was not Ren, then the Doll Maker in 2022 had had access to someone who had swapped documents inside the forensic office. Not an odontologist — a secretary or an assistant. That meant the Doll Maker had had a contact in their department back then, in 2022.
That meant — possibly — the Doll Maker had one now.
Endo finished the cigarette. Trod it out. Walked back.
She knew: when the time came, she would tell Kurosawa that too. But not before he was ready. He was not yet.

p.emphasis: The twenty-seventh of September, the night after the typhoon, the year he was thirty-nine.

section.subtitle: Chapter Nine
section.p: The plank under his knee was wet — not the wet of rain, but that particular wet salt water leaves behind after it has gone and the salt on the boards has not yet dried.

He stood on Pier Three in Otaru harbor. He knew it because his feet knew. The right foot stood on a plank with an old nail without a head — that nail had always stuck up two millimeters — and the left held further on, past the rusted clamp he had not trusted twenty years ago. He did not remember how he had come here. But the body remembered.
It was night. Twenty-two forty-seven. He did not know how he knew. He knew.

The typhoon had gone forty minutes ago. The sky was already that sky — drunk out, black with green at the rim — and only one hanging lantern on the right flickered — with kerosene, it seemed — though there had not been kerosene lanterns on Pier Three since ninety-two. He knew. Still the lantern flickered.
He was in his white cook's shirt. The two top buttons — fastened. Sleeves to the elbow. The right cuff was dry. The left — wet along the edge.
The water under the planks knocked. It knocked the way it knocks against an empty box set in water — dryly, with an echo.
Behind the pier's post, half a step from his right foot, stood Kenta.

Kenta Ono. Not that Kenta-brother — the other one — a cousin on his mother's side. Twenty-two years old. Had put on his navy work clothes three weeks ago, when he came back from service. They hung too big on him. He was holding the clamp under the lower edge of the post with one hand. The clamp was rusted. He was just checking it.
"Eiji-san," said Kenta, "hold the motor line, I'll look at it from below."
He held it.
The wave went out.

The wave went out — not a big one — not the kind that walk for hours after a typhoon — a small one, stealthily small — and it came back sooner than it should have — and Kenta — Kenta with two hands on the rusted clamp — Kenta, who said something — Kenta — Kenta —
The hand opened.

He saw it open. Saw the fingers — they were in sea salt — and the knuckles — which the water showed him for a second when the fingers were no longer on the clamp. He stood on the planks. The planks under him rocked two degrees. His right foot did not want to step.
Kenta cried out once. Once. From under the water.
He counted — not then — but afterward, many years afterward — and it always came to the same number. Forty seconds.
Forty seconds he stood.
Then the water came again — and there was no more cry.
He stood on the planks.

He knew that this was a room. He knew it in the part of himself that still knew how to tell. He knew it because Typhoon Vicki had ended in ninety-eight, and that was why Kenta could not be standing behind the post in his navy work clothes — because Kenta was at Cape Takashima on the third day, under a sheet — and Kenta's mother — his aunt on his mother's side — had asked him, Eiji, to tell her how it had been — and he had said, "I was behind the awning, making tea. I did not see anything."
He knew.
Knowing did not help.
The planks under him rocked. The lantern on the right flickered. Kenta stood behind the post.
"Eiji-san," said Kenta, "hold the motor line."
He held it.
The wave went out.
He no longer counted how many times.
The voice came from behind his left shoulder.
Not loud. Not close. It entered his ear not as sound, but as warmth enters a palm from a heated kettle.

He did not turn. He had nowhere to turn — behind his shoulder there was nothing — and still the voice was from there. He kept his eyes on the rusted clamp and on Kenta's fingers holding it — and thought, very quietly, that the fingers should not be so young. The body does not remember the fingers of forty years ago. Something else remembers them.
The wave went out.
The fingers opened.
He did not jump.
The room shook. Not with motion. With a shutter. The way an image shakes when a frame skips between two.
He stood on the planks.
Kenta held the clamp. The wave went out. The hand opened.
He set his right foot on the edge.

The pier under him rocked. The lantern on the right flickered. Far off, past the mole, where the water should have been — was not water. Was black gravel. He saw it for a second — when the light of the hanging lantern went through the gap between planks — and saw small stones — dry, sharp — and saw that they were a meter below the planks, no more.

He knew. He knew, in the part of himself, that this was not Otaru harbor, and that under the planks there was no water. The knowledge lay in him the way the wet salt lay on the boards — tightly — and did not move.
The voice behind his left shoulder:
He jumped.

Not into water. Into gravel. His knee struck a sharp stone — the right kneecap — the one he had spared for forty years. Pain went up his thigh into his lower back. He grabbed hold of a metal thing that was sticking out from the gap — a rod — the same one Kenta had held — and pulled.
The rod came out easily.

Along with the rod, out from under the planks came a body. Not a body. A rag doll in navy work clothes, filled with something heavy — sand, or a wet rag — the size of a person. The head — without a face. The hair — attached in a bunch. The clothes had soaked in sea salt the way real work clothes soak in real water.
He held the doll by the waist. The doll's left shoulder lay on his right shoulder — heavy — and the sea salt smelled of sea salt.
The voice behind his left shoulder said:

p.emphasis: — 見て。あなたは彼を救った.

section.p: He looked.
He cried.
He had not cried then, in ninety-eight — and he did not cry now — but something was in his throat — and in that small part of himself he thought — that he had saved him.
He did not know how long had passed.

He was sitting on the planks. The doll lay beside him, face — the one in which there was no face — to the sky. The lantern flickered. The sea knocked under the boards — but no longer knocked — now it was a dry sound — the knock of gravel under a load — but he did not hear it. He heard the water.
He knew he had saved him.
He knew it with the same knowing by which a man knows he has eaten breakfast — not remembering the menu, but only that fullness had been. Fullness had been. Rescue had been. Kenta was alive.
Kenta alive. Kenta on his mother's side, who worked on a launch at Otaru — the same one — who every July came to the izakaya Kingyo with his wife and son and ordered tofu steak.
Kenta alive.
He did not remember now whether Kenta had a wife. Did not remember whether there had been a son. But rescue had been. That was what mattered.
He turned his head.
In the corner of the planks, where the step went down to the mooring post — between two boards — stood a low black tray.
On the tray, a clay teapot the color of wet slate. One white cup, slightly crooked at the rim. A thin thread of steam rose from the spout in a patient, even line.
The tray did not belong on Pier Three in Otaru harbor. On Pier Three there had never been teapots. He knew this the way he knew the color of his mother's kitchen table.
He recognized the tray.
Not that one. But that. One like it had stood on the table in their kitchen — his and Michiko's — when Michiko still — when Michiko —
The name did not come.

The form came. A thin shoulder. A thin hand that held the teapot by the handle. Hair gathered into a knot at the nape. The taste of which tea — Asagiri — and the thin tartness — and the way she said, "Eiji-san, the tap water today isn't right."
The name did not come.
He looked at the tray.
The voice behind his left shoulder said nothing. The voice knew that one could wait.
He turned away from the tray.

He looked at the doll in the navy work clothes — at its hair fastened in a bunch — at the waxy skin where waxy skin might be — and thought, in that small part of himself, that the name of the woman from the kitchen would come later.
Later meant later.
The room shook.
He stood on the planks. Kenta held the clamp. The wave went out. The hand opened.
He set his right foot on the edge.
The voice behind his left shoulder:
He jumped.
He pulled the doll out from under the planks. His knee no longer hurt — it knew this motion — it knew it from the first time. He laid the doll on the planks. He sat beside it. He breathed evenly.
He knew it was the twenty-seventh of September. He knew it was the night after the typhoon. He knew he had saved Kenta in ninety-eight.
He knew.
He looked into the corner.
The tray stood. The steam rose.

p.emphasis: — あなたは忘れたのではない.

section.p: The voice waited. The steam went up in a thin line.
He nodded.
He did not know to whom he was nodding.
He sat on the planks — and somewhere in him — in that dry small part into which he had for a long time put nothing — something stirred — and fell silent.
The lantern on the right flickered.
The wave went out again.
Kenta held the clamp.
He stood up.

p.emphasis: "He left it twenty years ago — I don't even remember the face now."

section.subtitle: Chapter Ten
section.p: The road to Sounkyo went up in switchbacks, and the snow lay along the shoulder in a narrow white band — not the first November snow that would melt by noon, but already dense — the kind that gathers in the mountains a month earlier than in Sapporo.
Sasaki drove. Yukio sat on the right, holding a folder on his knees — thin — with two photocopies and one sheet of notes. The wipers went once every ten seconds.
"Two more hours," said Sasaki.
"I know."
"Did you sleep."
"No."
She did not argue.

He looked through the side glass at the slope on the left, where the pines stood evenly at the same distance from one another — a planting, not a natural forest — and thought about how the monastery Reisen-ji had not been on the list of his case three weeks ago. Had not been on the list at all. He had no grounds to go there, except one line from Toshi across the table in the detention center: "Find where he read."
That was nothing. You couldn't build a warrant from that.

But Kenji had pulled three entries from the 5channel archive — under the handle kazan-no-monogatari — and by style they were Toshi's before the monastery. In those three entries a library was mentioned, and an abbot, and a sheaf of haiku with no name, "left, they said, twenty years ago."
Yukio had a photocopy of this text in the folder.
If it was the same sheaf — and if the hand in it was the same — then the Doll Maker had been at Reisen-ji. Before Toshi. Perhaps long before.
Sasaki shifted gears.
"What's the abbot's name?" she asked.
"Gensho. Seventy-two. At the monastery since ninety-three."
"Memory?"
"By the local paper — clear. Gives an interview about haiku once every two years."
Sasaki nodded. Yukio knew she had memorized it.
The monastery stood on the mountainside, small, with two irimoya roofs — and a third roof, over the library, was covered in fresh copper tile not yet darkened — a recent repair.
Yukio looked at it and said nothing.

A young monk in a gray robe met them in the genkan and showed the place for shoes. Sasaki's shoes stood straight; Yukio set his down two centimeters crooked and did not straighten them. His feet in socks found the warm floor — under the tatami went heating.
"Gensho-roshi is waiting," said the young monk.
He led them down a corridor that smelled of cedar smoke and old paper. The shoji doors at the end were thin — they glowed amber.

Gensho sat on a cushion by a low table, with two cups of tea already poured. He was thin, with short-cropped gray hair — hands on his knees — and looked at them with that calm that was not indifference but a practice earned across forty years of morning silence.
"Kurosawa-keibu," he said. "Sasaki-junsa."
"Junsa-bucho," the young monk corrected quietly.
"Forgive me," Gensho said, without the intonation of shame. "Sasaki-junsa-bucho. Sit."
Sasaki sat.
Yukio sat.
He took the cup in his palms — did not drink — held it the way one holds a cup to understand what clay it is made of. The clay was local, Ashibetsu — he knew by the weight. He set the cup down.
"We won't be long," he said.
"I'm in no hurry," Gensho said.
That was not politeness. That was a statement of fact.
Yukio opened the folder. Took out the photocopy of five lines of haiku and put it on the low table — text toward Gensho.
Gensho took the sheet. Held it at a distance, brought it closer, moved it away again. Read slowly.
Yukio waited.
Sasaki did not look at the sheet. She looked at Gensho's hands — at the fingers — at how the fingers lay on the sheet — and whether they would tremble if the text was familiar.
The fingers did not tremble. The fingers lay.
"A good hand," said Gensho. "Not mine."
"We know it isn't yours," said Yukio. "We want to know whether this hand ever lived in your library."
Gensho looked at him.
"In a library many hands live," he said. "Some stay. Some don't."
"This one — stayed?"
Gensho looked at the sheet again. Not longer — the same amount of time — but Yukio noticed that Sasaki tilted her head slightly. That meant she had seen something he had not.
"Perhaps," said Gensho. "Come."
The library was long and low — three rows of open cedar shelves — and at the end a separate niche with thin sheaves tied with silk cord. It smelled of dry grass and rice paste.
Gensho ran a finger along the third row from the bottom. The fingers knew the way — it was clear — they were not searching. They came to one sheaf, stopped, took it out.
Thin. The cover, light ochre washi, no writing. The cord, dark red, slightly faded.
Gensho laid the sheaf on the low table by the window. Untied the cord. Opened it.
Yukio leaned in.

The first line of the first page was the same as on the photocopy. The same hand. The same wide pauses between the ideograms — the same characteristic elongated right stroke in the character 冬 (fuyu — "winter").
He said nothing.
Sasaki beside him was silent too. She knew.
Gensho turned the page. The second — different haiku, the same hand. The third. The fourth. Twelve pages, thirty-four verses.
"Who left it?" asked Yukio. "Was there a name?"
"There was a name," said Gensho. "On the first cover, inside. It's rubbed off now. I don't remember exactly."
"Who would have rubbed it off?"
"Anyone. We don't keep the library under lock and key."
Yukio looked at him.
Gensho held the look.
"You remember him," said Yukio.
"I remember the hand."
"Remember the hand, don't remember the name."

"I remember," said Gensho, "that he lived here for several winters. Was not a novice — did not want the tonsure. He was, how would I put it, a guest. We have guests sometimes. Those who ask permission to stay a while."
Sasaki shifted a little.
"A novice," she said.
Gensho looked at her.
"You said, 'not a novice,'" said Sasaki. "You paused before the word. Half a second."
Gensho smiled. Not with pleasure. Calmly.
"You are attentive, Sasaki-junsa-bucho."
"That is my work."

"Then I will answer you honestly," said Gensho. "The guest tried to be a novice. Tried for two years. Did not endure. Or endured, and understood that he did not want to. Left somewhere at the beginning of the two-thousands — perhaps two thousand one, perhaps two thousand two. I was not abbot then, but the second monk. The abbot then, the late Yoshida-roshi, knew him better."
"When did Yoshida-roshi die?"
"Two thousand ten."
Yukio was silent.
"Do you remember his appearance?" asked Sasaki.
"Not closely."
"Approximately."
Gensho thought.

"Medium height," he said. "Thin. Hands — I remember the hands. Long fingers. Left-handed, it seemed — wrote with the right, but ate with the left. I was not in conversation with him. He spoke little."
"The name," Yukio said again, quietly.
Gensho was silent.
Yukio did not press. He knew this kind of silence — when a person does not remember, and when a person remembers but will not say. This was the second. But it was not hostile. It was habit.
"Did he make a donation to the library?" asked Sasaki.
"Yes."
"Anything else?"
"To the roof," said Gensho. "Some seven years ago. A significant one."
"To that roof," said Sasaki — not as a question, but as a statement — "over the library."
"Yes."
"Through what company?"
Gensho looked at her for a long moment.
"I don't remember," he said. "That is the treasurer's decision."
"The treasurer at the monastery?"
"Yes. He is in Sapporo this week."
"We'll call him."
"Please."
Yukio kept his fingers on the sheaf.
"Can we take this for photographing?" he asked.
"I cannot give it to you," said Gensho. "This is the monastery's property."
"I'm not asking to give it. I'm asking permission to take pictures. Here. We brought equipment."
Gensho nodded.
"The young monk will help," he said. "I'll leave you."
He stood.
"Gensho-roshi," said Yukio when he was already at the door.
Gensho turned.
"You know why we ask."
Gensho looked at him.
"I don't know," he said. "But I knew that someone would come. That knowing came to me long ago. I carried it."
"When?"
"Fifteen years ago," said Gensho, "perhaps twelve."
Yukio was silent.
"You have come late," said Gensho. "I am not angry with you."
He went out.
The shoji doors closed softly.
Sasaki stood over the sheaf.
"That is one hand," she said.
"One."
"With the 5channel photocopy?"
"One."
She set up the camera.
"Kurosawa-san," she said, without lifting her head. "He has not forgotten the name."
"He hasn't."
"He won't say?"
"He will tell the treasurer. The treasurer will produce some paper in which the name will not be. But there will be a date of donation. And there will be a company."
Sasaki nodded.
She took the pictures, page by page, evenly, and the lamp over the table gave off a quiet electric hum.

Yukio stood by the window. He looked at the roof — new — copper — and at how the copper lay on the rafters — and at how the repair had been done well, very well — the way repair is done by people who know how to do repair.
Yuki-Kogei, he thought.
He did not say it aloud.
He knew.
In the car, on the drive back, Sasaki turned off the radio.
"He was here before Toshi," she said.
"Nineteen years before," said Yukio. "Perhaps more."
"Then Toshi came here in two thousand twenty-one."
"Yes."
"And this guest left at the beginning of the two-thousands."
"Yes."
"Then they could not have met."
"Not here."
Sasaki looked at him.
"You think they met somewhere else."

"I think," said Yukio, "that the monastery is not a meeting place. It is a place to which the Doll Maker directed Toshi. Directed him so that Toshi would come here twenty years later and see what he had left."
"The sheaf."
"And the roof."
She kept her hands on the wheel. The road went down, toward Sounkyo, and the snow on the shoulder was grayer now.
"He recruited Toshi in advance," she said.
"He recruited Toshi the way one plants a tree. You put down a seed. You come back in twenty years."
Sasaki was silent for a long time.
"Kurosawa-san," she said at last.
"Yes."
"How many seeds are still lying?"
Yukio did not answer.
He looked through the side glass at the slope on the right, where the pines stood evenly at the same distance from one another — a planting, not a natural forest.
An hour and a half later they stopped at the parking lot beside the Asahikawa-Daisetsu service station. Sasaki went to the toilet. Yukio got out of the car — to stretch his leg — and lit a cigarette.
One cigarette per case. This was the first in this one.
He smoked slowly. The taste was foreign — he had not smoked for a year — and the throat remembered worse than the mind thought.
He dialed Kenji.
"Kurosawa-san."
"Kenji. Reisen-do Sangyo. Sounkyo. Ceramics, tea sets."
"Written down."
"Find every invoice they issued to the monastery Reisen-ji over the last ten years. Especially large ones. And especially on the roof."
"Large ones on the roof," Kenji repeated. "I'm on it."

"One more thing. Find the list of monastery guests. Not novices. Guests. Those the monastery fed and did not tonsure. Nineties, two-thousands. It'll be in the tax office — if there was a stipend donation."
"Kurosawa-san, I'll be honest. This can be found, but it's twenty hours minimum. That's a hundred and sixty thousand yen."
"Do it."
"All right."
Yukio pressed "end." Drew on the cigarette once more. Put it out in the ashtray at the parking lot — metal, with rain in it and a black film from old ash.
Sasaki came back.
"You called Kenji," she said.
"Yes."
"You didn't wait for me to sit down."
"I wanted to catch it before I forgot the abbot's exact word."
"Which."
"'The guest tried to be a novice.'"
"Yes."
"'Tried for two years.'"
Sasaki nodded.
"'Did not endure. Or endured, and understood that he did not want to.'"
"He said 'or,'" said Sasaki. "That's important. He offered two versions. He did not know which was the real one."
"Which means," said Yukio, "that he did not know because the guest did not tell him. And did not know because the late Yoshida-roshi, who did know, had reason to keep silent."
"Or the guest left," said Sasaki, "and Yoshida-roshi a few years later came to think it had not been 'did not endure' but 'decided not to be.' That's a difference."
"A difference."
Sasaki got in behind the wheel.

"Kurosawa-san," she said, "and what if this person, who spent two years trying to be a novice in the mountains, and did not become one, and disappeared for twenty years, and then came back and made the roof, is not the Doll Maker?"
"Then who?"

"Someone the Doll Maker knew. Someone who was at the monastery before the Doll Maker. And who left the sheaf in the library. And whose haiku Toshi later read on 5channel — and did not know it was the same hand — until the Doll Maker showed him."
Yukio was silent.
"You think," he said, "that the Doll Maker was not the one who went to Reisen-ji."
"I think," said Sasaki, "that he perhaps learned from the one who did. And that this is one more person who may still be alive. Or dead. But who exists on the diagram."
Yukio closed his eyes for two seconds.
The diagram was growing. He saw it in his head — and it was not a tree with one root — it was mycelium — with many points that came up to the surface.
"Kenji," he said into the emptiness. "A month's worth of work ahead."
Sasaki turned the ignition.
The car pulled out.

The road went down toward Sounkyo, and the snow on the shoulder was grayer now, and Yukio was thinking about the person with the long fingers — left-handed — who ate with the left and wrote with the right — and about how this person, if still alive, would now be — by Gensho's reckoning — around sixty.
That was not the Doll Maker.
The Doll Maker was younger.
That was someone's teacher.

p.emphasis: "Eight thousand an hour plus hardware. No name of mine in the reports."

section.subtitle: Chapter Eleven
section.p: The café on the ground floor of the Susukino business center was the kind you go into not to drink coffee but to wait something out. Always fifty percent of the seats empty. You could always sit so as to see the door.

Yukio came in twelve minutes early. Ordered a short coffee — not from desire, but from ritual — and sat in the corner from which he could see the door, the stairs, and the exit into the back corridor. He put a thin notebook in front of him — not to write in, but so that something would lie in front of him.
At sixteen zero five the door opened.
Yukio did not lift his head.

The young man who came in was thin, one meter seventy-two, in a black hoodie with the hood thrown up and a light windbreaker over it. Glasses in round black frames. On his shoulders — a rucksack. In his right hand — a carrier.
The carrier was soft, dark gray, with a mesh window. In the window, a gray cat's face.
Yukio looked at the cat once. And relaxed his shoulders slightly. Those were the first shoulders that had relaxed in him in a week.
The young man came to the table. Looked at Yukio. Looked at the second chair. Sat.
Put the carrier on the floor by the wall, in shadow, so the waitress wouldn't look at it.
"Yamada-san," said Yukio.
"Kenji."
"Yukio Kurosawa. Keibu."

"You are not the first to find me," said Kenji. "I saw you three days ago on Chiebukuro. You were asking about the 5channel archives and doing it too specifically — not the way someone asks who is learning, and not the way someone asks who is looking to resell. I thought: who is this. So I answered when you wrote. That you were police I understood by your second reply in the exchange. You correctly named the internal 5channel API but made one mistake — used the old field timestamp_client instead of edited_at. That's how an amateur writes who has learned quickly — or a person who doesn't write scripts every day, but knows which circle to search in."
"And how did you understand I was police and not a journalist?"
"A journalist asks for it cheaper. You wrote about payment right away."
Yukio nodded.
"I apologize," he said, "for the cover. I had no other way to reach you that would not have gone through the department."
"I understand."
Kenji raised a hand. The waitress came over. He ordered coffee with no sugar. His voice was even, without intonation — not indifferent, just even.
Yukio waited for the waitress to move off.
Kenji lowered his hand into the carrier and touched the cat's ear with a finger. The cat closed its eyes. Opened them.
"Miso," said Kenji. "Last three weeks with me. He's stressed, strangers came to fix the air conditioning. I don't want to leave him."
Yukio nodded.
He saw, from the side, that Kenji was not timid. Thin, quiet — yes — but not timid. He had that particular quietness of people who work at night and count each word the way others count money.
"Kenji-san," said Yukio.
"Just Kenji."

"Kenji. I need to map a corporate network of four Japanese legal entities registered to dead directors. Each firm exists legally, pays tax, has held a bank account since two thousand eight. Through them houses are bought, electricity is paid for, furniture is ordered. I need to find how these four firms are connected to each other — and whether there is a common point between them. For example, a mailing address, a phone number, an IP, a signature, a bank."
"How much time will I have."
"A week."
"How many victims."
Yukio looked at him.
"Two are missing," he said. "One more will be missing by Friday."
Kenji nodded.
"And one girl," said Yukio, "went missing three years ago. She may still have time."
Kenji was silent. Not the silence that hides — the silence that counts.
The waitress brought the coffee. Kenji took the cup with two fingers by the rim and took one sip.
"I read about Kamishiroi," he said. "Not pompously. You did not give interviews yourself."
"I did not."
"I thought it would be either a dull story or a bare sensation. It turned out to be neither."
"I didn't come to be liked."
"I know. I came to explain why I didn't stand up and leave."
Yukio waited.
"Now for terms," said Kenji. "Eight thousand yen an hour. Hardware costs on top, with receipts."
"Good."
"No name of mine in the reports. I am 'external consultant,' in the documents — my freelance company."
"Good."
"No meetings with the press. If journalists see me with you even once — I disappear that same evening. I won't return the money."
"I won't show you."
"One more thing."
Yukio waited.

"If at some moment," said Kenji, "I tell you I don't want to any more — you will not press. You will not appeal to the girl, to the victims, to your boss, to anything. You'll just say 'understood' and we part."
"Understood," said Yukio.
Kenji smiled a little. Barely at all. The way a person smiles when another person has said the word at the right time — and added nothing to it.
"Then," he said, "we can begin."
"From tomorrow?"

"From today. Send me everything you have. Firms, dates, any invoices, any emails you could pull. Name of the contact person in each firm, even if that's someone long dead. I want to look at this tonight. Tomorrow at ten in the morning we meet, I'll tell you where to start."
"At the office?"
Kenji thought.

"Not at the office," he said. "First — here. I want to look at your team — that later — when I understand the work exists. I don't want to walk into a police station for no reason. I'm not one of those who like the police."
"Neither am I," said Yukio.
Kenji looked at him for a long moment.
"You just said," he said, "something I did not expect."
"I didn't want to please you. I said what I think."
"I believe you."
Yukio nodded.
Kenji reached into the carrier, took from his pocket a pouch of dried fish, and pushed a strip through the mesh window. The cat took it.
"What happens with him tomorrow?" asked Yukio.
"I take him with me. He sits quietly."
"You don't mind," said Kenji, "cats in the office?"
"I mind many things in the office. Cats aren't on the list."
"Then we're agreed."
Kenji finished his coffee. Stood up. Took out a thin wallet, put a thousand yen on the table.
"No need," said Yukio.
"There is need. This is my coffee. When I start work, you'll pay for coffee. Today I'm not yet working."
Yukio did not argue.
Kenji lifted the carrier.
Kenji started for the door.
Yukio stayed.
He sat for a long time. The coffee in his hands was cold.
He took out his phone. Wrote to Sasaki: "Found him. I'll introduce him tomorrow at ten."
"Good. What kind of person."
"Calm. Cat with him."
"A cat is a good sign."
Yukio did not smile, but something in his chest unclenched by a fine half-millimeter — for the first time that week — and he put the phone screen down and stood.
Outside, a fine snow was falling. The first of November in Sapporo.
He buttoned his coat.
He knew that tomorrow at ten Kenji would come on time. Knew it the way he knew the color of his mother's kitchen table.
He walked out into the street.

The next morning at nine fifty-seven Kenji was standing by reception with the carrier and rucksack. The duty sergeant, Yoshida, raised an eyebrow — but said nothing — because Yukio had already come down and nodded.
"Yamada-san is with me."
"Consultant guest?"
"Yes."
"The cat too?"
"The cat too."
Yoshida opened the service doors.

Yukio led Kenji down the corridor to the third floor — past the poster "Prevention of Domestic Violence" — past the cooler with warm water — past the door with the sign "Missing Persons Unit" — and brought him into his office.

Sasaki was already sitting at the side desk. On the desk was an open MacBook, a cup of green tea, and a photocopy of a Hokkaido map with four black squares — the preliminary sketch of what Kenji was to turn into a proper map.
Kenji put the carrier down in the corner by the radiator. Miso yawned loudly.
Sasaki lifted her eyes. Looked at the cat for two long beats. Then at Kenji. Then at Yukio.
"Kurosawa-san," she said, "you warned me about the person. Not about the cat."
"The cat was unforeseen," said Yukio.
"He's not a problem," said Sasaki. "He's nice."
Kenji nodded.
He set his MacBook Air on the corner desk Yukio had cleared for him the evening before. Plugged in the power, the external SSD, and began opening browser tabs.
"I'll give you the starting data," said Yukio. "Each of the four firms has a corporate number. Here."
He put on Kenji's desk a sheet with four numbers, four addresses, four names of deceased directors, and dates of registration.
Kenji looked. Took a pen. Corrected the fourth digit of one number — Yukio had miscopied it from the registry.
"Thank you," said Yukio.
"It happens."
Kenji began.

The keyboard tapped evenly — not fast — evenly. Yukio stood at the window, looking at the square in front of the department, where Ogawa's service Toyota Crown stood. Ogawa was at a briefing at the prefecture today.
"Kenji," said Yukio, not turning.
"Yes."
"One more question. Not about work."
"Go ahead."
"You live alone. The cat is with you. You sleep under a weighted blanket."
Kenji stopped typing.
"How do you know."
"I saw laundry-instruction stickers on the things in the carrier yesterday. Those come with weighted blankets after washing."
Kenji was silent for a few seconds. Then smiled a little.
"Are you testing me."
"No. I'm talking with you."
"Then, honestly. Yes. Nine kilograms. Helps with the fact that I live alone and the cat doesn't weigh nine kilograms."
Sasaki at the side desk tilted her head slightly. Yukio looked at her. She said nothing. She had remembered.
"All right," said Yukio. "Let's work."
"Let's work."
Kenji started typing again.
Yukio sat down at his desk. Opened the folder. Took out the photocopy of the haiku sheaf from Reisen-ji — the one Sasaki had photographed yesterday. Put it in front of him. Took a pencil.
The first verse was about snow on the rafters of an old temple.
He did not hurry.

He knew that Kenji would work until evening, and that Sasaki would call the treasurer at ten, and that Miso would sleep in the carrier by the radiator, and that Ogawa would come back from the briefing at four, and that this would be — perhaps — the week when the work would begin to move.
Yukio held the pencil over the verse.
Miso in the carrier sighed.
The office smelled of coffee, of cedar from the photocopy, and a little of dried fish from Kenji's pocket.
Yukio did not notice when he relaxed his shoulders a second time.

p.emphasis: The third of February, eleven forty in the morning, the year she was fifteen.

section.subtitle: Chapter Twelve
section.p: The fluorescent lamp over the couch gave a white light without shadow — that particular white that has two shades — the upper cold and the lower with a barely visible green — and in which skin never looks the way it is.

The room was two by three meters. The walls were white, smooth, under oil-based paint. The right wall was a cabinet with two glass doors, behind which stood metal boxes labeled in small handwriting in two rows. The left wall was a concertina screen, half folded. Directly in front of it, a narrow window with ribbed glass. Beyond the window — a light emptiness. No clouds, no line, no roof of a neighboring building. Only white.
Aoi sat on the couch.

The couch was covered with a paper sheet the color of cream ice-cream — it crackled when Aoi shifted by two millimeters. Aoi did not move. Her legs hung from the couch — she was in a white hospital gown with ties — and her feet in white socks touched the linoleum. The linoleum was cold.
She was fifteen years old. Her body knew that without her.

A metal-legged table stood to the left. On it, a metal tray. In the tray, three things: a plastic syringe in a sterile wrapper, a cotton swab, and a disposable towel with the clinic's logo. The logo was unfamiliar to her — pink, in the shape of a crescent — and she knew it was the logo of the Niigata Woman's clinic, and she knew the clinic was at Kamioshima 3-chome, and she knew she had come here on bus number seventeen, and had told her mother she was going to a school competition.
She knew.
The knowing lay in her evenly — did not burn — it was there the way a certificate lies in a folder.
The door of the room opened.
The door was not shoji. It was white, with a metal handle on a spring — a procedure-room door — and it opened quietly, on well-oiled hinges.
The nurse came in.
Aoi lifted her eyes.

The nurse was in a white knee-length coat, white trousers, white slip-on shoes. On the head, a white cap with a double fold. On the face, a surgical mask — white, covered nose and mouth entirely — and over the mask, large glasses in a white plastic frame, lenses slightly tinted, of the kind given out in dental offices to keep splashes from the eyes.
Above the glasses, a narrow band of forehead — and hair, also under the cap — not a strand outside.
Aoi did not see the face.
Aoi saw a silhouette.

The silhouette was tall — a head taller than she was — and the shoulders were wide — not the wide of a woman — but those shoulders that do not fit into a woman's coat armhole the way they should. The coat was stretched on the shoulders. The seam on the right shoulder — slightly parted.
Aoi did not notice this in the first second. In the fifth she noticed it. Did not think about it.
The nurse came up to the couch.
"Nakamura Aoi-san?" said the nurse.

The voice was female, neutral — that calm, friendly voice nurses have in clinics of this type — where many come alone and everyone is afraid. The voice went through the mask — but there was something else in it too — a small, thin, almost imperceptible electric note — the kind that happens when a voice is processed — when one frequency is cut and another added.
The note was on the "s" in the word "Aoi-san." Thin. One.
Aoi heard it. Forgot it half a second later.
"Yes," said Aoi.
"You are alone?"
"Yes."
"Your mother did not come?"
"No. She doesn't know."
"All right."
The nurse sat down on a low round stool on wheels beside the couch. Took a clipboard from the tray. A pen. Wrote.
"Allow me a few questions," she said.
"Yes."
"How many weeks of pregnancy?"
"Eight."
"You are certain?"
"The test was three weeks ago. The second one a week ago."
"What did it show?"
"Two lines. Both times."
"Last period?"
"Eighth of December."
The nurse wrote.
The pen went along the paper with that particular dry sound — the one that happens when the pen is good and the paper poor.
"The child's father," said the nurse, "does he know?"
"No."
"Do you want him to know?"
"No."
"Do you want the procedure medically or surgically?"
"Medically."
"You understand that this is two doses of tablets at intervals of forty-eight hours, and that the pain may be significant?"
"I understand."
"Do you want to think about it?"
Aoi looked at her.

The voice asked what had not been asked on that day. On that day — that real third of February two thousand eleven — the nurse had not asked "do you want to think about it." The nurse had simply given the tablet and watched Aoi swallow it and said "come back in forty-eight hours." It was eleven forty in the morning. It was carried out. It was finished.
"You can go to Doutor by the station," said the nurse. "Order a melon soda. Sit a while. Come back in an hour, if you're ready. In a week, if you need."
Aoi was silent.

Aoi knew that on that day she had gone to Doutor after the procedure and had ordered a melon soda, and had not drunk it, and had returned to the station and taken the bus to her grandmother's, because she could not meet her mother in the evening.
The knowing lay in her.
The knowing did not move.
"I'll think," said Aoi.
"Good," said the nurse. "Do you want to say anything more?"
Aoi thought.
The word she had written that night in her notebook — and never opened that page again after — came of its own.
"Haru," she said.
"What?"
"If it were a child. The name. I already made it up."

The nurse tilted her head slightly. That gesture was not feminine. It was feminine to 80 percent — and 20 percent it was male — a light, very light preponderance of the right shoulder — the way people tilt their head who have worn a uniform for many years.
"A good name," said the nurse.
The voice said it warmly.
The warmth was not a woman's warmth.
Aoi did not notice.
"Haru," Aoi repeated. "Spring."
"Yes."
"He'll be born in spring. If I —"
She did not finish.
The nurse said nothing. The nurse put the clipboard back on the tray. Stood. Went to the door.
"I'll leave you," she said. "You can lie down. Or sit. As you wish. I'll be back in fifteen minutes."
The door closed.
Aoi sat.
The room shook.
Not with movement. With a shutter. The way an image shakes when a frame skips between two.
Aoi sat on the couch. The paper sheet crackled. The table stood to the left. The tray, the syringe in its packet, the swab, the towel with the pink crescent.
The door opened.
The nurse came in.
"Nakamura Aoi-san?" said the nurse.
The voice was female. Neutral. Friendly. The warm electric note on the "s."
"Yes," said Aoi.
"You've thought?"
Aoi thought.
"I am not going to do this," said Aoi.
The nurse tilted her head 80 and 20.
"You are certain?"
"Yes."
"You understand this is a decision for life?"
"Yes."
"You will tell your mother?"
"I will tell her."
"You will call Koji?"
"I will call him."
"You will keep the name?"
"Haru."
"Haru," said the nurse. "Beautiful."

The nurse gave her a hand. Aoi stood up. The nurse walked her to the door. The door opened. Beyond the door was the corridor of the clinic — but the corridor was not that corridor — the corridor was warm, with cream wallpaper — and at the end of the corridor Aoi's mother stood. The mother was in a black coat. The mother was smiling. The mother said: "You did the right thing."
The room shook.
Aoi sat on the couch. The paper sheet crackled. The table stood to the left.
The door opened.
The nurse came in.
"Nakamura Aoi-san?" said the nurse.
"Yes," said Aoi.
"You've thought?"
Aoi knew.
Aoi knew — in the small, tiny, ever-smaller part of herself — that this was already the twenty-fourth time the door had opened. Or the forty-third. She could not count. The number scattered.
She knew that Haru was the name she had made up in a dream, and that she had given it to no one, and that there was no child — because there was no child — because —
The knowing scattered.

Haru was. Haru lived in Niigata, with grandmother, because Aoi worked in Sapporo — and Haru was fifteen — and Haru played the cello. Haru came to visit her on holidays twice a year. Haru liked miso soup.
Haru was.
Aoi looked at the nurse.
The nurse stood there with the same silhouette. Shoulders — wide. The seam on the right shoulder — slightly parted. The surgical mask — white. The glasses — tinted.
Behind the tinted glasses, for a second Aoi saw the eyes.
One eye.

Not two. The right one reflected green from the fluorescent lamp. The left was hidden by the shadow of the frame. The right eye was dark, calm — with that calm that does not calm — and it looked at Aoi without curiosity — the way a person looks at work — at work they know how to do.
The eye did not blink.
Aoi lowered her eyes.

She lowered her eyes to the metal tray, to the syringe, to the swab, to the towel with the pink crescent — and beyond the tray — in the corner between the table and the wall — on the floor — stood a low black tray.
The tray lacquered. On it, a clay teapot the color of wet slate. One white cup, slightly crooked at the rim. A thin thread of steam.
The tray did not belong in the procedure room of the Niigata Woman's clinic. Teapots were not kept in procedure rooms.
Aoi looked at the tray.
The thin thread of steam rose evenly.
Something in Aoi — in that dry, tiny, ever-smaller part — recognized the tray.
She could not have said from where. Could not remember whose teapot. Could not name a name — neither female nor male — neither mother's nor her own.
But the tray was familiar.
Aoi cried.

Not loudly. Not at once. First one tear went from the right eye down the cheek and stopped at the corner of her mouth. Then a second. Then she breathed out — and her shoulders lifted themselves once, and dropped — and after that she cried without shoulders, quietly, with open eyes.
She did not know why.
The nurse stood in the doorway. Did not move. The one green eye behind the tinted lens watched.
The nurse said nothing.
The nurse waited — exactly twenty seconds — and turned — and went out — and closed the door.
Aoi sat on the couch and cried at the tray.
Haru was.
Haru would be.
The tray stood.
The steam rose in a thin, patient line.
The fluorescent lamp over the couch gave a white light without shadow.

p.emphasis: "He does not keep one address. He keeps one pocket."

section.subtitle: Chapter Thirteen
section.p: Kenji brought the printout in a black plastic tube — the kind architects carry plans in — and stood the tube upright by the door of the office, the way one stands an umbrella in a genkan. Miso in the carrier was silent. It was ten forty-eight in the morning.
Yukio sat at his desk. Sasaki at the side desk, on the right. Endo stood in the doorway with two paper cups of coffee — did not come in — was looking to see if she could.
"Come in, Endo-san," said Yukio.
Endo came in. Set one cup in front of Yukio, the other in front of Sasaki. Kenji had his own Boss Coffee from the vending machine in the corridor — the can stood on his corner desk, still cold.
"All right," said Kenji. "Unrolling it."

He opened the tube. Drew out a sheet rolled into a tube — not an ordinary A1 but larger — a meter by a meter and a half — printed on a plotter. Unrolled it on the conference table in the middle of the room.
The table was small. The printout hung off the edges by fifteen centimeters on each side.
"Small table," said Kenji. "I knew it would be. I brought tape."

He weighted the four corners with small metal weights of the kind sold in stationery shops. The table turned out to be the dinner table of the Kurosawa family when Kurosawa Yukio and Kurosawa Ren had sat on one side and their mother on the other — only it was in the office — and on it lay a network.
Yukio stood over the table.
Sasaki stood on the right.
Endo — on the left, holding her coffee.
Kenji stood at the foot of the table, facing the map.
"Four legal entities," he said.
He set an index finger on the four squares in the four corners of the printout.

"Upper left: Yuki-Kogei LLC. Head office, Sapporo Chuo. Restoration of traditional architecture. Director — Tanaka Hideo, died in Otaru, September two thousand eight, kidney failure. The daughters who might have inherited — two — neither knows her father was director of anything."
Yukio nodded. He had known that.

"Upper right: Kita-Michi Zaimoku KK. Ashibetsu. Trade in cedar timber. Director — Sasaoka Yoshiro, died in Ashibetsu, February two thousand eleven, heart attack. Forest. Taiga. Was a local mountain ranger for thirty-seven years."
"Forest," said Sasaki. "Taiga."
"Yes," said Kenji. "Through this firm all the construction material comes into the network. Cedar, Japanese larch, bamboo for interior partitions."
He set his finger lower.

"Lower left: Reisen-do Sangyo KK. Sounkyo. Goods for the tea ceremony. Ceramics, tableware, teapots, lacquered trays. Director — Oshima Kiko, potter, died in Sounkyo, April two thousand seven, pancreatic cancer."
Yukio put a hand on this square.
He did not look at anyone.
"Reisen-do," he said quietly.
"Yes," said Kenji.
"Reisen-ji."
"I thought about it," said Kenji. "One root. One mountain. You spoke yesterday about the monastery. I don't think the coincidence is accidental."
Sasaki looked at Yukio.
Yukio was silent. He was not yet ready to speak about this aloud in front of everyone. He took his hand off the square.
"Go on," he said.

"Lower right: Ainu-Tabi Hosho LLC. Kotan, near Lake Shikaribetsu. 'Tourism insurance.' Director — Kaizawa Takeshi, an Ainu guide, died in Kotan, August two thousand fifteen, stroke. Through this firm electricity is paid for in —" he paused, looking at the left column, "twenty-eight properties across the prefecture. Twenty-seven of them in Hokkaido, one in Yamagata."
"Twenty-eight," said Endo. "Excuse me, I was thinking five."
"Five active," said Kenji. "Twenty-three sleeping. Plus the twenty-eighth itself, sleeping, in Yamagata. I put every property on this map."

He passed a palm over the central part of the printout. There was the space of Hokkaido — the outline of the island — and on it black squares — twenty-seven — and one separate square in the lower right corner as a plus to Yamagata. Each square had a number. Each number had a thin line running to one of the four corporate squares in the corners.
There were many lines.
Very many.
Yukio looked in silence.

"This is not a network," said Kenji. "This is a system. Each property is fed from three or four firms at once. Cedar comes from Kita-Michi, ceramics from Reisen-do, electricity through Ainu-Tabi, restoration through Yuki-Kogei. No firm holds a property on its own. They are woven together so that if one is taken away — the others compensate."
"But," said Sasaki, "something holds them all."
"Holds them," said Kenji.
He set a finger in the very center of the map. There was a small yellow square.

"One postal point. A rented box at the post office Sapporo Kita 1. All four firms receive their official correspondence there. The box is paid for in cash once a year — always on the first Wednesday of April. In the last six years, on those days, the same person appears in the post office cameras — but the cameras are low quality — and the person is in a cap and mask. Height — one hundred seventy-five to one seventy-eight. Movements economical. Right-handed. Carries a bag — dark — of soft material."
"In April," said Endo, "on the first Wednesday."
"Yes."
Endo looked at Yukio.
"The next first Wednesday of April is five months away," she said.
"I know," said Yukio.
He did not intend to wait five months.

He kept looking at the center of the map. Not at the yellow square of the postal point — but at the interweaving of lines — at how it spread across the whole island — and how it held the five active houses — and how it held the twenty-three sleeping ones — and how in Yamagata, on the southern slope of Mount Zao, there stood one property completely apart, outside Hokkaido.
One outside.
Yukio looked at it.
"That is outside Hokkaido," he said. "Zao-minami. One."
"One," said Kenji. "Plus the sleeping Zao-kita. Both — Yamagata prefecture."
"So," said Yukio, "Hokkaido isn't the border."
"Not the border."
