Sasaki opened a folder she was holding under her arm. Took out three thin sheets.
"Here are three," she said.
She put the first sheet in the middle of the map, over Ashibetsu.
"This is where Aoi was. Taken away five days ago."
The second sheet — on the right, over Lake Shikaribetsu.
"This is where she is now. With Sato. With Ito. Three victims in one house."
The third — to the northwest, over the island of Rebun.
"This is where Ito was. Taken earlier."
Three sheets. Three properties. Three victims in one place.
Kenji was silent.
Endo said:
"He is gathering them."
"Gathering them," said Yukio.
"That is either a breakthrough or a trap."
"A trap," said Yukio. "It is a trap. He knows that we know. He wants us to come there."
"Then we don't go," said Endo.
"We go," said Yukio.
Endo looked at him.

"But not today," said Yukio. "We go when he isn't expecting us. And we go not the way he is counting on. Kenji, how much time do you need to draw a schedule of Yamato deliveries to Kotan for the past six weeks?"
"Two days."
"Do it."
"Doing it."
Half an hour later Endo left. Kenji rolled up the printout — but left a small copy on the desk, A3 — and hung it on the office wall next to the prefecture map. Miso in the carrier was asleep.
Yukio sat at his desk. Sasaki opposite.
"Kurosawa-san," said Sasaki.
"Yes."
"Reisen-do. Reisen-ji."
"I know."
"You saw the treasurer yesterday?"
"I haven't called yet. I'll call today."
"Kurosawa-san," said Sasaki, "the treasurer will say nothing."
"I know."
"But the firm will. Reisen-do issued an invoice for the monastery roof. That invoice will be in the monastery's bookkeeping. It cannot not be. It's the tax office."
"Yes."
"So," said Sasaki, "we give the treasurer one day. On the second — we demand the documents officially. From the prosecutor we take a warrant. Through Fujiwara."
Yukio nodded.
"Fujiwara will only issue a warrant if we show him this map."
"We'll show him."
"He'll register it in the case. It will go into the official record."
"I know."
"The Doll Maker will find out."
"He will."
Sasaki was silent.
"Kurosawa-san," she said.
"Yes."
"He already knows."
"Yes," said Yukio. "He already knows."
He looked at the small A3 copy on the wall. At the four squares in the corners. At the twenty-eight black dots on the island. At the one yellow dot at the center.
He thought about Ashibetsu, where a week ago there had been a warm teapot.
He thought about the monastery Reisen-ji, where the new copper roof had not yet darkened.

He thought about the post box at Sapporo Kita 1, about the person in cap and mask, about the fact that the person came in once a year, about the fact that they had a bag of soft material, about the fact that they were right-handed and moved economically.
He thought about the one in Yamagata, apart from the island.
He thought about Ayano — not here, not on Kenji's map — but somewhere.

Somewhere on one of the twenty-eight properties — perhaps on the twenty-ninth Kenji had not yet found — sat a girl with a thin hand and hair gathered into a knot, and drew in a notebook with the pixiv stroke Sasaki had recognized on a screen two weeks ago.
Yukio reached for the phone.
"Kenji," he said.
Kenji lifted his head.
"You said twenty-seven and one. Twenty-eight."
"Yes."
"Could there be twenty-nine?"
Kenji looked at him for a long moment.
"Kurosawa-san," he said. "There could be thirty."
Yukio nodded.
He picked up the phone. Dialed the treasurer of the monastery Reisen-ji.
The tone went.

Outside, snow was falling — fine, November, the kind that does not stay on the asphalt longer than twenty seconds — and Yukio looked through the glass at it and thought about the first Wednesday of April.
Five months.
He did not have five months.
The tone went.
The treasurer picked up on the eighth.
The treasurer of the monastery Reisen-ji was a man of about sixty, with a thin, tired voice.
"Kurosawa-keibu," he said. "Gensho-roshi warned me."
"Thank you," said Yukio. "I will take little of your time."
"I'm listening."
"The roof over the library. The repair was done seven years ago. The donation went through the firm Reisen-do Sangyo. I need a copy of the invoice and a copy of the payment order."
"You could get them officially through the prosecutor."

"I could. But that would take a long time. I give you a day. If in a day the documents are not on my desk, I go to the prosecutor, and that path is a different one — with searches of the monastery's bookkeeping."
The pause was long. Yukio waited.
"Kurosawa-keibu."
"Yes."
"I will give you the documents. But I have to say one thing."
"Go on."
"Reisen-do Sangyo is not our only benefactor. We have many. I don't know why this firm in particular."
"I am not accusing the monastery," said Yukio. "I am accusing the firm. The monastery is a victim no less than the others."
"Thank you."
"One more thing."
"Yes."
"Do you remember the monastery's guests in the nineties and two-thousands? Not novices — guests."
"Not all. I remember those who made donations. We have a book."
"I need that book. The same term — one day."
"All right," said the treasurer. "I'll send them. Kurosawa-keibu."
"Yes."
"Gensho-roshi this morning asked me to pass on one more thing. He said, 'Kurosawa-san thinks he came late. Tell him he came in time.'"
Yukio was silent.
"You'll pass it on?" said the treasurer.
"I will."
"Good."
Yukio pressed "end." Put the phone face-down on the desk.
Sasaki was watching him.
"What did he say?"
"Gensho-roshi sent me a message. That I came in time."
"Is that good or bad?"
"It is," said Yukio, "what a person says when he doesn't want to say 'all right.'"
Sasaki nodded.
Kenji at the corner desk lifted his head.
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."
"I checked with the banks. Reisen-do issued an invoice to the monastery in December two thousand twenty. Seven hundred forty-five thousand yen. For 'goods for the tea room.' Not for the roof."
Yukio turned to him.
"For the tea room."
"Yes."
"But Gensho said — for the roof."
"So," said Kenji, "either Gensho didn't know about the invoice for the tea room. Or he knew and didn't name it."

"Or," said Sasaki, "Gensho is thinking of a different kind of donation. Not monetary. Material. People in monasteries sometimes speak that way. 'They gave us the roof.' And in fact they gave the tableware."
Yukio looked at her.
"Yes."
"And that means," said Sasaki, "that Reisen-do brought into the monastery ceramics, teapots, trays. Perhaps the same lacquered tray that stands in every one of the Doll Maker's rooms."
Yukio was silent.
That was right.
That was terrifying.

That meant that the same trays — from the same batch — that Aoi sees in her Clinic and that Sato sees on his Pier — stand right now in the monastery Reisen-ji, on the shelf of the tea room, where Gensho-roshi holds tea ceremonies once a month for a dozen local old people.
It meant that the Doll Maker distributed his mark not only to his victims. He distributed it to the world. He held the world on one tray.
"Kurosawa-san," said Sasaki quietly.
"Yes."
"We won't be taking the trays from the monastery."
"We won't."
"We won't be speaking about this to the press."
"We won't."
"We'll keep silent about this until —" she stopped. "Until we take him."
"Yes."
Kenji, who had been listening, was silent. He understood more than he spoke. That was his quality.

"Then," said Yukio, "we write a report for Ogawa. Short. Four firms, one postal point, twenty-eight properties, five active. Yamagata outside Hokkaido. Hypothesis: an event is being prepared at Lake Shikaribetsu. Validity of the hypothesis — a week."
"A week," said Sasaki.
"A week."
Yukio looked at the little A3 on the wall. At the four squares. At the twenty-eight dots. At the one yellow dot at the center.
He looked at the square for Reisen-do Sangyo.
Reisen-do.
Reisen-ji.
One root. One mountain. One hand in the library twenty years ago.
Yukio took a pen and on the small A3 circled the Reisen-do square with red.
"That one," he said, "is not the newest. That one is the oldest of the four. That one is the door into the past."
Kenji nodded.
Sasaki said nothing — but stood and brought Yukio a fresh coffee from the corridor — without asking — and set it on the desk.
Yukio did not thank her aloud. He nodded.

Outside, the fine November snow was falling in a thin, patient line — the same patient line — and Yukio for a second remembered the steam from the teapot on his own kitchen tray — the one on the upper shelf above the sink — and thought whether it had been bought, some long time ago, through the same Reisen-do Sangyo.
He did not remember where the tray had come from.
He set the thought in a corner. It would be for later.
Now — a week.
A week to the lake.

p.emphasis: "You're looking not where I was. You're looking where I will be."

section.subtitle: Chapter Fourteen
section.p: Kenji arrived at ten in the morning, in a black hoodie, a laptop in its sleeve, and a can of Boss Coffee in his pocket. He always came with a single can, as though the dose were a measure — not of thirst, but of the time he would stay.
"Uncle," he said, setting the bag on the corner table. "You didn't answer the mail yesterday."
"I was asleep," Kurosawa said.
"At two in the morning?"
"Asleep," he repeated, level.

Kenji glanced at him briefly — the way one glances at a computer that has begun to throw a new sort of error — and opened the laptop. The three monitors weren't set up yet; for these two weeks he'd been bringing one ThinkPad from home and adjusting to the office.
Sasaki sat at her desk, reading a protocol from Asahikawa. She did not lift her head.
"Coffee?" said Kurosawa.
"I've got mine," said Kenji, patting the can.

Kurosawa put the pot on. Twenty-two grams of coffee, three hundred and thirty grams of water — a motion made by the body, without thought. He had long since stopped thinking about this ritual; thought would begin only if he broke the proportion. He didn't break it.
The coffee boiled. He poured into two cups — his own and Sasaki's — set his own on the desk, set hers by her elbow. Sasaki nodded silently, not looking up from the paper.

Kurosawa's laptop chimed quietly — the way mail chimes — each time a new message came through the service. He opened it. Three protocols, two callouts, one letter from the prefectural archive. Nothing important.
Then a second notification came. Not from the mail. From the browser he kept open in the background on the mixi service.
He froze for a second — not visibly to the others — and turned his head to the monitor.

mixi was a dead network. People had used it back in 2008, when Kurosawa was still in Tokyo — a junior inspector with the organized-crime division who thought at the time that mixi was the place they told you to go to "keep tabs on the youth milieu." He'd set up an account, written fourteen posts over three months, then forgotten.
He didn't remember the password. The mail the account had been registered to — the old Tokyo corporate address — had ceased to exist long ago.
And yet on the screen was a notification: new post on your page.
Kurosawa clicked.

The page unfolded slowly — the old mixi layout, thin pink borders, Osaka font — all as he remembered. The avatar was his own — the same one taken in 2008 in the kitchen of the Tokyo apartment, when Ren was still alive — a shot from the windowsill, him in profile, short hair, cup in his hands, the gray Tokyo sky behind. He'd thought himself superfluous in his own photograph at the time. He didn't like himself in pictures. But he had kept this one because his brother had taken it.
Beneath the avatar — a new entry. Private. Dated today, 11:47.
One sentence:

p.emphasis: "You're looking not where I was. You're looking where I will be."

section.p: Beneath the text — one more picture. A thumbnail. Attached as though an illustration to the post.
Kurosawa did not move for a long time. He heard Sasaki turn a page of the protocol behind him — a dry, even paper. He heard Kenji click open the tab of his can.
Then he said:
"Kenji."
His voice came out in a way that made Kenji lift his head at once.
"What."
"Come here."
Kenji came, glanced at the screen. He read for three seconds, no more.
"This is your account."
"Yes."
"You didn't post that."
"I haven't had the password in seventeen years."
"Who did."
"No one," said Kurosawa. "It's dead, this account. I registered it in Tokyo in 2008. Haven't logged in since 2009."
Kenji lowered himself onto his heels beside Kurosawa's chair — his habitual pose when reading someone else's screen — and for several seconds simply read.
"Uncle. That thumbnail. Click."
"What will it give us."
"We'll see."

Kurosawa clicked. The picture opened to the whole screen. Gray winter sky, the thin branch of a pine in the lower-left corner — and nothing else. No hint. The frame was empty the way a frame is empty when it was made deliberately about nothing.
"Download the original," said Kenji. "Not the preview. Right-click, save as."
Kurosawa saved. Kenji sat at the next desk, plugged in a cable, pulled the file to his laptop.
"Sasaki," said Kurosawa. His voice level again. "Come here."
Sasaki came, glanced over his shoulder at the post. She read for as long as Kenji had. Then she put a hand on the back of his chair — not touching his shoulder — and said:
"This is the first direct address."
"Yes."
"To you."
"Yes."
She said nothing more. He was grateful.

Kurosawa sat. Did not move. He knew how to hold the weight of such notifications — he had learned in Tokyo back in 2005, the first time in his life he had seen a threat envelope arrive at a prosecutor colleague's service address. His senior had told him then: "Don't move for ten seconds. Then move the way you were moving before. There must be no difference."
He counted off ten seconds.

Then, with two fingers, he opened another tab in the browser. Entered the address of the prefectural mail-server archive. A search for "mixi" — over the last thirty days. Nothing. Over the last seventy-two. Nothing. He closed the tab.

Kenji was silent for fourteen minutes. Kurosawa counted it off by the clock on the wall. In that time Sasaki had managed to make two calls — both on other cases — and to brew herself a second cup of green tea from the thermos.
At twelve-o-seven Kenji lifted his head.
"Uncle."
"Yes."
"The EXIF on this file has been rewritten. Not wiped — rewritten. Someone wanted you to read it."
"What's there."
"Coordinates. A GPS tag. Latitude, longitude. Camera model is fake — Nikon D40, no such model exists with that firmware. Date of the shot — today, 06:14 in the morning. Time zone — JST."
"Coordinates to where."
Kenji turned his laptop screen toward him. On the screen — a map. One point marked in red.
Kurosawa looked.
Mountains. Northeast of Sunagawa, in the foothills. The area — Ashibetsu-yama. Not touristic, not residential. A reserve where an old mountain trail begins across the ridge.

He knew this place. Not because he had been there — he hadn't. Because it was on the map Kenji had assembled earlier — the layout of ryokan networks across Hokkaido. One of twenty-eight points. Not a priority. Not the highest in electricity consumption. Periphery.
"It's one of the ryokans," said Kurosawa. "Ashibetsu."
"Yes," said Kenji. "It's the tenth point on my list."
"How long to drive."
"Three hours forty," said Kenji, without checking. "Route 452, then a mountain track. The last five kilometers — on foot or by off-roader. In winter — off-roader only."
Sasaki stood behind, listening. Kurosawa felt her shift her weight from one foot to the other.
"Sir," she said. "It could be a trap."
"Yes."
"He's drawing you out personally."
"Yes."
"You're looking where I will be. That's future tense. He's saying he isn't there yet."
"Or telling us he isn't," said Kurosawa.
Kenji clicked at the keyboard. Did not lift his eyes.
"Uncle. One thing. There's another comment in the metadata, hidden. Three characters."
"Which."
Kenji turned the screen.
Against the black of the EXIF-editor hung three ideograms:
Kurosawa looked at them a long time. Kenji did not interrupt.
"What does it mean," Kenji said at last.
"It means," said Kurosawa, "that he is waiting for us, and that he can wait."
"That's bad."
"That's the worst thing he could have said."

Kurosawa went down to the canteen on the first floor — a small one, with four tables and one vending machine — bought a hot ō-mugi in a can from the machine, came back to the office, put the can on the desk, did not open it.
Sasaki asked:
"Sir, have you eaten today?"
"No."
"You should."
"I know."

She pulled a small packet of rice crackers from her drawer, laid it in front of him. He nodded — did not begin. The crackers lay between the keyboard and the phone for twenty minutes. He did not eat one.

Ogawa came in at one in the afternoon. Kurosawa showed him the screen — mixi, coordinates, comment. Ogawa read for a minute. Then he sat on the corner of Kurosawa's desk — the way he sat when he needed to think, not to stand — and rubbed the bridge of his nose with two fingers.
"Kurosawa," he said. "This is personal."
"I know."
"He's talking to you."
"I know."
"I have to pull you off."
"You won't."
Ogawa smiled briefly — the dry smile that meant I know I won't, but I had to say it out loud.
"What do you need."
"Two off-roaders. Three operatives. Sasaki with me. Kenji in the comms vehicle — not in the field. Timing — tomorrow at six in the morning."
"I'll have to inform the prosecutor."
"Inform him."
"He'll say to take tokushu with us."
"Tell him we're taking them," said Kurosawa. "We won't."
Ogawa looked at him for a long moment.
"Kurosawa."
"Ogawa-san."
"If it's a trap out there, I'll bury you at state expense with military honors. Don't promise my wife I won't."
"I don't promise," said Kurosawa.
Ogawa stood up, nodded briefly to Sasaki — she nodded back — and left.
Three remained in the office.
Kenji opened his second can of Boss — for half a day this was already a lot for him — and sat looking at his screen. Not at the mixi post. At the coordinates.
"Uncle," he said. "One question."
"Yes."
"Who restored that account for you."
"No one. It came back on its own."
"Someone reset the password. Through phone recovery. Or through a backup mail. Or someone knows your secret question."
"What was my secret question."

"Uncle," said Kenji, "I can't see. He rewrote the table in the database. That means he has access to mixi's servers, or he has access to someone who does. mixi was folded into Recruit's holding in 2019. A hole opened in 2020, publicly. Half the old accounts have been reachable through that hole to this day."
"So he just went in through the hole."
"Yes. And wrote a post from your name."
"Then," said Kurosawa, "he knew the account was mine."
"He knows a lot," said Kenji. Not as a supposition. As a fact.
Sasaki stood by the window, looking at the dense snow that was beginning beyond the glass. She did not turn.
"Sir," she said. "He was reading your page."
"What is there to read. Fourteen posts from 2008."
"He was reading your page," she repeated. "And he could also have been reading pages linked to yours. In your friends list."
Kurosawa froze.
He opened the friends list on mixi. Twelve names. All long-dead accounts. But the third from the top — Kurosawa Ren.
He clicked.
Ren's page loaded. The avatar — Ren in 2008, aged thirty, in a gray jacket, smiling at no one in particular. The last post — April 4, 2019, two days before Ren "disappeared." One line:
Kurosawa looked at this line a long time.
Then he asked, without turning his head:
"Kenji. Can you see whether anyone visited this page."
"Your brother's?"
"My brother's."
Kenji shifted closer, took control of the screen. He clicked for about five minutes.
"Uncle."
"Yes."
"The last visit to this page was today at six-fourteen in the morning."
"From what device."
"I can't see the device. Through Tor. But from the same session that posted to yours."
Kurosawa closed the laptop. Quietly, with both hands — the way one closes the lid of a chest in which something lies.
He stood up, went to the window, next to Sasaki. He looked at the same snow she was looking at.
"He's reading my brother," he said.
Sasaki did not answer.
"He's reading all of us," she said a minute later. "You knew that."
"I knew," said Kurosawa. "Now I know differently."

Kenji did not interrupt them from behind. He was clicking again — quietly, without pauses, in the rhythm from which an experienced listener could read that the keyboard did not intend to stop for a long while yet.
"Kenji."
"Yes."
"How much can you pull from the steps he took on my brother's page."

"Uncle," said Kenji, without lifting his eyes, "on the Tor network no steps remain. But he may have left local caches. If he was reading from a laptop — and if that laptop ever connects to an unwashed network — we'll see him."
"How long to wait."
"A week. Maybe a month. Maybe never."
"Do it."
"Doing."
Kurosawa looked at him one more second. Kenji was already looking at his screen again. Kurosawa nodded to himself and turned back to the mixi monitor.
Sasaki stood beside him. Did not move.
"Sir," she said quietly. "One more thing."
"Yes."
"He wrote will be. Not is. Not was."
"I know."
"So he is drawing you to a place he has not yet arrived at."
"Yes."
"Or wants us to work it out that way."
"Yes."

Kurosawa nodded grimly. Both readings equally weighted. Neither gave advantage. He had long since learned not to like texts from which both readings emerged equally plausible — these were texts written by someone who knew how to hold symmetry.
At six in the evening Kenji closed the laptop, dropped the can in the bin, took his bag.
"Uncle," he said at the door. "One small thing."
"Yes."
"I looked at that avatar of yours. The original. The metadata of the original has a comment too. One character. Not the one on the coordinates."
"Which."
Kenji raised his phone, showed him. On the screen — one ideogram.
Kurosawa looked. Then he nodded, briefly.
"Thank you, Kenji."
"Don't thank me," said Kenji. "It isn't a gift."
He went out, closing the door quietly.
Sasaki stayed. She stood by the window for a few minutes more — beside Kurosawa, who did not move — then took her jacket from the back of the chair.
"Sir."
"Yes."
"Tomorrow at six."
"Yes."
"Sleep well," she said.
He almost smiled. Didn't quite.
"You too," he said. "And, Sasaki — Nao is in Niigata today?"
Sasaki looked at him a long time. Not surprised — attentive.
"Yes," she said.
"Good."
She nodded. Didn't ask how he knew. Both knew he knew. Both silently agreed not to open that conversation now — but marked that it would come.
Sasaki nodded, went out.

Kurosawa stood at the window a long while. Snow beyond the glass fell slowly — in those large fat flakes that mean there is no wind — and each reached the sill in the rhythm that keeps only in Japanese winters, when darkness comes at exactly four o'clock.

He thought about Ren's little page. About that last post — tonight, snow — written two days before his brother left the apartment in Chiba on a working evening and did not return. About how Endo now said the body in the grave was not his. About how someone today at six-fourteen in the morning had visited that page. Not him. Not Endo. Not Kurosawa. A third person, who was reading his brother.
He thought about the phrase "You're looking not where I was. You're looking where I will be."
It was an invitation. Direct. For the first time.
But an invitation always has a second layer. He knew this. The one who sets a trap sets it so that the victim walks into it on her own feet — believing she is following her own trail.

Kurosawa opened the laptop once more. Clicked on the post — the new text on his page — and right-clicked on the picture itself. From the drop-down menu he chose "save page as complete." The computer rustled quietly for a few seconds, saving.
He knew that tomorrow at six in the morning they would drive to Ashibetsu-yama. He knew what they would find there. Or not find. He knew this would be a way station, not an end.
He knew one more thing, and from this knowledge it was hardest.
He knew that he wanted to go.
Not because the Doll Maker might be there. And not because victims might be there.
But because the trail of his brother might be there.
Kurosawa closed the laptop a second time.
He stood a minute more. Then took his jacket.
Went home.

The smell of boiled rice from Ryoko's apartment reached him on the stairs. He stood on the landing a second — not ready to go into his own straight away — then nodded to the invisible neighbor behind the door and turned the key in his own lock.
On the kitchen windowsill stood two white porcelain figurines without faces. One his. The other from Toshi's hut.
He did not glance at them.
He went to the kitchen — and began to set the pot on again.

Twenty-two grams. Three hundred and thirty grams. The water boiled faster than he had reckoned; the kitchen was colder than usual, and the kettle on the burner hummed differently. He poured into one cup. Carried it to the table, set it down — did not sit, stood beside it. Looked at the steam.
Then he said aloud — quietly, into the empty room — as quietly as one speaks only to those who hear without hearing:
"Ren."
The steam from the cup rose vertically — there was no draft — and vanished in the air half a meter above the surface.
He said nothing more.
He drew the phone from the inner pocket. He wrote Sasaki one message:
He put the phone down. Did not wait for a reply. He knew it would come in half a minute — short, one letter of confirmation. So it did.
He drank the coffee standing. Beyond the window the snow lay evenly on the sill. Two porcelain figurines without faces looked into the same emptiness — with a look they did not have.
Kurosawa finished the coffee — and only then sat down.

section.subtitle: Chapter Fifteen
section.p: The cab smelled of diesel and something third — perhaps varnish — that hadn't smelled on any truck he had worked in for twenty-one years.

Ito sat at the wheel. Held it at ten and two — not by habit: his wrists knew it before he had time to think. The engine hummed the way an Isuzu Giga from 1997 hums — his old cab from the first years at Nippon Express. On the panel the electronic clock glowed blue: three forty-two in the morning.

Beyond the windshield went winter. Route 39. Kamikawa pass. The forty-third kilometer before the summit. The blizzard was thin — only the first flakes — but visibility had already dropped to fifteen meters. The wipers moved unevenly: the right one a little slower than the left, and each time it left a thin streak on the glass.
He knew that streak.
You can hear it, said the voice.
The voice came from behind his left shoulder. Neither high nor low. Neither male nor female. He did not turn his head. He never turned.

The wheel this time turned when he turned it — with that small resistance a real wheel has on the road. Earlier, for some twenty cycles, it had spun like a toy, independent of anything. In the last cycle something had changed. They had given him the wheel.
He saw her.
A figure was on the right shoulder. Walking against his direction. Shoulders lowered, dark jacket, cap pulled low.
He knew that figure. He had known it for twenty-one years.

Watanabe Kōichi. Twenty-seven years old. A hydroelectric worker, his car had broken down ten kilometers up. Walking home on foot. Always took one more step nearer the road — precisely the one that put him into the right mirror's blind zone.
Ito pressed the brake. The truck slowed evenly. He drove past the figure at fifty. The figure did not turn its head.
Some two hundred meters on he stopped the truck on the shoulder. Turned on the hazards. Blue flashing reflected in the snow on both sides. Killed the engine.
Silence fell at once. Only the blizzard rustled thinly on the roof.
He opened the door. Wind broke in, struck his cheekbone. He threw on the old JR jacket and climbed out.
The road was wet-icy. He stepped slowly — the way a man steps whose feet once failed him at the wrong second — and walked in the reverse direction. Toward the figure.
Two hundred and forty-two steps.
The figure was still there. Standing. Not moving. The face was not visible.
He came within five meters. Stopped. Coughed. Quietly.
"Excuse me."
The figure did not answer.
"Excuse me," he said louder.
The figure did not stir.

Now he could see the jacket — dark-green, woolen, with a patch on the left elbow. Trousers spotted with fuel oil. Heavy boots, soles worn inward. This was Watanabe Kōichi's clothing. He had read the description in the newspaper in 1998 — three times. Could have listed every detail, including the size of the boots: twenty-seven.
He came within two meters.
"Watanabe-san."
The figure slowly turned its head.
A face was there. But it was not of details — of form. Oval, nose, mouth. Eyes not visible under the cap. But it was a face. He could have said one thing about it: it was not dead.
"You're going home," said Ito.
The figure nodded. Once.
"Far still."
"Eight kilometers or so."
The voice was low, calm, with the drawn Hokkaido o in or so.
"I'll give you a ride," said Ito. "To the bridge. From there it's close for you."
The figure looked at him. He felt the eyes though he could not see them.
"Thank you," said Watanabe.

They walked to the cab. Ito a little ahead — not because he was hurrying, but because he could not bear walking beside for longer. He opened the passenger door, held it. Watanabe climbed in heavily, with a short exhale.
Ito walked around the truck, sat behind the wheel. Started the engine. Pulled onto the road. The blizzard strengthened.
They drove five minutes in silence. Watanabe placed his hands on his knees. He smelled of wet wool and gasoline.
"You're local," said Watanabe quietly.
"Asahikawa."
"A ways off."
"I was in Kushiro."
"Long haul?"
"Nippon Express. Second year."
Watanabe nodded.
"My car broke down," he said. "Ten kilometers back. Starter went. I thought — maybe a lift."
"There are no lifts here at this hour."
"I know."
He did not say thank you a second time. He didn't need to.
They passed the turnaround loop — the one that had always tightened Ito's chest across all these years — and he did not notice the moment.
You came earlier than that time, said the voice. From behind the left shoulder.
Ito froze.
He saw — for a second — that beside him sat not Watanabe. Beside him sat a mannequin. Rag-cloth. With a cap low over the oval where the face should be. Rope-hands on knees.
He blinked. Watanabe was there again. Looking ahead. Breathing.
Ito drew a slow breath. Held it.
"I come here twenty-one years," he said quietly. "To this road. Twice a day."
Watanabe turned his head to him.
"Why."
"I don't remember."
Watanabe did not ask more. Nodded.
They drove another six kilometers. The wipers barely kept up.

On the dashboard, right under the clock, lay a small lacquered tray. The size of a palm. On the tray — a tiny clay teapot, one tiny cup. He knew this tray. Not from here. From somewhere else. He always looked at it at one and the same moment — when the clock read three fifty-five — and always felt that there was something to remember, but he could not.
The clock read three fifty-five.
He looked at the tray. Did not remember.
But today on the tray beside the tiny teapot stood two tiny cups. Not one.
He looked for several seconds.
Watanabe was not looking. Watanabe was looking ahead, at the road.
You came earlier than that time, said the voice, quieter still. One for you. One for him.
Ito nodded slowly.
He was not sure to whom.
The bridge went past. Watanabe asked to stop two hundred meters after it, by the fork.
"From here on foot. Thank you, driver."
"I'll take you to the village."
"No. That's my custom when I come back from the night shift."
Ito stopped the truck. Turned on the hazards. Watanabe opened the door — and before climbing out turned to him.
The face was visible now. Twenty-seven years old. Eyes — gray, Hokkaido. Not angry. Not sad.
"Driver," he said. "Get some sleep."
Ito nodded.
Watanabe climbed out, closed the door. Walked along the shoulder toward the fork. His steps were swallowed by the blizzard in ten seconds.
Ito sat. The engine ran quietly. The right wiper left the same thin streak.
After a minute he switched off the engine. Silence fell. He put his hands on the wheel and closed his eyes.
You came earlier than that time, the voice repeated, quite quietly. Next time you will come earlier still.
Ito sat. Did not contest.
He knew this.

p.emphasis: Next time he will live — as he lives today. And the day before. And three nights ago. And he will always live, because you will stop. Because you can stop. Because you can.

section.p: He held the wheel.
He held the wheel.
Beyond the windshield it was dark and white. The clock read four ten. Beyond the window to the right — the thin branch of a pine, under which Watanabe had passed.
He wanted — with all his strength, with all his years, with all his twenty-one years — for the tray on the panel to have two cups again. Not one.
He opened his eyes.
The tray had one.
He looked a long time. Did not move.
Then, quietly, like a small child from whom a toy has been taken — he said aloud:
"Do not take it."
The voice said nothing.
The wipers went. The right one left a streak.
Ito waited.

He always waited here. Knew it in every cycle. Waited until the voice said: begin again. Then he would appear once more on the forty-third kilometer before the summit, at three forty-two in the morning. A figure on the shoulder.
Sometimes he drove past. Sometimes he stopped. Sometimes he struck. Sometimes he took to the village.
He had long since stopped counting the times. He knew only one thing: each time he came a little earlier.
Maybe one day he would come before Watanabe left his own house in the mountains.
Maybe one day he would pull up to Watanabe's very door, and go with him into the kitchen, and Watanabe's mother would set before them both a cup of tea from the tray.
The voice had said as much one cycle. Promised.
Ito believed.

He could not remember his own name. Could not remember who was the woman who sometimes came to the dream and laid a hand on his shoulder. Could not remember what his son's name had been, and whether there had been a son. Could not remember who Issa was, why in the breast pocket of his jacket lay a thin volume of poems.

But he could remember the name Watanabe Kōichi, and the address of his village, and the color of his jacket, and how his hand trembled on the strap of his bag as he walked alone along Route 39 at three forty-two in the morning.
It was enough.
The voice said: begin again.
Ito pressed the brake though he was stopped. Started the engine. Pulled onto the road.
The clock showed three forty-two.
The blizzard grew thin.
The figure on the shoulder — in the distance — emerged from the white.
Walking against his direction.
The wheel was under his hands, at ten and two.
He held it steady.
He knew he would stop.
He knew that this time he would stop ten meters closer than the last. And that the voice would praise him. And that on the tray there would once again be two cups, if only for a second.
That second was all he had.
That second was all he wanted.
He held the wheel.
And the blizzard began to strengthen.

section.subtitle: Chapter Sixteen
section.p: The off-roader lifted onto the last rise — the engine dropping into a lower gear, wheels slipping a centimeter — and came out onto a small plateau from which the roof of the kominka opened to view.
Sasaki eased off the gas.

The roof was black, steep, covered under a good forty centimeters of snow. No smoke came from the chimney. No tire tracks on the approach — apart from old ones, left perhaps a week ago and then powdered over. No people. No sound but the engine.
"Stop," said Kurosawa.
Sasaki halted the vehicle twenty meters short of the door. Killed the engine.

The silence fell at once. It was the kind mountain forest carries in itself before a winter noon: no wind, no birds, no water. Only the thin creak of a pine somewhere to the left — the pine giving notice it was alive.
Kurosawa opened the door. Climbed out slowly. His boot cut into the snow to the ankle. He stood a second — inhaled air that smelled only of pine and cold — and nodded to Sasaki.
Sasaki got out from the other side. She held her pistol in the holster, under her unbuttoned jacket. She did not draw it. She simply kept a hand close.
Behind them, twenty meters back, stood the second off-roader. Three operatives. They did not move until Kurosawa gave the sign. He did not give it.
"Sir," said Sasaki. "No tracks."
"Yes."
"None fresh at all."
"No."
They walked to the door. Kurosawa in front, Sasaki half a step behind and a little to the left — the way partners walk in the field when they do not know what waits inside.

The kominka was old. Wood, roofed with red tile, with a wide eave beneath which mushrooms had once been dried. The sign above the door — faded — was hard to read, but the word yama-no-ya (mountain house) still showed through.
The door was shut but not locked. Kurosawa pressed. It creaked. Opened.
He froze on the threshold. Did not cross.
Inside it smelled of old tatami — dry, cooled — and faintly, barely, of burnt pine. Not today's. Yesterday's, or the day before. Smoke that had had time to soak into the walls and almost air out.
And one more thing. Faintly.
Coffee.
Not the smell of a fresh brew. The smell of grounds left in the filter and forgotten — the way one leaves them in a hurry — grounds that had dried but still remembered themselves.
"You smell it," Kurosawa said quietly.
"Yes."
"It's not today."
"No. But recent."
He crossed the threshold.
The genkan was empty. One pair of cold white zōri stood to the left, evenly — the way one sets them for a guest who is to come but did not. Or — the way one leaves them behind.

Kurosawa unlaced his boots. It was an automatic movement — not from custom, but from the fact that in another's house you do not enter shod, even when hunting a criminal. Sasaki also took off her boots. It was not in the video-protocol; it was simply what they did.
He took the flashlight, switched it on. The beam was white, wide.
The corridor. Wooden floor. To the right — zashiki, to the left — kitchen, at the end — a way out into the garden. He went right.
The zashiki was empty. Tatami, low table, alcove — tokonoma. In the alcove hung a scroll.
Kurosawa raised the flashlight to the scroll.
One ideogram. Large. Drawn with wet ink, recently; the paper at the edges was slightly darker where the ink had been drying. Not days ago. Two days at most. Perhaps less.
Kurosawa looked a long time. Sasaki stood at his shoulder, also looking.
"Sir."
"Yes."
"That's his hand."
"I know."
"He wrote this recently."
"I know."
Kurosawa nodded slowly. Lowered the flashlight.
They went to the kitchen.

He walked farther — to the kitchen. To the right of the entry a dozō showed through — a thin wall of clay plaster, coated by time's soot; the soot was not fresh, an old layer quietly shed with time. To the left hung a narrow shelf — dishes had once been kept on it, now empty, only two rings from old round bases.

The kitchen was small, cramped. A table, two shelf-boards, an old electric burner, an old tin kettle. In the corner — a Melitta filter with a wooden handle, in which lay dark dried coffee grounds. Kurosawa lifted the filter with two fingers. The grounds were dry — but not brittle. Three days, no more. He replaced the filter.
The sink — dry. No water came from the tap: Sasaki turned the handle — only one short cough in the pipe — and closed it.
The refrigerator — unplugged. Door held open a centimeter — the way one leaves it when one does not want the inside to spoil with smell. Empty.
On the kitchen windowsill stood three white porcelain figurines without faces. Not nine. Three.
Kurosawa looked at them a long time.
Sasaki said nothing.
She knew that nine was the full set. Three was a remainder.

He shifted the flashlight into his left hand. With his right, carefully — with two fingers — he took one of the figurines. It was cold, smooth, as always. On the base — a small, almost invisible stamp. He brought it closer to the light. The stamp read: 2019.
He replaced the figurine.
"Farther."
In the hallway — a long corridor with several doors. Kurosawa counted: one, two, three. At the end — a small one, with a padlock hasp — a storeroom. The door was ajar.
He went in.
The storeroom was small, a meter and a half by two. Shelves — floor to ceiling. On the shelves — boxes. All alike. Wooden, roughly thirty by twenty centimeters, with a thin lid on hinges.
He counted. Nine boxes.
He opened the first.
Empty. Only a scrap of soft silk on the bottom — pink, with a thin gold pattern — on which a figurine had once lain. A hollow in the silk held the shape.
The second. Empty. Hollow.
The third. Empty. Hollow.
The fourth. Empty.
The fifth. One white porcelain figurine without a face. Lay evenly in its hollow.
The sixth. One.
The seventh. One.
The eighth. Empty.
The ninth. Empty.
He counted again, aloud:
"Three here. Three in the kitchen. Together, six. Should be nine."
Sasaki stood behind him, in the storeroom doorway. She did not enter — there was no room for two.
"Sir. He took three with him."
"Yes."
"He's moving them."
"Yes."
Kurosawa closed the ninth box. Put it in place.

He stood a second more in the storeroom — held the flashlight, looked at the empty hollows. Three figurines on the kitchen he had left. Three in boxes. Three taken. Nine broken into three-three-three.
It was a move. Deliberate. He wanted them to count.
Kurosawa left the storeroom.

They went through all the rooms. Nine doors along the corridor. All empty. In the third — the tatami had a fresh stain, round, damp to the touch, the size of a palm; Sasaki sniffed it — no smell — and registered it on the phone. In the fifth — on the windowsill lay a pair of thin wool socks, black, rolled into a ball, men's, size twenty-seven. He did not touch. Sasaki also registered.

In the seventh — on the floor, at the center of the tatami, lay a single long gray hair. Kurosawa bent, looked closer. Some twenty centimeters. Straight, thick — not thin women's — with that particular sheen that hair has in a person past sixty, cared for, in soft water. He did not touch. Pointed with a finger to Sasaki. Sasaki nodded — photographed it, entered it in the protocol.
"His," she said quietly.
"May be. May be another."
"How many people cut his hair."
"One."
Kurosawa straightened. They went farther.
In the eighth — nothing.

In the ninth — on the futon, folded and set against the wall, lay a single sheet of paper. Thin, white, the size of a postcard. On the sheet — not a single word. Only one line in ink — short, made in one stroke — from the upper-left corner to the lower-right.
Kurosawa looked at this line a long time.
It was a diagonal. Just a diagonal.
Or it was a sign: from here to there. A course. A direction.
He photographed it.
Sasaki stood silently in the doorway. Then she said:
"Sir."
"Yes."
"He knows that we know."
"Yes."
"And he's telling us so."
"Yes."
"He's telling us he knows, and he doesn't care."
"Yes."
Kurosawa placed the sheet in a clear evidence bag. Left the ninth.
They walked back down the corridor. Three operatives waited in the genkan — they had come in — did not ask. Kurosawa said quietly:
"Perimeter. Log every room. Grounds from the filter — to analysis. Do not move the scroll. Call Endo-san to the site."
"Understood," said the senior of the group.
"Also," said Kurosawa. "The hair in the seventh. Log it separately, in its own bag. Not with the other biomaterials. It was placed — not dropped. This is not a routine sample."
"Understood."
"And one more. No smoking here. Not on the yard, not in the kitchen. He is sensitive to strangers' smells in his rooms. If he comes back — and he will not — I want him to know we didn't smoke."
"Understood."
They nodded, dispersed.
Kurosawa went out onto the threshold. Sasaki behind him.
The sky was low, gray. Snow was beginning again — thinly.
He stood on the wooden eave. Looked into the forest.
"How long," he said.
"Three, four days," said Sasaki. "By the grounds. By the smoke in the walls. By how the kettle dried out."
"He led them out."
"Yes."
"He knew we'd find the address."
"Yes."
"He gave us the address himself."
"Yes."
Kurosawa was silent a long time.
Then:
"So he wanted us to see exactly this."
"Yes."
"An empty storeroom. The scroll. The diagonal on the sheet."
"Yes."
He turned from the forest. Looked at her.
"Sasaki. We are in a game where he is giving us the moves."
"Yes, sir."
"I don't like it."
"Neither do I."
He almost smiled. Didn't quite. A smile wasn't possible now.
They drove back to Sapporo in the second vehicle. The three operatives stayed at the site, awaiting Endo and the forensics team.
Sasaki drove. Kurosawa sat on her right, looking out the window at the slopes of Ashibetsu-yama as they slowly fell behind.
"Sir."
"Yes."
"One more thing."
"Yes."
"The scroll. To move. That doesn't mean I am moving. It means — a command. Or an invitation."
Kurosawa thought.
"You're right."
"He's telling you: move."
"Yes."
"He wants us to move further."
"Yes."
"That means he is leading us somewhere."
"Yes."
"Not here."
"Not here."
Sasaki added a little gas. The off-roader ran smoother.
"Sir."
"Yes."
"I want to stop by Toshi's."
Kurosawa turned his head.
"Today?"
"Today. On the way. At the detention center."
"What do you want to ask him."
"I want to ask," said Sasaki, "who else knew about Ashibetsu."
Kurosawa looked at her a long time.
He knew Toshi would not answer that question. And he knew Sasaki also knew this. But she wanted to ask.
"All right," he said. "We'll stop."

At the Sapporo Chūō detention center they took walk-ins badly — they had no schedule for unplanned interviews — but Kurosawa had called in an hour ahead, and the duty officer, seeing the surnames, only sighed and nodded. Kurosawa and Sasaki entered a small room with two tables and one bench at four forty-two. Toshi came in from the other side five minutes later.

Kurosawa looked at the empty bench in front of him. He kept his hands on the table — palms open, downward. It was his old habit at interrogations — to show his hands. To hide nothing. He did not notice that he was doing it now, when the one across the table was not a suspect but a witness who had once been a suspect and who might, perhaps, be a witness again.
Toshi had thinned further. Shoulders lowered. Head freshly shaved — this morning — a small nick from the razor on his cheekbone. He sat. Put his hands on the table.
Kurosawa set down the thermos. Poured water into a plastic cup. Set it between them.
They did not drink.
"Nakamura-san," said Kurosawa. "We were in Ashibetsu-yama today."
Toshi did not stir. He listened.
"He left. Three, four days before we arrived. The room dry. The storeroom empty — three figurines he left. Scroll in the tokonoma: 動."
Toshi nodded slowly.
Kurosawa waited.
Toshi said:
"He moves faster than you."
"I know."
"Because he knows where he is going."
"I know."
Sasaki leaned slightly forward. Her voice was level.
"Nakamura-san. Who knew about Ashibetsu apart from you."
Toshi turned his eyes to her. Looked a long time. Not hostile — simply.
"Sasaki-san."
"Yes."
"I did not know about Ashibetsu when he kept me there. I knew only that it was mountains and that it wasn't Kamishiroi."
"You lived there."
"I did not live there. I was there. That's different."
"Who else was there."
Toshi did not answer.
He looked into the cup of water Kurosawa had set before him. Did not drink.
"I don't know," he said at last. "I'm not one of those who keeps a notebook."
"Then who does keep the notebook."
"He has no notebook," said Toshi. "He has memory."
Sasaki did not ask again.
Kurosawa watched the two of them — Toshi sitting straight, and Sasaki not looking away.
"Nakamura-san," said Kurosawa. "He wrote to me today."
Toshi slowly — very slowly — raised his eyes to him.
"To you."
"To me."
"Through what."
"Through mixi. My old account."
Toshi nodded.
"And what did he write."
"You're looking not where I was. You're looking where I will be."
Toshi closed his eyes for a second. Then opened them.
"He has begun with you," he said. "Now he will not stop."
"He began long ago."
"No, inspector. Before, he spoke with you through me. Now — directly. That is different."
Kurosawa sat. Kept his palms on his knees.
"Nakamura-san," he said quietly. "I need to know something. Where he went from Ashibetsu."
Toshi did not answer at once.
He looked into the cup of water. Long.
Then he said:
"Inspector. It is not that he left Ashibetsu. Ashibetsu is what he had long since already been leaving. You arrived at an empty place because he had long moved on."
"Then where was he moving to."
"To a lake."
Kurosawa froze.
"Which."
"I will not name it for you," said Toshi. "I do not know it myself. I know only that it is — and that it is the one out of which no one comes."
He raised his eyes. For the first time in the conversation he looked Kurosawa straight in the pupils.
"Inspector. He is taking them there now. All of them. Into one room."
"How many."
"As many as there are."
Kurosawa was silent for a long time.
Then he stood. Took the thermos. Nodded to Toshi.
"Thank you," he said.
Toshi did not answer. Looked into the cup.
In the car Sasaki did not hurry to switch on the ignition. She sat a minute, hands on the wheel.
"Sir."
"Yes."
"He says — a lake."
"Yes."
"We have twenty-eight points on Kenji's map. How many are by lakes."
"I don't remember. We'll get in and check."
"Sir."
"Yes."
"One more thing."
He turned his head to her.
"He is taking them all into one room. That means," she was speaking evenly, "they will be together. For the first time. If we find the lake — we find them all at once."
"Yes."
"Or lose them all at once."
Kurosawa did not answer.
Sasaki started the ignition.
"Sir."
"Yes."
"Kenji has to be told. About the lake."
"I'll tell him from the car."
"I'll tell him."
"All right."
Sasaki took out her phone, put it on speaker, laid it on the panel. Kenji answered on the second ring, briefly — he already knew the call was coming.
"Kenji," said Sasaki. "Priority. Every point from our map within a three-kilometer radius of a lake. Every lake in Hokkaido. Ponds, reservoirs. Anything with fresh water and a shore."
"Received."
"By morning."
"Received."
He hung up without a goodbye. It was his manner — it did not annoy Sasaki. She liked people who did not waste words.
The off-roader pulled quietly from the spot. The sky over Sapporo was already dark — four forty-two in the afternoon in December — and along the road shoulders the first yellow lamps were coming on.
Kurosawa looked out the window.

He remembered the seventh room. One hair in the middle of the tatami. Not dropped — placed. He saw it now, as the vehicle went through the darkness of Route 452, and understood it differently: the hair lay evenly parallel to one of the seams between the mats. It was not a hair that had fallen. It was a gesture.

p.emphasis: I was here. I placed this for you.

section.p: Kurosawa looked out the side window. The forest had lost its outlines — become black masses — and at the edge of the road the marker posts flashed briefly.
He thought about the diagonal on the sheet in the ninth room. About the scroll 動 in the tokonoma. About the three porcelain figurines without faces on the kitchen windowsill, set in a row.
He thought, for the first time in many days, not of Ayano. But of Ogawa, whom tomorrow he would have to tell that the lake existed.
He placed his palms on his knees. Looked forward. The wipers went evenly, both of them.
Sasaki was silent.
Beyond the window a sign flashed by — Ashibetsu 2 — the town waking to winter evening, a few windows already yellow — and the vehicle bypassed it, going around by the highway without entering.

Kurosawa closed his eyes for ten seconds. He needed ten seconds not to think of the scroll 動, not to think of the photographs of hollows in silk, not to think of Endo, who tomorrow would come with the result of the grounds and say: "Kurosawa-san, he brewed coffee in a Melitta with four holes. That's not a household filter. That's a restorer's. Such filters are used in workshops where furniture is restored and gourmet-grade coffee is brewed alongside. Fourteen such filters have been sold in Hokkaido in the last two years. I've passed the list to Kenji." He knew Endo would say this — he knew it already by the form of the grounds — and he needed ten seconds not to hold it in his head together with all the rest.
He opened his eyes.
Route 452 went to Sapporo.
He did not yet know that tomorrow he would not manage to tell Ogawa.

section.subtitle: Chapter Seventeen
section.p: Ogawa left Asahikawa at two-ten in the afternoon.

He'd risen that morning earlier than needed — at five-forty — and sat half an hour in the kitchen, while his wife still slept, with a cup of coffee and Hokkaido Shimbun. He read the sports column. Nippon-Ham had lost in Komagazawa — not a league game, a friendly — but someone young, an understudy at third base, had turned a triple, and the column was about him. Ogawa read it twice. He liked short pieces about young men. He liked seeing the start of someone's road.

At six he dressed — gray suit, blue overcoat, the old cashmere scarf his wife had folded into his bag on Monday. He wrote his wife a note: "Back by eight. Don't warm anything." Fixed the note to the fridge with a Hokkaido-maru magnet.
Left Sapporo at six-forty.

Route 39 ran southwest through a thin layer of fresh snow. The plow had come through at ten in the morning — an even dark-gray stripe down the middle, white banks to the sides — and Ogawa kept the Toyota Crown at forty-eight kilometers an hour, no faster. He did not like speed. Never had.

The meeting in Asahikawa was brief: the deputy chief of the city police, an old colleague from Tokyo days, apologized for not being able to come to Sapporo himself, and for half an hour they drank coffee in the duty office. Ogawa reported on the general shape of the case. The deputy nodded, listened. On the way out he asked quietly:
"Ogawa-san. Your inspector."
"Yes."
"Kurosawa."
"Yes."
"Is it hard for him now?"
"It's always hard for him," said Ogawa. "That's how he lives."
The deputy nodded once more. Shook his hand. Ogawa stepped into the piercing sun of an Asahikawa afternoon — the sky was clear, with thin gray clouds at the edges — and got into the car.

On the back seat he set two bento he'd bought at the station. One for himself, one for Sasaki. Sasaki's wife — as he sometimes joked when he loaded them with evening work — didn't warm their supper. He did. It was one of those old-fashioned gestures at which Kurosawa slightly shrugged and Sasaki accepted with a barely visible nod.
He cracked the window a centimeter — fresh air on his cheek — and drove out of the city.

Thirty minutes on he turned off Route 39 onto 452. This was a narrower mountain road — the one that led toward Ashibetsu. He was not planning to go to the ryokan itself — that was Kurosawa's business, he'd sort it out — but he had a small detour: in the roadside settlement, twenty kilometers before the mountain itself, lived an old forester who had given an unofficial account of an unmarked car that had twice in the past month driven up toward the kominka.
Kurosawa had wanted to send one of the operatives. Ogawa had said:
"No need. I'll stop by from Asahikawa myself. It's on my way."
"Ogawa-san."
"Kurosawa. I'm not going up the mountain. I'm going to the village. A village is not a ryokan. A village is a village."

Kurosawa looked at him a long time with that look of his in which Ogawa always read a little more than had been said. But he didn't object. Kurosawa never objected to his elder — if his elder was Ogawa.
Ogawa had smiled to himself then, inside. Kurosawa trusted him. That was that.
Now he was driving Route 452. Forest on both sides. Snow in the branches. The sky had darkened a little — low clouds from the northwest — but visibility was normal.

He turned on the radio. Local Asahikawa station. Weather forecast — by evening, possible blizzard in the mountains. Then an old enka, a man's voice, calm, about a port and a woman. Ogawa hummed quietly along — the refrain he'd known since youth.
The clock showed fourteen forty-seven.

He thought briefly, without weight, that Kurosawa had looked tired today. This morning at the briefing. That mixi post. Ogawa had glanced at the screen over Kurosawa's shoulder, read it twice, nodded — and then spent half a day thinking about what to say. Said nothing. He knew: Kurosawa knew. Words would have been superfluous here. The best thing he could do for Kurosawa was not to keep him from thinking. And — not to show that he was worried.

He decided: on the way back tonight he'd stop by that bento shop at the station, take two. One for Sasaki. One for Kurosawa. Kurosawa would refuse. That was nothing. Ogawa would make him eat at least the rice.
He smiled to himself. Quietly.

Eight kilometers ahead slow equipment appeared. First only the yellow flash of a beacon among the white-gray landscape. Then — the outline of a tractor. A small agricultural tractor with a front dozer blade — the kind municipal services use to clear side roads. Moving slowly — maybe fifteen kilometers an hour — in its own lane.

Ogawa slowed. Assessed the distance. The oncoming lane was clear — a straight sight line of some four hundred meters — and he could pass calmly. He switched on the left indicator, glanced in the rearview mirror, checked oncoming once more.
Clear.
He pulled into the oncoming lane and began to pass.
At the second the front of his Toyota drew even with the tractor's cab — the tractor, sharply, without a signal, without prior braking, turned its wheel to the left.
The bucket went toward the Toyota.

Ogawa had two tenths of a second to react. He managed to press the brake and crank the wheel to the right. It was the right decision — from the physics of it — but the tractor was no longer going straight; it was going at a diagonal, and the oncoming vector of the bucket struck the driver-side door of the Toyota at fifteen kilometers plus fifty — sixty-five combined.
The Toyota took the strike full into the center of the driver-side door.
The A-pillar deformed inward. Glass shattered. The airbag deployed — but from the side, not the front — and not where it should have.
Ogawa lost consciousness at once. The second event — aortic rupture from blunt chest trauma — occurred in the next three seconds.
He did not manage to notice either.
The car slid off the highway onto the shoulder, fell on its right side into a snowbank. The engine ran another twenty seconds — then stopped by itself.
The radio kept playing. The man's voice was finishing the song about the port.
The tractor stopped. From the cab, slowly, a man in a blue work coverall climbed out. Around sixty, short-cropped gray, a good face.
He came to the Toyota. Looked through the broken glass. Saw.
He drew a phone from the chest pocket of the coverall. Dialed 110.
"Accident," he said evenly. "Route 452, somewhere on the seventh kilometer from the crossing. Car against a tractor. The driver, it seems, is not moving."
He gave his name. Katsushi Matsuda, sixty-two, municipal worker of Ashibetsu. Dictated the number of his ID. The dispatcher said a team would be there in ten minutes.

Matsuda ended the call. Stood beside Ogawa's car a few more seconds — the way a man stands who has just done everything he could. Then he went back to the tractor, took a thermos of tea from the cab, poured into the lid. Drank, standing on the shoulder, looking down the road from the Asahikawa side.
Waiting for the ambulance.
Sasaki took the call at three-eight in the afternoon. Kurosawa sat opposite, at his desk, reading someone's protocol. He watched her.
She listened for half a minute. Did not say a single word. Only — once — briefly closed her eyes. Then opened them.
"Yes," she said. "Yes. We're leaving."
She put the phone down.
Kurosawa was watching.
"Sir," said Sasaki. "Ogawa."
Kurosawa said nothing. Waited.
"Accident. Route 452. A tractor."
"Alive?"
"No."

Kurosawa looked at her a long time. Then he lowered his eyes. On the protocol in front of him was written something about a Yamato delivery schedule to Ashibetsu village for October. He read the first line again — mechanically — did not understand a word. He read it a second time.
Then he said, quietly:
"Who."
"The tractor driver. Local. Sixty-two. Sober. No record."
"Where did he swerve."
"Into the oncoming lane. Ogawa was passing him — the driver turned left. Without a signal."
Kurosawa nodded.
"We're going."
Sasaki was already standing with her jacket in her hands. She had known he would say it. She had known it when she was on the phone.
Kenji stood up from his corner desk.
"Uncle," he said. "Am I with you?"
"No," said Kurosawa. His voice level. "You stay. Keep working the Hokkaiden power-pattern. Find the lake."
"Uncle."
"Kenji. This isn't about you. We need you here."
Kenji sat down. Did not object. Did not look at the screen at once. Just sat — held his fingers on the keyboard, did not move them.
Kurosawa took his jacket.
Sasaki drove. Kurosawa sat on her right, looking out at Route 12, then at the interchange with 39, then at 452.
They were silent.
Twenty minutes short of the place the snow began. Fine, not yet a blizzard. The Corolla's wipers went. The right one left a thin streak — Kurosawa noticed this for a second — and forgot at once.

He thought about Ogawa. About how Ogawa had stood up at his desk in the January meeting and said aloud: "Kurosawa is leading this series." About how Ogawa would step out with him on the balcony and smoke one cigarette. About his wife, whom Kurosawa had seen twice in ten years — a small woman with a long braid, smiling quietly. About his elder daughter — a teacher — whom Ogawa had once shown him on the phone, with a pride in which there was no fatherly pathos, only fact.
He was not yet thinking why this had happened today. Not yet. That would come.
Sasaki glanced at him once.
"Sir."
"Yes."
"I'm sorry."
"I know."
She said nothing more.
He said nothing either.
The blizzard began to strengthen.

The site was ten kilometers before Ashibetsu-yama. A straight stretch. Two patrol cars already stood — blue-red flashing. The ambulance too — a stretcher being unloaded from the rear doors, empty. No one was hurrying.
Kurosawa got out of the Corolla before Sasaki had killed the engine. Walked slowly.
The Toyota Crown lay on its right side in a snowbank. Driver-side door broken and crushed inward. Glass on the road. One rear number plate, bent, lay separately.
He came closer. A police officer from the local station — a junior inspector, about thirty — recognized Kurosawa from his shoulders and straightened. Wanted to salute.
"Don't," said Kurosawa. "Show me."
The junior inspector nodded. Led him to the car.
Ogawa sat in his seat. His seatbelt was fastened. His head bowed to the left, toward the broken door. Right shoulder turned forward. Eyes closed.

On his lap lay a paper — pulled from the brown envelope in which, from the look of it, he had kept the report after the meeting with the Asahikawa deputy. The paper was slightly bent, but dry — no blood on it. There was very little blood at all. Only on the left cheek — a thin line from the mouth.
Kurosawa looked for a minute.

Then he slowly bent and with the tips of his fingers fastened two buttons on Ogawa's overcoat collar — the top button was unfastened, the collar turned aside. It was a gesture Ogawa himself would have made had he woken in the morgue and seen himself laid out. Small — but Kurosawa could not not do it.
He straightened.
Sasaki stood half a step behind.
"The tractor driver," said Kurosawa, without turning.
"Over there," said Sasaki. Quietly.
Kurosawa turned his head.

Fifteen meters off, by the tractor, stood an elderly man in a blue coverall. Held a plastic cup — most likely, tea. Talking with another officer. He didn't look shaken — not calm, but with the look of a man who has just reassigned his own life, telling the story in detail, slowly, without tears.
Kurosawa went to him.
The tractor driver saw, fell silent.
"Matsuda-san," said Kurosawa. He'd caught the name on the badge.
"Yes, sir."
"Kurosawa, prefectural police."
"Yes, sir."

Kurosawa looked him in the eyes a long time. Matsuda held the gaze. Did not look away. In his eyes was that particular emptiness that comes to people who have been told what time to get into the cab at six in the evening, and who got in — and did what they were told.
Kurosawa did not see fear in them. He also did not see a lie. He saw a third thing — and, unlike with Toshi, had no dictionary for it.
"Tell me," he said quietly, "when did you last work this road before today."
"Yesterday, sir. And the day before. And on Monday."
"Every day."
"Yes, sir. The chief gave the order. Clear the sides."
"Who is your chief."
"The Ashibetsu municipality. Head of public works."
"His name."
"Suzuki-san."
"Thank you."
Kurosawa turned to Sasaki. He said nothing. She understood: check Suzuki. She nodded.
Kurosawa looked at Matsuda again.
"You're sober."
"Yes, sir."
"You haven't taken any medications today."
"No, sir."
"You see well."
"Yes, sir. Glasses only for reading."
"Did you see the car you were being passed by?"
"Sir," said Matsuda, "I didn't notice it."
Kurosawa looked at him a minute. Then nodded.
"Thank you," he said. "Someone will speak with you again."
Matsuda nodded. Lifted the cup to his lips. Swallowed. His hand did not tremble.
Kurosawa stepped away from him to the shoulder. Sasaki came up in ten seconds. Both stood above the highway, looking at Ogawa's Toyota lying on its right side in the snow.
"Sir."
"Yes."
"This is not an accident."
"I know."
"Matsuda is not the one who did this."
"I know."
"Matsuda is the one who was told."
"Yes."
Sasaki was silent.
"Sir."
"Yes."
"I'll check Suzuki. In two hours I'll have his biography. In six — his accounts."
"I know."
"I'll find nothing there. He'll be clean. Through him someone paid someone, who through someone else paid the one who hired Matsuda."
"I know."
Kurosawa was silent a long time.
Then he said:
"He knew Ogawa was going there."
"Yes."
"He knew it no later than this morning. We decided it last night in the office."
"Yes."
"That means we have someone in the department."
Sasaki turned her head to him.
"Toshi said as much then, at the detention center."
"I know."
"Then you thought he was bluffing."
"I know."
Kurosawa looked down at his boots, covered with fresh snow. The toe of the right was black from melted ice — he had not noticed when.
"Then I thought he was bluffing."
He did not add now I do not think so. It was unnecessary.
Kurosawa looked once more at the Toyota.

The radio in Ogawa's car was still playing — quietly, muffled through the broken glass. Now it was another song — a woman's voice, old, of the sort Ogawa would not have chosen himself, and would only have listened to because the station had chosen for him.
Kurosawa came closer. Stretched his arm through the broken side glass — carefully, around the sharp edge — and turned off the radio with a short flick of the finger. The button clicked.
The silence became complete.
The junior inspector, standing a meter behind, bowed briefly.
"Sir," he said, "we were awaiting your instructions, or —"
"That's fine," said Kurosawa. "The radio was on. That's how it should have been. I turned it off."

The junior inspector nodded — did not understand why, but noted in himself: "at sixteen seventeen the radio was turned off by Inspector Kurosawa by personal decision." It would go in the protocol. Someone in Tokyo would read this someday.
Kurosawa turned back to Sasaki.
"Tell Kenji," he said. "To check Suzuki's calls over the last three days. All of them. And the calls of the number Suzuki called most often. Then — every number in contact with that number."
"A ring."
"Yes. Three levels. No further — three is enough to see who's really steering."
Sasaki nodded. Stepped five meters away — the signal was better there — and began dialing.
The ambulance took Ogawa at four-twenty. The forensics team worked until late night. Kurosawa stayed until dusk — stood by the shoulder — then Sasaki came up and said quietly:
"Sir. Let's go. They'll finish here without you."
He nodded. Went to the Corolla.

She opened the passenger door for him. He got in. Not at once. He stood a second before the door — a hand on the top — and looked once more at the place where the Toyota had stood. It had already been towed away. Only tracks in the snowbank remained — deep, black on white.
He sat down in the car. Belted in. Sasaki closed the door behind him, walked round, sat in the driver's seat.
The engine came to life. The wipers switched on.
The right wiper left a streak.
Sasaki did not pull away at once.
Looked forward.
Kurosawa also looked — not at the road — just forward.

Beyond the windshield the blue-red pulses of the patrol cars still flashed. One of the officers was waving a flashlight, directing the occasional oncoming driver around. Someone from the forensics team was setting up a portable floodlight on a tripod — evening was falling fast, and they still had work.
Sasaki opened the glove box. Drew out a small white towel — she kept it there for all occasions — and laid it on Kurosawa's lap. Did not put it in his hand. Just laid it. Kurosawa did not move.
She took the shifter. Engaged first.
"Sir."
"Yes."
"Where."
Kurosawa thought. Did not answer at once.
"To his wife," he said at last. "She should be told in person."
"To Hiragishi."
"Yes."
Sasaki nodded. Released the clutch. The car pulled slowly from the shoulder onto the road.
Beyond the window drifted the place where the Toyota had stood. Tracks in the snow. One broken side mirror flashed once in the headlight of a passing car — and vanished around the curve.
Kurosawa sat. Held the towel on his lap. Did not wipe anything. He had nothing to wipe.
Kurosawa sat in Sasaki's car by the roadside. He did not cry. He did not yet know how many times this would not be the final price.

p.emphasis: In the second cupboard — a shirt no one will take back.

section.subtitle: Chapter Seventeen and a Half
section.p: Kingyo had been closed for two hours when Yukio unlocked the back door.

He did not switch on the overhead light. Only the lamp above the counter — the one Sato left burning all night so the fish in the round tank could see each other — and its faint reflection in the bottles on the shelf. It smelled of warm wood and the remnant of ginger broth.
Yukio did not sit in his own place.

He sat one stool over to the left — the one Ogawa took once every two months, after work, on a Thursday when his wife was at her sister's in Otaru. Ogawa would order one sake, warmed, and one small plate of edamame. Drank slowly. Spoke little. Sometimes he'd take a folded newspaper from his pocket and lay it on the counter — not to read, just to lay it there — as though he needed an ordinary object on the surface.
The stool was empty.

Yukio drew a pack of Peace from his inner pocket. Set it on the counter. Opened it. Turned it upside-down, shook the cigarettes into a neat row — evened them with his little finger — fourteen. Sato used to do this before a long shift: he would lay out the pack and not smoke a single one, only look. He said it was his way of testing whether he would hold the night.
Yukio did not smoke a single one.

Beside the row he laid what he'd taken from the car — before the photographer from the department arrived, before all of it became evidence. The glove. The left one. Ogawa could never find the right one in his overcoat pocket in time and always put on the left first — his wife had laughed at him for it twenty-two years. The leather was dark, worn on the pad of the thumb. Inside, under the lining, warm — Yukio touched it with a finger — still warm, it seemed, though it was impossible, the car had been standing in the cold nearly an hour before they arrived.
He laid the glove palm-up. Straightened the fingers.
The clock on the wall in Kingyo ticked the way it always ticked. One of the fish knocked its nose against the glass and turned back.
Yukio sat.

He was not thinking about the case. Not thinking about Endo, not thinking about the photographs, not thinking about the fact that tomorrow was morning and he'd have to go to Ogawa's wife and say what had to be said. He looked at the row of cigarettes and at the glove and at the empty stool, and inside him was one simple, dull, good thought: Ogawa liked coming here.
After a long time he gathered the cigarettes back into the pack. One by one, without hurry. Closed the lid. Put it in his inner pocket.
He did not take the glove. He laid it on the stool — where a palm would have been — and pushed it slightly toward the counter so it wouldn't fall.
Kingyo he did not take with him. Kingyo was Sato's, and Sato was to come back tomorrow at ten, and everything had to be in place.

Yukio switched off the lamp above the counter. In the dark the tank still glowed for another minute with its own faint light — Sato kept a night-light in the water for the fish — then his eyes adjusted, and he saw only the outlines of the bottles.

He went out through the back door. Locked it with his own key — Sato had given him a spare three years ago, after the fire in the neighboring building, "just in case," and Yukio had never once used it.
The key turned stiffly. The frost had drawn the lock tight.
Yukio stood a second more beneath the door, holding the key in the lock. Then drew it out.

p.emphasis: He'll release him tomorrow. Not today.
"The name," she said, "you'll have to invent again."

section.subtitle: Chapter Eighteen
section.p: The morgue of Sapporo Kōsei stood on the north side of the hospital block, in the shadow of the eight-story clinic, and the sun in November never reached it. Kurosawa parked in the staff lane. Nobody checked the placards there.

Endo waited on the second-floor balcony. In a coat over a sweater, in worn-out sneakers that had been hers, it seemed, since their first meeting in 2019. She held a cigarette in her palm — not raised, just held. She saw him — did not wave, only nodded.
He came up by the service stairs.
"Kurosawa."
"Endo-san."
"Let's go."
She did not ask how the funeral had gone. He did not say. They kept between them the distance of profession that neither checked more often than needed.

In the corridor it smelled of formalin and, faintly, of vending-machine coffee. The fluorescent lamps hummed on one note. Two assistants greeted them and walked past. Endo went ahead, not looking back.

She led him not into the anatomical room but to her own office — a narrow room at the end of the corridor, with a single window that gave onto an inner courtyard with rubbish bins and one stunted oak.
On the working desk, on a clean sheet of paper, lay a folder. Old, cardboard, pasted over with two layers of tape.
"Sit."
He sat.
She closed the door. Did not go to the desk at once — stood with her back to him, arms folded, rubbed with two fingers under her left eye.
"I'm sorry about Ogawa," she said, without turning.
"I know."
"He came here on Monday. Was asking about the 1998 archive. I didn't have time to speak with him."
"I know."
She turned.
"Kurosawa, I didn't want to say this today. I wanted to wait a week. But you came yourself, and I'm not in the habit of keeping folders closed on the desk."
He was silent.
She came over, pulled out the chair on the other side and sat — not in her own place, but opposite him, as to a patient.
"We've finished the analysis," she said.
"And."
"First — one thing. The guardian of the mother in Sendai signed on Monday. I spoke with him personally, not through a notary. He said: if this isn't Ren, then where has the body gone."
Kurosawa nodded. Once.
"The body in your brother's grave — is not your brother."
He laid his palms on his knees. Kept them there. Did not look down.
"Say it more slowly."

She opened the folder. Inside was a thin stack — two protocols, three photographs, a printout of the DNA report with lines underlined. She did not give him anything to hold; she laid them out in the order convenient to her.
"First. The molar."
She placed the first photograph before him — a digital photo of a tooth, black and white, with a millimeter ruler alongside.

"This is the lower left M1 from the body exhumed from the Shukotsu-dō cemetery in Hiragishi. Twenty-eighth of October. An ordinary molar, healthy, no implant. One filling entry in the occlusal pit — old, amalgam."
"Ren did not have this tooth."

"He did not. In Ren's place stood a ceramic implant with a titanium post. Installed at the Midori clinic in Tokyo, 2018. I have a copy of the chart. I have the post-operative control X-ray. The post does not burn in a fire, Kurosawa. It can deform, but it's there. Here it isn't."
He nodded. Once.
"Second. A rib."
The second photograph. A fragment of a curved bone, with an oval outlined in chalk in the middle.

"The eighth left rib. Here — a microcalcification, long healed, consolidated. An old fracture, mended with a small bulge. Such things stay long. There is nothing like it in your brother's medical history. He never broke a rib. Not in childhood, not later — I asked Kioko-san, she confirmed."
"You spoke with my mother."
"Yes. I told her nothing. I asked about fractures as though gathering a family-history brief. She believed."
"Thank you."
"Don't thank me. Third."
She laid down the DNA printout.
"Mitochondrial. Samples from the dental pulp. Comparison with your sample and with the archival sample of your mother. No match."
"Mother."
"She's been in the bone-marrow donor registry since '99. We have her mt-profile in the archive. It is unambiguous."
"What's the margin for error."
"One in something that doesn't happen."
He was silent. A long time. Endo did not fill the silence.
The breath of a lab assistant in the corridor — through the crack under the door — showed once and then didn't.
"Who is this man," said Kurosawa.
"Unidentified. Thirty to forty-five. By enamel isotope analysis — grew up on Hokkaido, likely the northeast. Diet — fish-based. I can't give more without opening the case."
"Don't open it."
"I don't intend to. For now."
He at last looked at her hands. At the thumb of her right, on which was a small cut — fresh, two days old, already dried. She noticed his glance.
"Envelope knife," she said. "Funny."
"Not funny."
"Not funny."

She stood. Went to the window. Took an ashtray from the sill — small, ceramic, with two grooves — and set it on the edge of the desk between them, as one might who wanted her guest to do at least one ordinary thing.
He did not light one. Nor did she.
"Kurosawa."
"Yes."
"I won't tell you what this means. I know you know it better than I do."
"I know."
"But I have to say one thing."
He waited.
"If he wasn't in that car — it doesn't mean he is alive now. It means he wasn't in that car."
"I understand."
"These are different things. I've seen too many people confuse them. Don't."
"I won't."
She nodded. It was one of those nods of hers in which there was more attention than in most of her words.
He looked at the DNA printout. At the underlined line. At the date of the analysis — yesterday, 22:14. She had worked in the night.
"You slept," he said.
"No."
"How long."
"Three hours. I don't like to hold a result more than a day."
"You should sleep."
"I should do my work. So should you."
He rose. Not at once — hesitating, bracing one palm on the knee. The rib on the right, the sixth, twinged with old memory. He set his foot down more firmly, and it quieted.
"Thank you, Endo-san."
"Kurosawa."
He stopped on the threshold.
"One more thing."
