She came to the door — not close, left a step and a half between them — and looked at him the way she had not looked at him in this office before. Not as a forensic. As a person who knows that after her next sentence will come years of another's life.
"You searched for Ren for five years. Those were years with a name. Now the name doesn't work."
He was silent.
"The name," she said, "you'll have to invent again."

p.emphasis: Everything is paid for by someone not in the room.

section.subtitle: Chapter Nineteen
section.p: The courtroom on the fourth floor of the Sapporo District Court was the smallest of the three used for motions. Twelve seats for the public. One window, closed at two turns. The heating warmed the air as though there were syrup in it — and everyone who came in from the corridor stood a few seconds on the threshold, waiting for their eyes to stop watering.

Kurosawa sat in the second public row. Alone. Sasaki had not come — she'd stayed at the department, working the new Yamato delivery block Kenji had pulled at dawn. Kenji had not come either. It was the right call.

Toshi was brought in wearing a gray sweatsuit. Not the prison blue — the lawyer had negotiated the change at the previous hearing. The cuffs were removed at the threshold; two guards remained in the doorway. Toshi walked to the defense table evenly, without wavering — the way he had always walked in Furano between the house and the well: not fast, not slow, exactly as long as needed.
He did not look toward Kurosawa.
The prosecutor — Fujiwara, in the same black suit as a month ago — opened the folder, cleared his throat, and began by the protocol. The crisp pages in his hands rustled slowly.

Kurosawa did not listen for the first four minutes. He watched the back of Toshi's head. Clean, shaved two days ago — a faint whitish undergrowth in the hollow above the collar. Thin. In seven months of detention Toshi had lost some fourteen kilograms, as the doctor had written in the petition. From this angle it was visible how it looked.

Toshi's lawyer was new. Not the one from the start. That one had been state-assigned, sluggish, read from an iPad and mixed up dates. This one Kurosawa was seeing for the first time: about forty, slim, suit not from the prefectural catalog — Tokyo cut, thin wool — rimless glasses. Briefcase — shadowy brown leather, thin stack, well worn.
The name on the badge — Sudo, Sudo Kenji. Kurosawa noted it briefly in a notebook.

Sudo spoke evenly. He repeated three points of justification — cooperation with the investigation, voluntary surrender, deteriorating health — but did it not the way one speaks by the protocol, but the way one speaks when one knows the court will hear him out to the end. He laid before the judge three certificates, four recommendations, and one billing statement from the Hokuto clinic. Everything — properly filed. Everything — in stitched folders with the same cloth spine.
Kurosawa narrowed his eyes. Cloth spine. Bound in two places in Sapporo — one of them, an old one in the Chūō district, serving the city's leading law firms. Expensive.

The judge — a woman in her fifties, with a thin scarf at her neck — asked two clarifying questions. About internet access outside service purposes. About the possibility of a trip to Aomori for the funeral of a distant relative, which might happen in the coming months. Sudo answered clearly: internet — only from a police workstation, under Kenji Yamada's log; travel — only with prior coordination from the prosecutor. He knew the staff's names. He knew the department's schedule.
Kurosawa slowly turned a page of the notebook.
The prosecutor objected briefly, by form. Not seriously, without insistence. His formulations, too, even, shorter than they might have been.

The judge heard him out. Recorded it. Announced the ruling: the defense motion is granted; recognizance not to depart; electronic bracelet on the lower limb; daily check-in at the Chūō-minami station; consultative work with Sapporo police under an agreed program; contact with any possible witness in the Kamishiroi case prohibited.
Toshi did not move. Only once he lowered and raised his eyelids — longer than an ordinary blink.
Kurosawa looked at his hands. Folded on his knees, relaxed. Callused palms. The calluses — old. He had not held wood for seven months, but the hands had not forgotten the shape.
In the corridor before the stairs Sudo was waiting for him.
He did not come near — he stood by the fire hydrant, back to the window — but nodded to Kurosawa the way one nods to a person with whom one has a brief business exchange.
Kurosawa came over.
"Sudo-sensei."
"Kurosawa-keibu."
"Who hired you."
Sudo smiled — briefly, without offense.
"You know I can't answer that question."
"I know. I'm asking anyway."
"The client is a legal entity financing a rehabilitation program for former Zen novices who have found themselves in difficult circumstances. It's in my materials."
"I read them. In your materials — the name 'Reisen-dō Sangyō.'"
"Yes."
"That's the restoration of temple interiors. Hokkaido, Tokyo. Four branches."
"Correct."
"You know who else this firm finances."
Sudo adjusted the temple of his glasses. Calmly.

"Kurosawa-keibu. I know that you know. I know that you know that I know. It doesn't change my work. My client has the right to pay for the defense of its ward. In all the documents — cleaner than most corporate cases that pass through this corridor."
"I don't doubt it."
"Don't. Good day."
Sudo nodded, took his briefcase, walked to the elevator. He went unhurriedly.

Kurosawa stood a second. Looked at the glass of the fire hydrant. Saw his own reflection in it — slightly bent — and saw that the right brow, with the old scar, stood a little higher than the left. It had been standing so for several weeks now. Only now had he noticed.
He looked away.
Toshi came out through the service exit — not the main one. Kurosawa waited for him in his car in the side lot, heater on. Toshi recognized the car, came over, stopped by the passenger side.
Kurosawa opened it from inside.
Toshi sat. Cautiously — as though the car were a stranger not only to him but to his body after seven months of a cell. He belted in. Placed his palms on his knees.
"Where to," said Kurosawa.
"Wherever you take me."
"Your studio on Kita-nine."
"Yes."
"Your lawyer has already brought your things there."
"I know."
"Did he tell you?"
"No."
"Then how do you know?"
Toshi looked out the window. Did not answer at once.
"Because otherwise he wouldn't be that lawyer."

Kurosawa pulled the car out of the lot. The warmed engine hummed evenly. Snow fell in a fine grain — not from yesterday's cloud, but from a new, thinner one — and beyond the windshield filled the emptiness of the intersection.
They drove three blocks in silence.
"Toshi."
"Yes."
"I would have taken you into the department as a consultant regardless."
"I know."
"But Fujiwara signed faster than I thought."
"I know."
"You understand why."
"I understand."
"Then say it yourself."
Toshi turned his head to him. For the first time in the conversation — directly.

"Because it's convenient to him too," he said. "Me on the outside is easier for him to find if he wants to find. And me on the outside is easier for you to show to others if you want to show. Everyone who needed it got theirs."
"And you."
"I got the way out."
"And what will you do with it."
Toshi looked ahead a long time. In the light of oncoming headlights his profile seemed unfamiliar — not Toshi from the hut in Furano, but someone from the road, picked up on the highway.
"I'll do what I did."
"That's not an answer."
"I know."
Kurosawa did not press. He knew the rules. Toshi's answer came once per meeting; he had given it today with that one "got the way out." No more.
They came up to the right building — a five-story manshon with a steel-sheathed entry. Kurosawa stopped the car. Toshi slowly unbuckled.
"Toshi."
"Yes."
"We leave the day after tomorrow. North. Shiribetsu."
"I know."
"You come with us."
"Yes."
"It's not an offer."
"Not an offer."
Toshi opened the door. Did not get out at once — held the handle.
"Kurosawa."
"Yes."
"I won't go to the other side of the lake with you."
"I didn't ask."
"I know."

He got out. A thin figure in a gray sweatsuit under the entry-lamp. Did not look back. Did not wave. Opened the door with a key, went in, and through the glass Kurosawa watched him climb to the second landing — holding the rail with his left hand — and vanish.
Kurosawa sat another minute with the engine on. He looked at the entry. At the yellow rectangle of the lamp. At the fine snow that fell into that light and vanished before reaching the asphalt.
He dialed Sasaki.
"Kurosawa."
"Dropped him off."
"How is he."
"Thin."
"Understood."
"Sasaki."
"Yes."
"Sudo. The lawyer."

"Pulled him on the registry while you were still in the corridor. Tokyo, partner at 'Sudo-Yamaguchi-Mori.' Clients — three religious foundations, four construction, one pharmaceutical. Reisen-dō on the list the last five years. Funds flow through a sub-account for the 'rehabilitation program for former novices.' Legally — clean."
"Legally."
"Legally."
He was silent.
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."
"He's playing chess with us through him."
"I know."
"You took the piece that was handed to you."
"I know."
"That's nothing. We know it's his. We move on."
"We move on."
He hung up. Pulled the car out of the yard. Onto the ring road.

Streetlamps stood sparser than downtown. Snow from the second cloud had now settled to a steady fall, and in the light of each lamp it fell at the same angle — as though someone had set one light source on the whole district and did not wish to change it.
Kurosawa drove home. Not home — to the department.

p.emphasis: I think I have someone who listens to me differently.

section.subtitle: Chapter Twenty
section.p: Ren set the meeting in a small kissaten on the second floor of Otaru Station. Not in the café on the first — the tourists sat there — but in the old one, with wooden paneling and a menu that hadn't been changed since the nineties. Kurosawa had flown in that morning from Tokyo on a matter that wasn't a matter: a second-order witness in a fraud case he was tangentially attached to. He had two hours before his return flight. Ren had proposed it — himself — and Kurosawa had been surprised, because Ren rarely asked for meetings on a working weekday.
He came up the stairs at ten-forty.

Ren sat by the window, back to the door. He had hung his coat on the chair back — dark blue, right elbow worn through — and was himself in a beige sweater Kurosawa remembered from their last winter in the parental home, some ten years ago. Ren's hair had gone grayer — not like Yukio, who had grayed evenly at both temples, but in patches — and one such lock stood above his right ear like a brushstroke someone had forgotten to wipe away.
Ren turned when he heard the step. Smiled quickly. Stood.
"Yukio."
"Ren."

They did not embrace. They never embraced. They nodded to one another — the way brothers nod who have four years between them and one shared memory of the night their father first failed to return — and sat.

The waitress was alone, elderly, hair lacquered into immobility. She brought water in glass tumblers. She did not ask — she knew Ren took a pot of coffee with milk, and the guest would decide for himself. Kurosawa asked for black.
Beyond the window — Otaru, snow-covered, with steam from the fish stalls below rising to the sill and vanishing.
"How are things," said Kurosawa.
"Quiet."
"Quiet is good."
"Quiet is what is."
Ren always answered that way. Kurosawa forgot it every visit and began with the same phrase. Every time got the same back.

They spoke first about Ayano. She was fourteen. She'd just started her second year of middle school, chosen the drawing club instead of tennis — and Ren was pleased and not pleased at once, in that particular way a single father is pleased that a child is quiet, and not pleased that the child is quiet — and could not say it. Kurosawa listened. Did not hurry.
"Does she show you her work?" he asked.
"She shows me."
"Good?"
"I don't know. She draws small things. Corners of rooms. Tables. Once — a coat sleeve on a chair. I don't know if that's good. I only see that she looks at such things more attentively than I do."
"That's already something."
"Yes."
Ren fell silent for a moment. Stirred the coffee. The spoon knocked the side of the cup once.
"Yukio."
"Yes."
"I've recently started going to one meeting."
"Where."
"Not exactly a club. Not a group. It's a person."
Kurosawa did not immediately understand which.
"A therapist?"
"No." Ren smiled at the corner of his mouth. "I don't think so. He doesn't call himself that."
"Then what."
Ren looked out the window. At the steam. At a woman's figure below, carrying a box with something long, wrapped in paper, and vanishing into a side street.
"I don't know how to explain. He's like — an interlocutor. He listens. Doesn't propose. Doesn't give advice. Doesn't assign homework."
"How much does it cost."
"He offers it free."
Kurosawa slowly set the cup down.
"Ren."
"I know what you're about to say."
"That's not the point."
"That too."
"Who is he."

"An acquaintance of an acquaintance. I don't want to explain how we met — because you'll be asking questions until evening, and I won't give you answers to all of them. He's — quiet. He lives far away. I go to him once every two months, on a Sunday. One hour."
"What do you tell him."
"What happens."
"About Ayano?"
"About everything."
Kurosawa was silent.

He had many questions. He had professional questions — about addresses, about registries, about prior records — and he had brotherly questions — why not me — and he had one question with which the rest began and ended: is this man well.
He asked none of them.

He knew how to speak with a witness. He did not know how to speak with a brother who had just laid on the table between them something that was not quite a complaint and not quite a trust, but something third, for which Kurosawa had no name.
"Are you happy at these meetings?" he said at last.
Ren thought. Looked into the cup.
"Not 'happy.' That's not the word. I think I have someone who listens to me differently."
"Differently — how."
Ren raised his eyes.
"Not like you. You listen the way you put questions. He listens the way one stands by the door and holds it open."
Kurosawa nodded. Said nothing.

He'd thought at the time that it was an offense. He wasn't offended — such things did not work as offenses between them — but he'd thought about it aloud in the night, flying back to Tokyo, and forgotten by morning. He remembered that Ren had said something about doors. He didn't remember what.
He would forget also what Ren said next.
"Yukio."
"Yes."
"If ever — I don't know why — I don't pick up the phone for two weeks running — don't worry right away."
"Why might that happen."
"I don't know. Just — don't worry right away."
"Ayano."
"Ayano I'll leave with the neighbor. Mizuki, from the flat below. She has the key. She's kind. She knows whom to call, if anything."
"Are you going somewhere?"
"No. I'm only saying — just in case. You know that these last six months my heart has been giving me small warnings. Aunt Kioko had the same."
"Have you been to a doctor?"
"I have. They say it's stress. They say cut down the work. I'm cutting down."
"How many hours a week."
"Fifty-five, now forty."
"That isn't forty."
"That's approaching forty."
They smiled at one another briefly. Very briefly.

Kurosawa took these words about "two weeks" the way one takes another's superstitious wishes — with polite seriousness and without weight. He was forty-one, his brother forty-five, both full of blood and alive, and Kurosawa did not live in a world in which men at forty-five vanished.
"All right," he said. "I won't worry right away."
"Thank you."
Later, even later, this moment with "thank you" Kurosawa would play out aloud for five years. First as a lapse of hearing. Then as a lapse of attention. Then as a lapse of love itself.
They walked out of the station together. Ren was going to the parking lot — he'd parked in back — Kurosawa was going to the express bus to Chitose.
At the crossing they stopped.
"See you at New Year," said Kurosawa.
"For sure."
"Give my love to Ayano."
"I will."
Ren for a second seemed as though he wanted to add something. He stood, looked past Kurosawa's shoulder — not at him — at something behind him, or at nothing. Then he shrugged his right shoulder.
"Well."
"Well."
They did not embrace.
Ren turned, went to the parking lot. Kurosawa went to the bus.

Having walked ten steps, Kurosawa looked back. Not because he felt something — he felt nothing then — but because at the traffic light he had to wait, and the head movement was simple. He saw Ren's back, in the coat with the worn elbow, in the gray lock above the right ear. He saw Ren slow beside an old man with a cart and patiently go around him along the curb.
It was the last thing he saw.
Two weeks later Ren did not pick up the phone.
Three — Kurosawa began to worry.

Four — the call came from the Asahikawa police: Ren's car, off the highway into snow, burned down to the frame. Inside — a body, identified by the teeth. Formal examination. Formal conclusion. Formal funeral a week later, at which Kurosawa stood beside his uncle and listened to the priest and could not recall anything from that morning in Otaru except one phrase — "heart giving warnings" — and one more, which he never recalled as a phrase, only as an intonation, as something about doors.
He did not recall it on the ninth day. Nor on the fortieth. Nor on the anniversary.
He would recall it now, on the night after Endo would set before him the DNA report with the non-matching mitochondrial.

He would sit in the kitchen. Brew coffee in the pot — twenty-two grams, three hundred and thirty grams of water — and drink it standing at the window. And between two sips the phrase would surface on its own from beneath the gray years, clearer than when it had been spoken.

p.emphasis: I think I have someone who listens to me differently.

section.p: The night in Sapporo would hold its shape. Kurosawa would set the cup on the windowsill and not wipe it.

p.emphasis: In a car of four people — the fifth is always the one not named.

section.subtitle: Chapter Twenty-One
section.p: The minibus was brought out of the department's service bay at four in the morning. A Toyota HiAce, steel-gray, with chains on all four wheels and two spare cans beneath the floor of the rear row. Sasaki checked tire pressures by flashlight, crouched down; the vapor of her breath rose briefly over her shoulder and vanished in the blue light beneath the bay lamp.

Kurosawa stood by the open rear doors. Counting silently — thermos, first-aid kit, winter blankets, two coils of rope, flashlights, spare batteries for the radios, Kenji's laptop in the yellow waterproof bag. Kenji stood beside him, hands in the pockets of his hoodie, not reaching for the vape. He kept a distance.

Toshi came up in a taxi at four-ten. Got out without a bag — only one strap over the shoulder, a thin backpack in which, it seemed, were two jumpers, two pairs of socks, and a tin of tea. The electronic bracelet under the trouser cuff made a thin thickening. He went to the minibus, stopped a meter from Kenji. Kenji stepped back half a pace.
"Good morning," said Toshi.
"Morning," said Sasaki, without rising from the wheel.
Kenji said nothing. Kurosawa looked at him.
"Kenji."
"Morning."

Kurosawa seated them briefly. He and Sasaki — up front; Sasaki at the wheel (Kurosawa bore long stretches badly, everyone knew), Kurosawa in the passenger seat. Kenji and Toshi — on the middle row, backs to the doors. The rear row — free, for bags and for anywhere anyone had to be moved if he became unwell.

Kenji lingered at the minibus door two seconds longer than needed. Then he got in, sat by the window, on the left. Toshi got in after him, sat on the right, leaving half a meter between them. Did not lean against the door.
Sasaki closed the rear. Walked around the vehicle. Sat behind the wheel. Belted in. Turned the key. The warmed engine hummed evenly.
"We move," she said.
Kurosawa nodded.

Sapporo at four-forty was empty. The Eneos station at the exit still burned in the black air with a yellow lamp, but no attendant was visible — sitting in the booth somewhere, warming up. The chains rumbled softly on the asphalt. In forty minutes they came out onto Route 274, heading southeast, toward Taiki and beyond, over the pass, into the Tokachi mountains.
The sky began to gray at half past five.

The first two hours they drove in silence. Kenji switched on his laptop on his lap, tapped quietly at the keyboard — Kurosawa saw from the mirror how his pale face was reflected in the screen — then closed it. He took out an apple vape from his pocket, spun it in his fingers, did not draw. Put it away.
Toshi did not shift his pose the whole time.

Kurosawa looked in the rearview mirror once. Toshi sat straight — not leaning into the seat — and stared into the back of the driver's headrest, as though at some point in it. Not out the window. Not at Kenji. At the point.
Sasaki saw this too. She said nothing.

Past the Hidaka pass the road grew narrower and the snow thicker. The chains left asphalt for compressed pack. The speed dropped to forty. Kenji coughed — a dry cough — pressed a fist to his mouth, endured, asked for water.
Kurosawa passed a bottle back over his shoulder.
Kenji drank, holding the bottle in both hands. A long time. Lowered it.
"Kenji-san," said Toshi quietly, without turning his head.
"Yes."
"Breathe through your nose. The bus is long. Do it three times — inhale four counts, hold four, exhale seven. Don't count more."
Kenji did not answer. Kurosawa looked in the mirror. Saw Kenji glance briefly at Toshi from the side, and after a pause nod. He began to breathe.
In a minute he evened out.
Kurosawa turned back to the road.
"Thank you," Kenji said. Quietly.
"You're welcome," said Toshi. As quietly.
Sasaki glanced at Kurosawa. Kurosawa at Sasaki. Not a word.

They stopped at a small lot by a closed village shop — about the middle of the road — to change drivers, refill the thermos with boiling water from a carried thermos-kettle, and take both bodies from the middle row out of the minibus for ten minutes while Sasaki checked the chains again.
Kenji stepped out first. Stood, stretched his shoulders, inhaled the cold air through his nose, exhaled briefly. Took out the vape. Drew.

Toshi stepped out slowly, holding the door frame. Stretched — a short movement of both hands over his head — and lowered them. Did not move on. Stood by the front fender, looked at the slope beyond the lot: snow, black trunks, mist behind the trees.
Kurosawa got out last. Came over to Sasaki.
"How is she."
"The chains on the rear loosened by half a turn. Tightened them."
"Three more hours."
"Three and a half. With lunch — four."
"We don't eat here."
"Not here."
He nodded. Turned to Toshi. Toshi did not move.
Kurosawa came and stood alongside him. Not close — a meter.
"Toshi."
"Yes."
"You've been down this road."
"Once."
"When."
"Twenty twenty-three. Summer."
"With whom."
Toshi turned his head. Looked at Kurosawa. Did not answer at once.
"Not with whom. Where."
"Where."
"To the village of Kotan. To Nabesawa Sae. I was sent with the photograph of a haiku. She received me. I stayed the night, left in the morning."
"Who sent you."
"You know who."
Kurosawa nodded. Looked again at the mist behind the trees.
"Does she remember you."
"I think so."
"That complicates it."
"I don't think so."
"Why."
"Because your visit and my visit will become to her two different visits. She's older. She knows how."

Kurosawa looked at him from the side. Toshi stood straight, thin, in the gray sweatsuit, with the shaved head, in the winter morning light that made his face ten years older. He did not take his eyes off the mist.
"Toshi."
"Yes."
"You understand that someone is waiting behind that lake in case you get further than you should."
"I understand."
"You won't get through."
"I won't."
"That isn't a question."
"Not a question."
Kurosawa turned back to the bus.

Sasaki took the wheel for the second shift. Kurosawa glanced once more in the rearview mirror when the bus pulled off — and saw Toshi already inside, again in the same pose: back not leaning, gaze on a point on the driver's headrest. Sasaki did not see this. Kurosawa did not say.
They drove another hour.
Then Sasaki, not looking at him, said:
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."
"Endo."
"I know."
"You haven't spoken to the team yet."
"No."
"You will."
"I will."
"When."
"Not today."
She nodded. He looked in the mirror. Kenji was tapping the keys again. Toshi was looking at the same point.
"Kurosawa-san," said Sasaki, quieter still.
"Yes."
"If the body in the grave — is not him — then he is either alive or killed later. Yes?"
"Yes."
"Both options mean that between us and the one we're chasing — there is not only Toshi and not only Ayano. There is also your brother. Or the memory of him."
"I know."
"I won't tell you 'hold on.'"
"Don't."
"I don't."

She shifted the gear. The engine whined briefly on the climb, then evened out. The mists in the valley below lay in layers — the lower one white, the upper one dun — and in the breaks between them was visible the black water of one of the Tokachi tributaries.
"Sasaki."
"Yes."
"Thank you."
"For what."
"For not saying it."
She squeezed the wheel a little tighter. One second.
"You're welcome."

They ate at a roadside kaiten-soba before the village of Shikaoi. Three bowls of hot soba with daikon, one portion without buckwheat — Toshi said his stomach after the detention center wouldn't take cold buckwheat, asked only for broth with thin slivers of yellow radish. The proprietress — a woman past sixty, in a blue kitchen apron — brought a bowl without comment. Toshi bowed to her a little deeper than needed. She noticed. Did not show that she noticed.

Kenji ate his portion quickly. Kurosawa watched him — and saw that a little color came back into Kenji's cheeks — and thought that it mattered to him, that they were eating together at one table; that this was, perhaps, the first joint meal in the team in eight months, since he had joined — and it would need to be repeated in Sapporo when they got back.
If four of them got back.
He pushed the thought aside. Did not hold it.

Sasaki paid with the department card. The proprietress printed the receipt, folded it carefully, put it into a paper envelope with an advertisement for her own place — and, handing it to Kurosawa, said quietly:
"Careful past Shikaoi. The road to Shiribetsu after the fifth turn — black ice under fresh snow. That's how it was yesterday for my son-in-law."
"Thank you."
"You're welcome."

They went out. In the time they'd eaten the snow had fallen thicker again. The minibus was white on the roof; Kurosawa passed a palm over the windshield, scraped a curve with his sleeve. Kenji cleaned the sides.
"Who drives on," said Sasaki.
"I do," said Kurosawa. "The last stretch."
"Then I'll listen to the road."
"Listen."
He sat behind the wheel. Belted in. Turned the key. The engine hummed evenly, as it had at four in the morning in the bay.

He looked in the rearview mirror. Kenji and Toshi sat in the same poses. Kenji — by the window, hands over the laptop, gaze on the white road beyond the glass. Toshi — straight, on the point on the back of Kurosawa's headrest.
Kurosawa for a moment met Toshi's gaze in the mirror.
Toshi briefly lowered and raised his eyelids. The same as in the courtroom.
Kurosawa looked away.

They pulled onto the highway. The village of Kotan was still an hour and forty minutes to the northeast, past three passes. Beyond the window, evenly, without wind, the snow fell — the sort of snow that in Hokkaido in winter falls without beginning and without end, and to a person in a vehicle it begins to seem that it is she who is standing still, and the snow is moving toward her in a single white sheet.
Kurosawa held the wheel with both hands. The right brow, with the old scar, stood a little higher than the left. He knew this now.
He thought about Ren, briefly, and pushed the thought aside too, because on this curve one had to watch for the ice.
The chains rumbled evenly on the pack.

p.emphasis: Three behind the doors. One — behind the paper.

section.subtitle: Chapter Twenty-Two
section.p: Lake Shikaribetsu lay under the morning light like something that had learned not to move. The ice on it was not white but of that dark glass through which one sees the next layer of ice and, deeper still, a third — there, where the water had forgotten how to be water. The cedars on the southern bank stood in a row, motionless, with the Hokkaidan attitude in which old things stand together when there is nothing left between them to talk about.

The road from the village of Kotan to the ryokan — four kilometers of gravel. The minibus they left half a kilometer short, among the trunks. Kenji slung the waterproof bag with the laptop over his shoulder. Sasaki checked the magazine once, slid it back, patted the holster with her palm — not to make sure, but because that was what she always did when it was time for the hand to know where things were. Toshi got out last. Stood at the minibus door, glanced toward the lake, then toward the house. Did not walk on.
"From here — it's you, inspector."

Kurosawa nodded. He did not ask again. He already knew the answer: I don't want to forget more than I remember. Toshi had said it back in Kotan, in the light of the elder Nabesawa Sae's lamp, and Kurosawa had set it away in the part of memory from which he did not burn.

He laid on the stump at the gate the ikubasui tag Nabesawa had given. Wooden, darkened on one side — the one that remembers the place. Not for the house. For the one who one day returns to the house and does not find it.

The gate was ajar. The yard — empty. The snow lay in an even layer without tracks, save for a single trail from the back porch — narrow, like a person who knew where to step so his print would not be seen at once.
"Kenji — here, at the genkan. Keep the link. Sasaki — the back slope, then down, into the cellar. Do not come up here without a signal. I take the corridor."
Kenji nodded, pressed the bag with his shoulder.

Sasaki did not nod. She looked at him for half a second — that look of hers that made him hesitate a small hesitation each time he was to go first — and set off to the right, into the snow, around the corner.
Kurosawa slid the ryokan door open with his shoulder by one palm's width.
The house did not answer.

The genkan smelled of old damp cedar and tea. The earthen floor beneath the feet was dry at the steps and damp at the threshold. The shoe shelves — empty. On a wooden peg to the left — one felt jacket, dark, a man's, one size smaller than his own. He did not touch it.
Kenji sank onto his heels at the entrance, opened the laptop, connected the cord to a small battery. The screen lit his face from below.
"Kurosawa-san, link's up. I'm not going farther."
"Don't."
Kurosawa took off his boots, set them against the wall toes to the exit, took two steps onto the tatami.
The zashiki lay before him in the gray pre-dawn light. Seven tatami. A low table — not at the center, shifted to the far wall. The tokonoma alcove — with a scroll bearing one wide inked ideogram:
待
"Wait." He recognized the hand — the same that had hung in Kamishiroi — the same by which the Doll Maker held his objects under control. The vase beneath the scroll — with water, poured today. Empty.
He walked to the kitchen.

The kettle stood on the stove. Metal, plain. He set a palm against its side — hot. Above the spout held a thin stream of steam. Ten minutes. Maybe less. On the thin cherry cutting board — the same batch — a crumb of dry tea at the edge. The magnetic rail empty. The knives had gone somewhere.

In the corner of the kitchen, on a low stand, stood a tray. Black lacquer, corners rubbed. On the tray — a white cup with a thin crack in the base, a clay teapot the color of wet slate. Steam was rising.
He did not touch either.
From the radio in his pocket came a rustle.
"Kurosawa-san," Sasaki, quietly. "Back entrance open. I'm inside, found the cellar. Going down."
"Watch your step."
"Yes."
He slid the partition into the right corridor.
He recognized it not with his eyes — with his body. Thirteen meters of dark cedar. Amber of washi lamps at knee height, set every three steps. Nine shōji doors along the right wall. The left — bare.
He set off.

The tatami muted the step. The rib — that old one, from Noboribetsu — was silent this moment. He did not hurry. He knew what was behind the doors. He knew whom he was looking for. He wanted to find what he found, not what he would force by his haste.
He stopped at the first.

The room was empty. Not the way it is when a person has just gone out. The way it is when a room has not been activated. Fresh tatami. Empty corner. A lacquered tray with a teapot — yes, contrary to logic, stood here too — but the teapot was cold, the cup dry, and no tea was in the teapot. A prop without a show.
He closed the door.
The second door.
He slid it open slowly.

The room was a clinic cubicle. White walls, a fluorescent lamp under the ceiling — flickering once every four seconds with the lazy uneven tremor a lamp has just before it gives up. A gurney with paper covering. A folding screen. A small table with a metal tray.
On the gurney sat a woman.

Thin, in a white hospital gown, feet bare. Chestnut hair to the shoulders, cut evenly, without styling. Glasses in a thin frame — not hers, someone else's, with the look a person has who is used to wearing her own pair for five years. Fingers rested on her knees, backs of hands up.
She raised her eyes to him.
Calm. Not sleepy. The kind with which people look who have long been waiting for someone to come in — and had somewhat stopped counting when.
"Nakamura-san," he said quietly. "Aoi. I'm Kurosawa, from Sapporo."
She tilted her head half a finger to one side.
"Where is Haru?"

He did not answer at once. He knew this name from the file — from a private mixi entry of 2011, from one word in a diary margin. Haru. The name that had not been. The name the Doll Maker had put in her head in place of a child that had not been.
"At home," he said. "Waiting."
He knew he was lying. He knew he would remember this lie all the coming days. He said it evenly, because otherwise he could not have said it.
Aoi closed her eyes for a second. Then opened them.
"Thank you."
He extended a hand — not grasping, only placing a palm alongside. She placed her elbow in his palm. Stood. Came with him into the corridor.
He sat her by the far solid wall, in the corner between the ninth door and the blind wall.
"Stay here. Don't move."
She nodded.
The third door.
He slid it open more slowly than the second.

The room smelled of sea salt and wet wood. Walls dark, without detail. The floor — actual decking of wet boards, slightly tilted. One wall lantern to the right, imitation kerosene. In a corner — a heap of dry kelp. The sound of a wave came from a hidden audio system, quietly, from the direction of the decking.
At the center of the decking stood a rag figure — a mannequin in navy work clothes, hands gripping a metal rod that came up through a slit in the boards.

At the edge of the decking sat an elderly man. Squat, hunched, with a bald crown. A white cook's shirt, buttoned at the throat by two buttons. His right leg tucked under, like a man who is used to carrying his weight on the right. Right cuff — with a thin white scar from an old cut. He was smoking Peace — without a filter. Deep draws. The smoke hung in the room in an even layer.
He did not turn to the doors at once.
He kept looking at the mannequin. At the rod.
"Kenta?" he said.
The voice — low, with that dry aftertone in the exhalation that stays in the chest when a man has worked fifty years by the open fire of a small kitchen.
Kurosawa did not answer at once.
He took a step onto the decking. The boards under his feet gave two degrees — the Doll Maker's cradle. He placed a palm on the decking to hold himself, then took it away.
"Sato-san. It's me."
Sato slowly turned his head.
He recognized him not at once. A second — his face was neutral, then — the empty face with which a man searches memory for the shelf where he once placed this thing. Then — he found it.
"Kurosawa-keibu," said Sato quietly. "You are late."
He did not look at him in reproach. He said it as a regular guest would say: you're late, the counter's been wiped, I'll find you something.

Kurosawa held out his hand. Sato looked at it a long time. Then he laid his callused palm on it — not to grip, but to touch. Then he stood himself, slowly, with the caution people use who rise after a long shift behind a counter.
He did not look at the mannequin when he went out.
Kurosawa seated him beside Aoi — at one meter — so they did not touch.
The fourth door.
He slid it — and inside the room something was humming. An engine. Wipers. Low vibration — of a platform.
An Isuzu truck cab stood on a low platform. The windshield looked into an LED panel with a looped video of a winter pass. The wipers went. The seat vibrated at low frequencies.
In the cab sat a man. Stocky, broad shoulders, short graying hair, in a JR Hokkaido bomber jacket. A thin scar along the right cheekbone. One hand on the wheel. The other on the gear lever.
He did not look at Kurosawa.
Kurosawa came to the open cab door.
"Ito-san."
Ito turned his head — not fast, like a man torn from the road for a second who knows the road will not drive itself until he looks back at it.
"I didn't hit you, inspector."
The voice calm, precise. A plain assertion.
"I know," said Kurosawa. "Come."

Ito looked at the LED panel another long second. Then he reached with his right hand to the dash, took from the magnetic mount a small lacquered miniature tray with the tiny teapot and one cup — and placed it in the breast pocket of his jacket.
"I'll take this. If I may."
"You may."
He climbed down from the cab himself. His feet knew how to descend from height.
Kurosawa led him into the corridor. Sat him beside Sato. Three at the blind wall. No one looked at anyone.

He stopped one step from them. Placed a palm on the shōji board. Three sat behind his back and did not move — Sato in a white cook's shirt, Aoi with her silence, Ito with the trace of the wheel on his palms. Three living people with other days inside them. He did not know where to take them after this.
He took the palm from the board.
From the radio came a rustle.
"Kurosawa-san," Sasaki, quieter still. "I found it."
"What."
"A thin notebook. Leather cover. Dates. Codes. Listen: P-3, C-5, H-1... and W-2."
He froze in the middle of the corridor.
"Repeat it."
"W-2. And a list of ryokans. And notes of resettlements. I'm photographing."
"Keep it on you. Do not let it out of your hands."
Something drummed somewhere in his temples. W. Wood, two. The Doll Maker gives a code by type of room. In the forest, the second. Ayano.
He made his feet go on.
The fifth door — empty. Fresh tatami. Empty corner.
The sixth door — dust in the corners. Months, perhaps a year.
The seventh door.
He slid it — and for a second hesitated.

The room was half assembled. In the corners stood cardboard boxes — three — neatly closed, twine-tied. Against the wall lay a rolled thin mattress. On the low table lay one book with a bookmark at the middle.
In one of the boxes, the nearest to the door — the box unsealed — the sleeve of something small showed. He bent. Dark blue. He opened the lid.

Inside was a folded child's backpack. Small, school-sized, dark blue, with a short orange trim. On the front pocket — a rectangular fabric badge. Through the badge someone had stitched a new patch — white — and on the new patch a new name was to have been embroidered. It was not. Or was, and had been scoured off with some abrasive cloth to the ground where only hints of two or three vertical lines remained.
Nothing was legible.
He stood over the box one second longer than he should have.
He had seen this before.

Kamishiroi. The seventh door. The same backpack — not the same, but the same — with the same stitched patch, with the same scoured name. The Doll Maker had known Kurosawa would come here. The Doll Maker had known Kurosawa would recognize.
The Doll Maker had signed.
He lowered the lid. Did not touch the book. Went out, closed the door.
The eighth — empty, clean, with the faintly sweet smell of dried grass that new tatami has. Ready to receive.
The ninth.
He slid it slowly.
The room almost empty. Only — on the futon, at the center, neatly folded and laid — one object. A woman's scarf. Silk. Light-gray.
Folded in three.
The same scarf.
He did not enter. He stood on the threshold. Looked at the scarf.
Did not take it. The Doll Maker wanted him to take it. The Doll Maker wanted him to put it once again in the pocket over his heart. The Doll Maker wanted the repetition.
Kurosawa closed the door.
Nine. Three living. Three he had taken. One box with a backpack. One scarf. Three empty. One lamp under the ceiling flickering once every four seconds.
He went back to the far wall.
Aoi sat. Sato sat. Ito sat. No one looked at anyone.
"Kenji," he said into the radio. "Ambulance. Three. Careful with them."
"Three minutes."
He set off back along the corridor — to the zashiki — to the kitchen — to Sasaki — to the cellar — to the way by which the Doll Maker had gone out.
He got halfway.
Behind the fourth door — the one with the Isuzu cab — a board creaked.
Not inside the cab. Behind it. In the narrow gap between the room wall and the back of the cab — there, where in such a room there should have been a solid wall — something had shifted by five grams.
Kurosawa froze.

Then — quietly, of the sort that comes when a person holds his breath — through the shōji paper reached him a man's voice. Not from inside the room. From that side. From behind the back wall. From a passage that should not have been in the ryokan's plan.
"Kurosawa-keibu."
Quietly. Level. Without pressure. The kind of voice with which a man who has been waiting for someone a long time says: you have come — and adds nothing more.
Kurosawa slowly turned his head toward the door.
He did not draw the pistol. Both his hands remained free.
"Yes," he said.
Pause. The voice on the other side was in no hurry.
"You've come closer."

Kurosawa took a step. Another. Stopped at the paper — at a meter — as close as one could stand without touching. On the paper he saw a shadow — not a silhouette, but a hint of something standing on the other side — a shoulder, perhaps — the top of a head — a figure lower than himself and a little broader in the shoulders than he had expected. The shoulders did not move.
"You won't find him today," said the voice.
"I know."
"You won't find him tomorrow."
"I know."
"But you're going the right way."
Toshi had said the same, word for word — in the zashiki of Kamishiroi, three years ago. Kurosawa heard it and did not show that he had heard.
He allowed himself one even breath.
"I know who you were at Reisen-ji."
On the other side — not at once. The silence was not empty; it was the kind of silence with which a person wipes his palms on his trousers and considers whether to smile.
"Ah."
One sound — not a word, but an exhale — from which Kurosawa could pull nothing more. Neither recognition nor denial.
Then, just as evenly, without pressure, in that same voice that held something deeper than voice:
"You know one of me. I have others."
Kurosawa did not move.
He looked at the shadow on the paper. The shadow lingered a second — the shoulders lifted slightly and lowered, the way the shoulders are when a person makes one short bow — and vanished.
A board creaked. Once. Then — nothing.
Kurosawa still stood.
Then he slid the fourth door aside — with the care with which one slides a door behind which there is already no one.
The cab stood. The LED panel looped. The wipers went.

Behind the cab — a narrow passage. In the room's blind wall — where there should have been a blind wall — a plank panel had been slid aside. The passage went into blackness, downward, at an incline. A thin current of cold air came from it. It smelled of damp earth and lake.
From the radio rustled again.
"Kurosawa-san," Sasaki, quieter still. "In the corner of the cellar — a hatch. Metal. Unlocked. Goes down. Smells of the lake."
"Tunnel. He passed there."
"Do you want me to go."
"No. Not alone. I'm coming to you."
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."

"One more. In a niche by the wall — a small cabinet. I opened it. Inside — nine photographs. Nine. Polaroids. Small. Each — with someone's face. Three of them — Sato, Aoi, Ito. One — Hiroshi Maeda. That's Book 1. One — a woman I don't know. One — a man I don't know. And one — Ayano."
Kurosawa closed his eyes. For one second. Then opened them.
"Take them all. Do not describe them on site. We describe in Sapporo."
"Yes."
"Wait for me."
He set off farther down the corridor — to the zashiki — to the partition — to the kitchen — to the cellar doors. He did not look back at the fourth door.
Kurosawa descended.
The tunnel was low — he walked with head bent. Walls — clay, reinforced with old wooden beams. He counted fifteen steps. Twenty. Thirty. The earth went down, then — even. Then — up.
He came out through a hatch in an abandoned boathouse on the southern shore of the lake.
The door of the boathouse was ajar. He looked out.
On the ice of the lake — a fresh snowmobile trail. Thin, clear. Led eastward — to the far bank, beyond which rose dark cedars, and beyond the cedars — the Shiretoko forest.

Kurosawa stood by the door. He did not run. He knew he would not catch up. He knew the Doll Maker had appeared and gone not so he could be caught — but so that Kurosawa would know he had been spoken to.
He took out the radio.
"Kenji. Trail. Southern shore. Log the track on the lake while it's visible. Sasaki — into the cellar. Take the notebook."
"Yes."
He stood another second, looking at the trail. Then turned and went back through the tunnel.

In the ryokan's corridor Aoi, Sato, and Ito were being lifted by paramedics. Kenji stood at the genkan, held a tablet, showed the officer the map with the snowmobile track. Sasaki was coming out of the cellar — with the thin notebook in her hand — and in her eyes was what she now knew and had not yet told him.
Toshi stood beyond the gate, past the line. Did not come in. Did not ask. Only when Kurosawa passed him toward the minibus — Toshi said quietly:
"He spoke with you."
"Yes."
"He has never spoken with you before."
"Yes."
Toshi nodded once.

Kurosawa got into the minibus. Sasaki — beside him, with the notebook on her lap. Kenji — behind the wheel, with the gray face of a man who has not slept three days and now understands he will not sleep another.
The engine caught quietly.
Behind, at the gate, Toshi still stood. He did not wave.
In Kotan, Nabesawa Sae met them on the threshold of the guest house. She looked into Kurosawa's eyes longer than she had allowed herself at the first meeting the evening before.
"You went," she said.
"I went."
"And left the tag."
"Left it."
"The house heard you out."
Kurosawa did not answer at once. He knew she was not speaking of the ryokan.
"Yes," he said. "Heard me out."

She nodded. Asked no more. One of the village women — younger, in a gray down jacket — led two of the found ones from the sled and led them to a neighboring house; the paramedics from Obihiro already stood by their van and waited.
Kurosawa went into the guest house, into the same room with the irori. Sasaki laid the notebook on the low table. Kenji set the laptop beside it. He sat between them, not taking off his coat.

Aoi sat in another room of the guest house, in the elder Nabesawa's blanket, drinking tea in small sips. Sato lay on a futon, eyes on the ceiling. Ito sat straight, in his JR jacket, holding in the breast pocket the small lacquered miniature tray. Three paramedics from Obihiro worked with them by turns. None of the three asked anything. None of the three remembered how he'd come to be here.
Kurosawa let himself look at each of them for one minute. No more. He knew that more would already be transferring theirs onto himself, and he had no right to transfer now.
Then he came back to the room where the notebook lay on the low table.

He opened the notebook to the first page. The Doll Maker's calligraphy — the same — even, thin, with the barely perceptible slant downward to the right that the hand has when it writes quickly and yet cautiously.
Dates. Codes. Notes of resettlements. He ran his eyes to the end — the last five pages were already empty — the notebook was half full, half open.
The last entry — three days ago. The code W-2. One number. One arrow. The mark of place — only the first letter. Sh.
He closed the notebook.
Sasaki said nothing. Kenji did not either.
Kurosawa laid his palms on the cover. Did not move them.
The house at his back held the shape of a house without them.

section.subtitle: Chapter Twenty-Three
section.p: The village of Kotan lay in the blue pre-dawn light. The lamp in the window of the elder Nabesawa Sae — the one about which she had said "twelve years" — burned quietly, as it should.
They had rented her far room in the guest house. Six tatami. A low table by the window. In the corner — an irori with residual coals.

Kenji had been sitting at the table for the third hour now. The laptop in front of him was open. A second machine — a small gray box with a connected disk — stood beside it, with cables running to three USB hubs. His face was lit from below in cold blue. His hair had come loose from the ponytail. The IQOS lay beside him, forgotten, with a thin red heating indicator. He had not smoked in two hours.
Sasaki slept at the wall, under a blanket, palm to cheek. Breathing evenly.

Toshi, who had reached them on a snowmobile from the direction of the old gravel track an hour after the ryokan, was sitting by the shōji in the next room — they could hear him shift a cup — and did not come in without invitation.
Kurosawa sat opposite Kenji. Did not drink. Did not smoke. He looked at the screen, not to read anything from it, but because he could not now look at anything else.
On the screen was one work from pixiv. Profile @ayano.k.16. Tag — "snow room". Date of publication — six weeks before the raid.

The interior of a small room. Tatami. A futon. A low table. A small window with ribbed glass. In the corner — a lacquered tray with a teapot. The stroke of a thin line — the same one — with that barely perceptible microtouch with which she had drawn deer in January of 2024 and sent him a phone photo from the station at Utoro.
In the foreground — a woman's hand. Long fingers. Hair drawn into a knot.
There was no face.

Kurosawa had been looking at the work since the third hour of the night. He had studied it by heart to the level where you stop seeing the whole — only the enumeration of details is left: the window with ribbed glass, the wooden beam with a scratch, the shadow on the futon, the lacquered tray.
He waited.
Kenji swallowed from a can of Boss Coffee, empty — with the care with which one swallows from a can in which nothing is left. Set the can into the heap of the others. Wiped his palms on his trousers.
"Kurosawa-san."
Quietly.
"Yes."
Kenji did not go on at once. He clicked twice with the mouse. Three times. On the screen a window opened with a line of code — long, of the sort that only programmers manage to befriend.
"There's an EXIF comment here. Three characters. Hidden."
Kurosawa did not answer at once. He felt his breath go deeper — not by will, but by the way the body itself takes in air when it understands it will need a lot.
"Which."
Kenji with one motion selected three characters in the line — they lit yellow — and turned the screen toward him.
「まだ待つ」
Kurosawa looked. He knew these ideograms. Each of them. Mada matsu.

He did not at once see below, in small Latin letters, in brackets, Kenji's own comment. A technical note: "encoded in the EXIF field UserComment, UTF-8 BOM, length 12 bytes, preserved on file regeneration from Clip Studio 2.0."
Kurosawa read the Japanese aloud.
"Mada matsu."
Kenji nodded.
"Still waiting," said Kurosawa.

He said it as one might to a person who does not know Japanese — evenly, with the care with which one translates something important. Only in this moment there was no such person in the room. He translated it to himself.

From childhood Ayano used to write him small notes and slip them under the door of his apartment in Maruyama. She did it every time he was angry with her for something — a truancy, a missed dinner, going to Otaru for the day without her phone. The notes were short. Three characters. Mada matsu. Or four. Sono mama. Or five. Daijōbu da yo. He would find them when he came back late from work. He would read. He would answer with his own — also short, also under her door — and go to sleep.

He did not remember when they stopped doing this. Probably when she turned fourteen. Probably not. Probably one such note was still lying in his kitchen drawer — under the upper tray — dated the twenty-third of November, two thousand and twenty. He had not been into that drawer for years.
Three characters. Mada matsu. Her code.
No one in the world knew it. No one but him and Ren. Ren died on the seventieth kilometer from Tokachi in February of two thousand twenty-two. Now — after Endo — even this was no longer true.
But the code was known only to him and Ren. And, now, to whoever had made Ayano write this code into the EXIF.
Or Ayano herself.
Or Ayano herself.
He pressed a palm to his mouth. Held it there three seconds. Removed it.
"Kurosawa-san," Kenji, quieter.
Kurosawa did not answer at once.
Sasaki at the wall turned quietly in her sleep. Did not wake. Only her palm slid from beneath the blanket and lay on the tatami, back of hand up.
"Three years," said Kurosawa.
He said it evenly, as a number.
Pause.
He stood up. His legs did not move at once — for a second they did not know whether to stand. Then they stood. He stepped over the tatami and went to the window.
The window gave onto the lake. The sky was lightening by two tones. The ice glinted.
He placed a palm on the paper edge of the window. He looked at nothing. He held his palm there because his body needed something under his palm.
"I'm going," he said.
Softly at first, to himself.
Then, turning — to Kenji:
"I'm going."
Kenji did not understand at once.
"Where."
"After her."
"We don't know where."
"I know she's alive," said Kurosawa. "The rest — is a question of maps."
Kenji closed his mouth. Nodded once.

From the next room, through the thin paper partition, came a quiet, short exhalation from Toshi — the way one breathes on recognizing something one had predicted but hoped would not come to pass. He said nothing.
Kurosawa sat back at the table.
"Kenji," he said. "I need to know everything. IP of the publication. Device. Time. The stroke. Comparison with the archive. Not today. But begin today."
"Already begun."
"Give me forty minutes."
Kenji nodded.

Kurosawa stood. Walked to the kettle over the irori, with its dead coal. Did not pour. He understood now that for three years he had held two versions of one thing separately. One: Ayano is alive, and must be found. Two: Ayano is dead, and must be lived with. He had held both versions at once because neither could be chosen without more information than he had. Now the greater information was three characters in an EXIF field. It did not make the first true entirely. It only ruled out the second.
He took a step back to the table.

Kurosawa closed the laptop gently — the way one closes a child's notebook — and laid his palms on top of it. He sat like that a long time. Kenji beside him did not move. He knew now was not the time to move.

Kenji started to speak on — quietly, in the rhythm a person uses when he knows the listener does not need to listen right now, but continues anyway, because a human voice in the room is sometimes more useful than silence.
"File generated in Clip Studio Paint 2.0. That version came out in March 2026. Ayano didn't use one like that before she disappeared. That means the work was made after the disappearance."
"Yes."

"IP of the publication — Tor node. Amsterdam-exit. Device — MacBook Air, M3 chip. That's a heap of info that won't get us a provider. But in Clip Studio's metadata a unique license ID remains. I'm pulling it. It's not a name. It's a number. But the number's tied to the date of activation. If it was activated by purchase — there's a card with it. If a card — a city with it. If a city — that's a circle in which the device lies. A month or two."
"A month or two."
"I've started."
Kurosawa did not immediately understand. Then:
"Kenji."
"Yes."
"Thank you."
Kenji did not answer at once. He reached for the IQOS, saw the indicator had gone out, put it back.
"You don't have to, Kurosawa-san."
"I have to."
Pause.
Kenji lowered his eyes. He did not know how to receive such things and so he did not try.
Then Kurosawa opened the inner pocket of his coat and drew from it a photograph.

Old. Corners bent. Ayano at sixteen, the platform of Shiretoko station, a winter morning. Dark jacket. A backpack with a scratched festival pin. Hair fallen across one eye. A scarf — not hers, light-gray, silk, wrapped twice.

He held the photograph three centimeters from his eyes. He looked at her face. He let his memory set beside it the face of the one who was now on the pixiv work without a face. He looked for what remained the same in them. The hair — yes. The thin turn of the wrist on the pencil — perhaps. The stroke style — yes.
He knew.
He had long known.
He had not let himself believe for three years.
He exhaled one long, even breath — the one on six counts — and set the photograph face-up beside the laptop. Did not put it away.
"Mada," he said, "matsu."
Pause.
"Mada," quietly, "matsu. Aya-chan."
He held his palm alongside the photograph. Did not touch.
Kenji did not look at him.

Beyond the window the ice of the lake had taken on two more tones of blue. Somewhere toward the far shore, very far — so far that this was more a supposition of hearing than the sound itself — a cedar branch creaked under snow and shed a light white avalanche from itself, which broke apart in air before reaching the ground.
He stood again. Went to the sliding partition and pushed it aside by one shoulder's width.
Toshi sat in the neighboring room exactly at the center of the tatami, in seiza. Before him — a cup with cold tea. He was not drinking. He was looking at the partition. He was waiting.
Kurosawa stepped across the threshold and stopped. He did not sit.
"You knew," he said.
Toshi slowly raised his eyes to him.
"I told you, inspector," he said quietly. "In the zashiki of Kamishiroi."
"You said she was alive. You didn't say she was alive in a net, with a code W-2, in a room he had built for her before she disappeared."
Toshi did not answer.
Kurosawa allowed himself one long pause.
"You knew," he repeated. "How long."
"Not as long as you think," said Toshi. "And longer than I let myself. That's not the same answer. Kurosawa-keibu."
"I'm listening."
"I will not lead you to her. Not because I don't want to. I do not know for certain."
"I know."
"But I know where he will not take her. And that — is a small map. A small exception from a large one."
"Give it to me."
Toshi nodded.
"I will. Not today. Today you don't need me. Today I will only get in the way of your head putting in place what I just clarified for you."
Kurosawa did not move.
"Toshi-san."
"Yes."
"Why did you not say three years ago."
Toshi was long in answering.
"Because three years ago," he said quietly, "I was not the one who says this. And because I would have lied to you if I had said it then. And because I am still not sure I am not lying now."
Kurosawa looked at him. Long.
Kurosawa slid the partition back and returned to Kenji.
Sasaki turned in her sleep and woke.
She saw the photograph on the table. She saw Kurosawa's face. She did not rise. She only turned her head on the pillow and looked at him. Long.
Kurosawa did not look at her.

He kept his palm alongside the photograph. He knew that this was already a different photograph — the same piece of cardboard, the same grainy shot — but now it weighed differently, because from it a room had opened in which someone was still drawing.

For three years he had never allowed himself to remember Ayano's face whole. He held it in parts — the left eye in the moment she raised her head from a notebook in eighth grade; the right turn of the wrist when she held a pencil; the thin shadow of a strand on the temple in the carriage. He did not let the parts converge. He knew — as those who work with missing persons for twenty years know — that if you let the parts converge and they do not converge, then memory begins to fill in, and from the face you remembered something else remains, which never was. He preferred to leave the parts as parts.
Now — on the pixiv work, with the face that was not drawn — all the parts were opened to him at once. And he could stop keeping them separate.
He allowed it.

He allowed the left eye to converge with the right turn of the wrist. He allowed the shadow of the strand to converge with that left eye. He allowed everything. In the room it became one tone lighter — as it becomes when you draw back a curtain on a winter noon.
He smiled.

Once. Briefly. The way people smile who suddenly see a person they had considered lost at the table across from them, and in the first half-second do not know how to react; and therefore they smile, because for "for now" there is no other gesture.
"Still waiting," he said.
Pause.
He put his palm on Kenji's shoulder. Held it there two seconds.
Kenji — with the look of a boy on whose shoulder an older man is placing a hand for the first time in his life — froze for a second. Then he patted Kurosawa on the back twice. Briefly, awkwardly.
Kurosawa nodded.
Then — to Sasaki:
"We go."
Pause.
「まだ待つ」
Pause.

section.subtitle: Chapter Twenty-Four
section.p: Ashibetsu-yama received them on the second day after Shiretoko-ko with the same face it had shown the first time: gravel road, partly cleared, empty yard, kitchen with a kettle — this time cold — and a corridor with nine doors, behind not one of which was anything now.

Kurosawa walked the whole of it. He had not expected to find. He did not find. In the seventh room stood a box — sealed this time — and inside it was not a backpack. Inside were bags of grass for tatami. In the alcove of the tokonoma hung a scroll with the ideogram 静, quietly — and for that reason Kurosawa stood before it longer than he needed to.
The Doll Maker had taken from here everything that could speak. He left what speaks by its very absence.
In the kitchen — under the thin cherry board — Sasaki found a single scrap of paper. Palm-sized. A thin calligraphic hand. Three lines of haiku. Unsigned.

p.emphasis: Yuki no ma ni / koe no nai koe o / dareka kiku.

section.p: Toshi, when they showed it to him, nodded once and said:
"It's his."
"He was here."
"He was always here."
He handed the paper back to Sasaki — between two fingers — and did not look at it again.
The Shiretoko forest that following week gave them a thin trail.

Kenji, who on the first night after the ryokan had pulled the data from the tunnel and the snowmobile trail, drew out of Hokkaiden-billing across eastern Hokkaido six anomalies over three days. Three of them lay within a day's walk from Shiretoko-ko. He filtered out two (a ski base, an emergency station). One remained — an abandoned watch hut on the slope of Mount Rausudake, where the last payment for electricity was in 2015. Over the past six days there had been nine hundred and forty watt-hours consumed.
It was not a ryokan. It was a portable node — the place where the Doll Maker could come to sleep two or three days while preparing the next move.
Kurosawa looked at the map. Then he said:
"Kenji, I want you working with me and Sasaki from home now. No office. Don't leave Miso alone."
Kenji nodded. Did not argue.
"Toshi."
Toshi, from the other end of the room, raised his eyes.
"I will not go with you further, inspector," he said.
Kurosawa nodded. He knew.
Toshi looked at him a long time.
"I will not be useful in the forest," he said. "I will be useful here. I will stay in Sapporo. I will read what you bring. I will not run. I have nowhere."
"You're a consultant."
"I'm a consultant."
Pause.
"I will not see him," Toshi said quietly. "Ever. That — is your part."
Kurosawa did not answer.
"Kurosawa-keibu."
"Yes."
"Go without me. I am not holding you."
Kurosawa looked at him. He wanted to say something — not a thanks and not a reproach — but that short I know he usually kept in himself. He did not say it.
Toshi nodded once — for him — and lowered his eyes.
Ogawa's funeral had passed a month and a half before this. But now — after Shiretoko-ko — on the forty-ninth day — Kurosawa went to the cemetery alone.

He did not love the ritual. He knew he was coming not for Ogawa — Ogawa did not need him — but for himself, because otherwise this whole story would begin to stand in the corner of his apartment and wait until he spoke with it.
He walked in through the gates of Hiraoka cemetery at ten in the morning. The sky was low, snow grains fell finely, with that dry insistence with which it falls when the winter is testing itself.
Ogawa's grave lay in the third row, on the right side. The stone slab new. The name cut cleanly, without excess. Family marks — Ogawa. Dates. Two. Very close together.
He set down flowers — one white chrysanthemum — and folded his palms on his chest.

He did not pray. He stood. He let the wind set before him all the scenes in which Ogawa still was: the office balcony with that single cigarette per shift — a hand on the shoulder at the first walk out of the hospital after Noboribetsu — the soundless "Kurosawa is leading this series" at the meeting in January — and, last, that slip of paper with a four-digit number that Ogawa had wordlessly slid across the table. Just in case.
Kurosawa looked at the slab a long time.
Then, quietly:
"Sir."
Pause.
"He appeared."
Pause.
"I will catch him. Not today. But I will catch him."
He turned and walked. He did not look back. He did not need to look back.
That evening Sasaki brought bento.

She came in without knocking — she'd had the key since January — and set the bag on the kitchen table. The kitchen smelled of coffee, once-smoked, and cold rice from yesterday. Kurosawa was washing the pot in the sink.
"You haven't eaten," she said.
"Not hungry."
"Eat anyway."
He wiped his hands on the towel and sat. She laid out the bento — two. Both alike. Vegetables, steamed salmon, rice with black sesame. She began to eat first, in silence.
He ate three spoons. Then set the chopsticks aside.
"Sasaki."
"Yes."
"The notebook."
"I'm reading. Every evening."
"What's there."
She did not answer a long time. Then:

"Twenty-eight ryokans. Of them nine — with names. Nine — with dates of entry into service, some before 2010. Nine codes of victims — active. Of these we know four. Three are now home. One — with the code W-2."
"Yes."
Pause.
"And one more thing, Kurosawa-san. The one who held the key to Ogawa's schedule — he is on our floor. We are still looking. That is a separate line."
"I know. That's not for now."
"Not for now."
Pause.
"Kurosawa-san."
He raised his eyes to her.
She sat straight. Palms on knees. Gaze lowered to the bento — on the boundary between the salad and the rice — not on him.
"I did not tell you everything about Nao," she said.
He did not answer at once. He knew. He had known since March — and in March had decided not to ask. He was not sure now he wanted to.
"I'm listening."
She took one even breath.
"Her LiveJournal entry — the one I told you about, with the gap — I told you it was one entry."
"Yes."

"It isn't one. It's three. One — for the third of January 2019, mother's memorial. The second — for November 2023. The third — for April of this year. In all of them — one edit. One gap. Timestamp of edit — the fifteenth of October. The same day as Sato, Aoi, Ito. The very same day."
Pause.
"He was filtering her for three years."
Kurosawa closed his eyes. Only for one second.
"You took her out of the system."

"I did. My parents and I. She's not in any service now. She doesn't have a phone. She has a new address, I don't even have her in my contacts. Father takes her out on walks by a single route. That's for now, not forever. That's until he finds another way."
"And you didn't tell me."
"I didn't tell you."
Pause.

"I thought that if I told you — you would take me off. I thought you would say: 'Sasaki, you cannot lead a case in which your kin is a potential victim.' And you would be right. But then we don't find him. You alone. Kenji alone. We are not enough for each other, Kurosawa-san."
He did not answer at once.
He looked at her — not in reproach. In the way one person looks at another who has just laid on the table between them a thing she has carried with her for a year.
"Sasaki."
"Yes."
"You are right."
She closed her eyes for a second.
"I would have taken you off," he said. "And we would not have found him."
Pause.
"But I have to know. Not because I will order you. Because I have to know why, when you lift your cup earlier than I do, I know why."
"I know."
"That's once."
"Yes."
"Twice is not the way it goes."
She nodded — a small nod, without posture.
He took the chopsticks. He put one piece of salmon in his mouth. He chewed a long time. She finished her bento. He finished half of his. He set the bento aside. She gathered the dishes.
She stood.
By the door, tying her scarf — the gray one from which she had not removed the tag — she turned back.
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."
"Ayano is alive."
He looked at her.
"Yes."
"We will find her."
He did not answer at once.
"Yes."
She went out. The door shut quietly. He heard her go down the stairs and her steps fall silent on the first floor. He sat at the table a minute. Then he stood and put the pot on the burner.
Kenji that week made a preliminary map.

Twenty-eight ryokans. Nine active — all known. Three freed. One lives in Shiretoko-ko (now empty). One — Ashibetsu-yama (empty before this). One — Rebun-jima (not reached). One — Zao-minami (Yamagata, no). One — code W-2. Location — within the old Shiretoko forest, where the border with the national park holds a line between two old Ainu settlements. Exact coordinates — Kenji did not have. But the circle was twenty kilometers in diameter.
He printed the map. Stitched it in a folder. Brought it to Kurosawa.
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."
"It's not an address. It's a district."
"I know."
"Twenty kilometers — a lot."
"Yes."

"But here," Kenji opened the laptop, showed the power-consumption anomaly, "from 2024 to this year the same transformer has been giving out steadily nine percent more than it should by spec. It's a small anomaly. You won't see it unless you're looking. I was looking."
Kurosawa looked at the map a long time.
"When we go," said Kenji, "I'm with you."
Kurosawa looked at him.
"You haven't been in the forest."
"I haven't."
"Then you're home."
"I'm with you."
Pause.
Kurosawa nodded.
"You're in the minibus. You don't come out until signal. Your link with us — is you."
"Yes."
"Not the hero."
"Not the hero."
He put the map into the inner pocket of his coat, over his heart, beside the photograph.

He switched off the lamp in the room. Went to the kitchen. Sat there a long time with the cold pot from which he had not poured coffee. He listened as somewhere in the neighboring apartment Ryoko quietly moved the dishes on the shelf. He listened as beyond the window on Maruyama someone's car went past. Not in a hurry.
He knew he would not sleep this night.
He opened the kitchen drawer — the one under the upper tray — and lowered a hand into it. His fingers felt a folded twice slip of thin paper. He drew it out.
Three characters. Her handwriting. Childish, with a slight lean to the left.
まだ待つ

He had read this on the twenty-third of November two thousand twenty. He had been angry with her at the time for something he no longer remembered. She had slipped the note under the door of his apartment while he slept. He had found it in the morning. He had not answered then with his own note. He had forgotten.
He now put the paper back into the drawer. Carefully. Into the same position. He slid the drawer to the end.
The next day other news came.

Aoi Nakamura had begun to talk with her mother by phone. Not about Haru. About work. About the fact that she did not remember when she had last been at Ezo Systems. About the fact that when she closed her eyes her right shoulder ached, and she did not know why.

Ito Kazuo had asked Miho to move the JR Hokkaido badge into the pocket of his old jacket. He said he wanted to go to the Kamikazu hydroelectric station — just for one day — to apologize to Watanabe-san.
Miho nodded. Did not correct.

Sato was silent. He sat in the rehabilitation ward of Sapporo Kōsei-ren, straight on his bed, in the white cook's shirt — the same one — and looked out of the window at the grain of snow. Kurosawa visited him on Thursday. Brought him one pack of "Peace."
"Sato-san."
Sato did not answer at once. He looked at the pack. His thin fingers — the same scar on the left cuff — took it carefully, the way one takes something one recognizes but does not remember from where.
"Kurosawa-keibu."
"Yes."
"You are late."
Kurosawa did not answer at once.
"I know."
Sato opened the pack. Did not light one. Only smelled it. Then closed it and put it on the nightstand.
"Kenta," Sato said quietly.
"Yes."
"He is alive."
Kurosawa did not answer at once.

He knew that Kenta the nephew of Sato-san had died underwater on the twenty-seventh of September, nineteen ninety-eight, and that Kenta the elder brother of Sato had died of pneumonia in nineteen sixty-nine, and that both Kentas now lived in Sato-san's head as some one, other, that was Kenta neither the one nor the other. He knew Endo on the balcony of the morgue had promised him not to ask him the name in the first hour. He knew this concerned Ayano, not Sato.
He did not correct.
"Yes," he said quietly. "Alive."
Sato nodded. Once. Did not look at him again. Looked out the window.
Kurosawa sat another five minutes. Then he stood, laid a palm on Sato's shoulder — carefully, as one lays it on glass. Said nothing. Went.

In the corridor of the rehabilitation ward he stood by the window. Beyond the window was the parking lot. It smelled of disinfectant and the faint smell of morning soup from the canteen. He allowed himself one cigarette — there, on the balcony for visitors — the second by the book.
He finished it. Drew once deeply. Extinguished it.
He knew that the Doll Maker now held Sato in his head. He knew that he would not pull him out of there entirely. He knew that this was not a victory — this was only a transport.
He drove to the office.

On Monday evening he went to Endo at the morgue. Not on the protocol; for the conversation. She met him on the balcony, with a cigarette, in a white coat over a gray pullover. The sky over Sapporo was black with a pink orange at the lower edge.
"Kurosawa."
"Machiko-san."
"You look bad."
"I know."
She exhaled the smoke away from him.
"The body in Ren's grave — is not Ren. I already told you that. I cannot now tell you whose. That may take a year. Or — never."
"I know."
"Ayano is alive."
"I know."
She looked at him longer than she usually allowed herself.
"Kurosawa," she said. "If you find her, do not ask her her name in the first hour. Let her recognize you without the question."
He did not answer at once. He knew she was saying this not as an expert but as a person who had held her sister's file in the morgue already twenty-four years.
"Yes," he said.
She finished the cigarette. Extinguished it on the metal rim of the rail. Dropped it into the coat pocket.
"Go, Kurosawa. Don't sit. Don't think too much. He does this so that you sit and think."
"I know."
He went.
Toshi came to the office on Friday. Kenji that day was again working from home. Sasaki was not there — she had gone to her parents in Sapporo-Higashi.

Toshi arrived exactly at ten. He brought with him a small plastic folder with printed pages. Haiku. Thirty-one of them. All found over ten months on 5channel, under different aliases. He laid them on Kurosawa's desk.
"They are his," said Toshi. "All."
Kurosawa looked at the sheets a long time.
"You're sure."
"Yes."
"What is to be done with them."
"I don't know. I only identified them."
Pause.
Toshi sat across from him. The electronic bracelet on his ankle was visible from beneath the trouser leg. He was not hiding it.
"Toshi-san," said Kurosawa.
"Yes."
"You are staying in Sapporo."
"Yes."
"I want you to confirm it once more. Before witnesses. To Prosecutor Fujiwara."
Toshi nodded.
"I'll confirm."
Pause.
"And one more thing."
"Yes."
Kurosawa looked at him a long time.
"If you ever," he said quietly, "decide to go from us to him — I want to know first."
Toshi did not answer at once.
Then:
"Yes."
Pause.
"Kurosawa-keibu."
"Yes."
"I will not go."
"I know."
"I will not go not because I do not want to."
"I know."
Kurosawa nodded once and lowered his eyes to the sheets of haiku.
Toshi stood. Went to the door. At the door he stopped.
"Kurosawa-keibu."
"Yes."
"You will catch him."
"I know."
"Not because you are better."
"I know."
"But because you are not tired."
Kurosawa raised his eyes to him.
Toshi looked back.
"And he is tired, inspector."
He opened the door and went out.
Kurosawa sat. Long. Then he laid a palm on the sheets of haiku and did not move it.
In the corridor behind the glass partition stood Tanaka. In a coat, briefcase by his leg. Did not come in — waiting until Kurosawa lifted his eyes to him.
Kurosawa lifted.
Tanaka came in two steps. Did not sit. Did not take off his coat.
"Ashibetsu empty?"
"Empty."
"I knew."
He said nothing more. Nodded once, turned, went out. In the corridor a second later the elevator doors clicked.
Kurosawa remained sitting. Looked at the closed office door. Tanaka had not asked from curiosity; Tanaka had asked to confirm what he already had within himself. That was new — and that was bad news.
He knows more than we do, thought Kurosawa. He has known this for a long time. And he is not with us.

He stood from the desk, went to the window. Beyond the window on Maruyama the lamps still burned. One — the one by the turn to the next street — flickered every few seconds. It had always flickered like that. No one changed it.

He stood by the window a long time. Then he placed a palm on the glass. The glass was cold; the warmth of the palm on it left a mark, and the mark became clearer, until he took his hand away. The mark held another second and then vanished.

He knew that tomorrow he would put a red pin on the map in the center of that twenty-kilometer circle. He knew that it would not be an address — it would be only the center of the circle. He knew that with the same center he could sit here another six months. He knew he would not.
He lifted the pot and began to grind the beans.
He knew he would not sleep. He knew he would be at work in the morning earlier than anyone. He knew that the Shiretoko forest would be waiting.
The night, beyond the window, held the shape of the night.

p.emphasis: I knew you would come closer.

section.subtitle: Epilogue
