section.p: The Shiretoko forest held the winter the way one holds a bowl — with thin edges, not spilling.

The hut stood in a saddle between two hillocks, hidden by old cedar branches. The roof — of cold. The walls — of cold. Inside — the thin, hair-thin warm shaft that lays itself down in an abandoned house where in the corner stands a small kerosene stove.

He set the stove to the lowest flame. Took off his felt jacket. Laid it on the wooden crate beside him. Took from the shelf over the bed the clay teapot the color of wet slate and the white cup with the thin crack in the base. Set them on the board. Poured water from a ceramic jug — not from the tap. There was no tap here.

The radio receiver stood by the window. Old, wooden, with a needle-scale and one regulator knob with a metal notch. Batteries — fresh, inserted today. The antenna — short, pulled out by hand to its end.
He switched it on.

White noise came. Then — the thin whine of the search. Then, on the short wave — even, with those grains of the atmospheric tick-tick that had always been in the Hokkaido police ether — a woman's dispatch voice. He set the search-flame at this frequency.

p.emphasis: "Tokachi-two. Route confirmed. Segment of the three-twenty-second, from Obihiro east. Over."

section.p: Pause. Atmospheric crackle.

p.emphasis: "...all patrols of the eastern district. Priority three. Person search. Description without description. Style-mark: a traveling man, age forty-five to sixty, possibly with a rucksack. Particular attention — the Rausudake district, the border line of Shiretoko National Park. Kurosawa-keibu, operation head. On contact — do not approach. Call for reinforcement. Over."

section.p: He held his hand near the receiver. Did not touch the knob. He let the voice pass through the room evenly, the way one lets a guest through.
Voices came one after another, from nine patrols, from nine points of Hokkaido. He counted them — not to know the number, but because the number kept his hands at work. Nine.
He poured water into the teapot. Set the teapot on the stove. The water took its time to warm.

He sat on the crate. Placed his palms on his knees, backs of hands up. The walls of the hut smelled of long-ago wood and the light smell of old tea that had settled in the corners. In the niche at the far wall — not a tokonoma, but a shelf of two boards — stood one small porcelain figurine without a face. Old. He had brought it here first, before anything else. That was the law.
The radio continued.

p.emphasis: "...report any movement in huts above a thousand meters. Key word — 'find,' not 'detain.' Kurosawa-keibu asks: no single-man actions. Over."

section.p: He for a moment closed his eyes. Not from tiredness. With that brief gesture with which a person who has heard the names of other people for many years in the ether recognizes one name with which he has his own conversation.
He opened his eyes.

The kettle whistled on the stove — with the thin whistle of boiling that always begins a half-second before a person expects it. He took the kettle off. Poured water into the cup through a fine strainer. A thin steam rose in that vertical thread which is easy to break if you place the cup badly.
He set the cup on the board evenly.
The radio did not stop.

p.emphasis: "Abashiri-one. In the points Utoro and Rausu — silence. We are heading toward Shiretoko-yamaguchi. Over."

section.p: He took the cup. Held it in both hands. The warmth came through the porcelain into his palms — the kind that always arrives later than a person expects it — and stayed.
He sipped.
The tea was simple. Hot. As he liked it.

Beyond the window of the hut — a winter forest, gray and even, with those vertical black lines of cedars that always stand where they were placed and never where they were thought to be. Snow fell in a fine grain, without wind. The sky had that August-lead cast with which Hokkaido holds noon in the second week of December.

He knew how long it took a patrol to walk from Utoro to the road on Rausudake — three hours. He knew a patrol would pass the hut at half a kilometer. That they would not climb this slope today. That tomorrow, perhaps, a dog handler would be sent.
He knew this and did not move.

He knew that when they came, he would go on — to the second hut, to the third, to the six points between Memuro and Cape Erimo, in each of which lay a single steering clavicle. He knew that all of this had been prepared twenty years ago.
He also knew that Inspector Kurosawa Yukio now knew his voice.

For twenty years he had held his "I" one paper-shōji further away. For twenty years he had not entered the room Inspector Kurosawa had entered. Now — as quietly as he held himself — he had entered it himself, not by body, but by voice, and now that voice could no longer be taken off the tape.
He did not regret it.

He allowed himself one thin gesture — with the index finger of his right hand he touched the porcelain figurine on the shelf. Very briefly. The way one touches a photograph of a child one hasn't seen in years.

Then, with the same evenness with which one pours water into the teapot, he spoke into the empty room one sentence. Not to the receiver. Not to a sleeping man. Not to himself. Into the air of the hut, which he trusted more than people.
"I knew you would come closer."

section.subtitle: The Doll Maker Files concludes in the next book
section.p: Cape Erimo held the wind like a taut string.

Kurosawa stood beside the eighth of nine pillars of the old fishing pier. It was meant to be empty. He set his palm against the inner face, where the bronze clamp entered the wood, and the clamp gave.
Behind it was a niche.
In the niche — one child's clavicle, with a fine crack down its center. And one sheet of paper, folded in fours, with one word written in black ink.
He put the clavicle back.
He kept the paper.
The road to the last room began here.
Yehor Selin is the author of «The Doll Maker Files».
